    );
  }
  • What does the "scripts" section mean in package.json?
    The "scripts" section in package.json defines custom commands that can be run using npm or yarn. Each command in the script section is a shortcut to run a specific terminal command related to the project. Here's what each script does in the given example:
    • dev: Runs the Vite development server, allowing you to work on the app locally with fast hot-module reloading. Run using "npm run dev".
    • build: Builds the app for production by generating optimized static files using Vite's build command. Run using "npm run build".
    • lint: Runs ESLint on all JavaScript and JSX files to check for code quality issues. It also ensures there are no unused eslint-disable comments and fails the build if any warnings are found. Run using "npm run lint".
    • preview: Starts a local preview server to test the production build output. This simulates how the app will behave in production. Run using "npm run preview".
    These scripts help automate common development tasks and enforce consistency across the team.
  • Explain in detail the "scripts" section with dev, build, lint, and preview
    The "scripts" section in package.json is used to define command-line shortcuts for common tasks during development and deployment. Here's a detailed explanation of each script:
    • dev: "vite"
      This command runs the Vite development server. It starts your project in development mode with features like hot module replacement (HMR), fast file serving, and live reloading. It is typically used during active development. You can run it using "npm run dev".
    • build: "vite build"
      This command creates an optimized, production-ready version of your application. Vite bundles and minifies all JavaScript, CSS, and assets, and outputs them to a "dist" folder. You can deploy the contents of this folder to a web server. It is run using "npm run build".
    • lint: "eslint . --ext js,jsx --report-unused-disable-directives --max-warnings 0"
      This command runs ESLint on all JavaScript and JSX files in the current directory and subdirectories. It checks for code quality, stylistic issues, and potential bugs. The additional options mean:
      • --ext js,jsx: Lint files with .js and .jsx extensions.
      • --report-unused-disable-directives: Report any unused ESLint disable comments in the code.
      • --max-warnings 0: Treat warnings as errors and fail the command if any warnings are found.
      It helps enforce clean and maintainable code.
    • preview: "vite preview"
      This command runs a local server to preview the production build output. It's used to test the app after building but before deploying it. It simulates how the app will behave in a real production environment. You can run it using "npm run preview".
    These scripts simplify workflows for development, testing, and production deployment, and ensure consistency across environments and teams.
  • How does the web work?
    The web operates on a client-server model where the client (browser) sends requests to a server, and the server responds with the required data or HTML. In the context of ReactJS, here's how it works:
    • The user opens a web page in a browser, which sends an HTTP request to the server.
    • The server responds by sending a static HTML file with a small root div and linked JavaScript files containing the React app.
    • The browser downloads and parses the HTML and then fetches and executes the React JavaScript bundle.
    • React takes control of the root div and renders the user interface dynamically using the Virtual DOM.
    • React handles client-side routing using libraries like React Router, so navigating between pages doesn't require full-page reloads.
    • When needed, React fetches data from the server using asynchronous APIs (e.g., fetch or axios) and updates the UI accordingly.
    • The entire app runs in the browser (client-side rendering), although React also supports server-side rendering and static site generation with tools like Next.js.
    This approach allows React to deliver fast, dynamic, and interactive user experiences on the web.
  • ReactJS: Why This useEffect Code Causes an Error 
            useEffect(async () => {
          console.log('hello world');
          return true;
        }, []);

    ❌ Why This is Incorrect

    • React does not allow the function passed to useEffect to be async directly.
    • An async function always returns a Promise.
    • React expects useEffect to return either:
      • Nothing (undefined), or
      • A cleanup function (a regular function, not a Promise)
    • Returning a Promise causes this warning or error:
      "Effect callbacks are synchronous to prevent race conditions. Put the async logic inside."

    ✅ Correct Usage (with inner async function)

            useEffect(() => {
          const fetchData = async () => {
            console.log('hello world');
          };
        
          fetchData();
        }, []);

    ✅ Or Use an Immediately-Invoked Async Function

            useEffect(() => {
          (async () => {
            console.log('hello world');
          })();
        }, []);

    ⚠️ About "return true"

    • Returning true from useEffect is also incorrect.
    • React expects a cleanup function, not a boolean.
    • You may see a warning like:
      "Effect function must not return anything besides a function, which is used for cleanup."

    ✅ Proper Cleanup Example

            useEffect(() => {
          console.log('Component mounted');
        
          return () => {
            console.log('Component unmounted');
          };
        }, []);

    ✅ Final Correct Version of Your Code

            useEffect(() => {
          (async () => {
            console.log('hello world');
          })();
        }, []);
  • ReactJS: Lazy Loading in Detail

    Lazy loading in React refers to the technique of loading components only when they are needed, rather than at the initial page load. This improves performance by reducing the bundle size.

    🔧 How Lazy Loading Works
    React provides a built-in function React.lazy which allows you to dynamically import components.
    When a lazily loaded component is rendered, React will wait for the import to resolve before showing the component.

    📦 Required Features
    1. React.lazy for dynamic imports
    2. Suspense for fallback loading indicators

    Explanation
    1. React.lazy: Used to define the lazy-loaded component.
    2. Suspense: Wraps the lazy-loaded component and shows fallback UI while it's loading.

    🚀 Real-World Use Case
    Suppose you have a dashboard with many widgets. Instead of loading all widgets upfront, you can load them lazily:

    🧩 Chunk Splitting : Each lazy-loaded component is split into a separate JavaScript chunk. These are downloaded only when needed, reducing the initial payload.

    🛑 Limitations :
    1. Only supports default exports.
    2. Needs Suspense as a wrapper.
    3. Not usable in server-side rendering (SSR) without additional setup like React 18 streaming.

    🆚 Lazy vs Dynamic Imports
    1. React.lazy: For components (UI)
    2. Dynamic import: For utility modules, data, or any JS logic

    ✅ Best Practices
    1. Group related components in one chunk if used together
    2. Show meaningful fallback UI (skeletons, spinners)
    3. Use error boundaries to handle lazy load failures

        import React, { Suspense } from 'react';
    
    const LazyComponent = React.lazy(() => import('./MyComponent'));
    
    function App() {
      return (
        <div>
          <h1>Main App
            <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
            <LazyComponent />
            </Suspense>
          </div>
      );
    }
  
    
    const ChartWidget = React.lazy(() => import('./ChartWidget'));
    const TableWidget = React.lazy(() => import('./TableWidget'));
    
    function Dashboard() {
      return (
        <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading widgets...</p>}>
          <ChartWidget />
          <TableWidget />
        </Suspense>
      );
    }
  
    
    🌐 Dynamic Import Example (non-UI)          
    async function loadUtil() {
      const math = await import('./math-utils');
      console.log(math.add(2, 3));
    }
  • ReactJS: Suspense in Detail

    Suspense is a React component used to handle the loading state of components that are being lazily loaded using React.lazy or when using concurrent features like data fetching in React 18.

    🎯 Purpose of Suspense

    • To show fallback UI while a component is loading
    • To manage async behavior in UI (especially with React.lazy or concurrent features)

    🛠 When to Use Suspense

    • With React.lazy for code-splitting
    • With data-fetching libraries like Relay, SWR, or React Query (React 18+)
    • In routing for lazy loading page components

    🧪 Basic Example with React.lazy

            import React, { Suspense } from 'react';
        
        const LazyComponent = React.lazy(() => import('./LazyComponent'));
        
        function App() {
          return (
            <div>
              <h1>Main Page</h1>
              <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
                <LazyComponent />
              </Suspense>
            </div>
          );
        }

    Explanation

    • The component LazyComponent is loaded asynchronously.
    • Until it's fully loaded, the text "Loading..." is shown as a fallback.
    • Once loaded, the actual component is rendered.

    📦 Nested Suspense

    React allows nesting multiple Suspense components for fine-grained control of loading UI.

              <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading outer...</div>}>
            <ComponentA />
            <Loading inner...</div>}>
              <ComponentB />
            </Suspense>
          </Suspense>

    🚀 React 18+ Suspense for Data Fetching (Experimental)

    In React 18, Suspense is extended to support data fetching with frameworks like Relay or loaders in React Router v6.4+

              <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading profile...</p>}>
            <UserProfile />
          </Suspense>

    🧯 Error Boundaries 123

    If lazy loading or data fetching fails, Suspense will not catch the error. Use an Error Boundary to handle errors gracefully.

              <ErrorBoundary fallback={<div>Something went wrong.</div>}>
            <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
              <LazyComponent />
            </Suspense>
          </ErrorBoundary>

    ✅ Best Practices

    • Always provide meaningful fallback content
    • Use nested Suspense to isolate long-loading sections
    • Combine with Error Boundaries for robust async UI

    📌 Summary

    • Suspense helps build better user experience by allowing components to load asynchronously.
    • It is often used with lazy-loaded components and data fetching patterns.
    • It improves performance and responsiveness when used correctly.
  • ReactJS: Custom Error Boundary

    ReactJS: Custom Error Boundary

    An Error Boundary is a special React component that catches JavaScript errors anywhere in its child component tree, logs them, and displays a fallback UI instead of crashing the app.

    📌 Why Use Error Boundaries?

    1. To gracefully handle unexpected runtime errors
    2. To avoid a complete app crash due to an error in a child component
    3. To show a user-friendly error message or recovery UI

    📌 Key Rules

    1. Only class components can be error boundaries (function components cannot use componentDidCatch)
    2. They catch errors during rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors of their children
    3. They do NOT catch errors in:
      1. Event handlers
      2. Asynchronous code (setTimeout, fetch, etc.)
      3. Server-side rendering

      ✅ Custom Error Boundary Example
  import React from 'react';
  
  class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
    constructor(props) {
      super(props);
      this.state = { hasError: false };
    }
  
    static getDerivedStateFromError(error) {
      return { hasError: true };
    }
  
    componentDidCatch(error, errorInfo) {
      console.error("Caught by Error Boundary:", error, errorInfo);
      // You can also log error to a service
    }
  
    render() {
      if (this.state.hasError) {
        return <h2>Something went wrong.</h2>;
      }  
      return this.props.children;
    }
  }

  
    
  🧪 Usage Example

  function BuggyComponent() {
    throw new Error("I crashed!");
  }
  
  function App() {
    return (
      <div>
        <h1>My App</h1>
        <ErrorBoundary>
          <BuggyComponent />
        </ErrorBoundary>
      </div>
    );
  }

  
      
  🔄 Resetting the Error Boundary
  If you want the error boundary to reset when props or state changes, you can add a key to force remount:

  <ErrorBoundary key={someValue}>
    <Component />
  </ErrorBoundary>

    🎯 Best Practices

    1. Wrap only parts of your UI that may fail, not the entire app
    2. Log error details for debugging
    3. Provide useful fallback UI and guidance to the user

    🧩 Combine with Suspense

    Wrap Suspense inside an ErrorBoundary to catch lazy loading or data loading failures:

      <ErrorBoundary>
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading...</p>}>
      <LazyComponent />
    </Suspense>
  </ErrorBoundary>
  • ReactJS: Micro Frontend?

    🔍 What is Micro Frontend?

    Micro Frontend is an architectural style where a frontend application is divided into smaller, independent pieces (micro apps) that are developed, deployed, and maintained by different teams. Each micro app is responsible for a distinct feature or domain, similar to microservices on the backend.

    🎯 Key Features

    • Independent deployment
    • Technology-agnostic (can use different frameworks)
    • Team autonomy
    • Better scalability

    🏗️ Common Micro Frontend Approaches

    • Module Federation (Webpack 5)
    • iframes (legacy, less preferred)
    • Single SPA framework
    • Import maps (with SystemJS)

    📦 Example Architecture

    • Container App (Host) – Loads and manages micro apps
    • Micro App 1 (e.g., Dashboard) – Independent React app
    • Micro App 2 (e.g., Profile) – Another independent React or Vue app

    🛠️ Simple Micro Frontend Example Using Webpack Module Federation

    1. Container App (host)

            // webpack.config.js
        module.exports = {
          name: 'container',
          remotes: {
            dashboard: 'dashboard@http://localhost:3001/remoteEntry.js',
          },
        };
        
        
    
        // App.jsx
        import React from 'react';
        const DashboardApp = React.lazy(() => import('dashboard/DashboardApp'));
        
        function App() {
          return (
            <div>
              <h1>Host Container</h1>
              <React.Suspense fallback="Loading...">
                <DashboardApp />
              </React.Suspense>
            </div>
          );
        }
        
        export default App;
        
        
    
        2. Remote App (dashboard)

        // webpack.config.js
        module.exports = {
          name: 'dashboard',
          filename: 'remoteEntry.js',
          exposes: {
            './DashboardApp': './src/App',
          },
        };
        
        
    
        // App.jsx
        import React from 'react';
        
        const DashboardApp = () => {
          return <h2>Dashboard Micro App</h2>;
        };
        
        export default DashboardApp;
        
        
    
        
        3. Module Federation Setup
        Both apps use Webpack 5's ModuleFederationPlugin. Ensure they share React via singleton configuration.
        
        shared: {
          react: { singleton: true, eager: true, requiredVersion: '^18.0.0' },
          'react-dom': { singleton: true, eager: true },
        }

    🧪 Run the Apps

    1. Container runs on port 3000
    2. Dashboard runs on port 3001
    3. Dashboard is imported and rendered dynamically in Container

    ✅ Benefits

    1. Faster development with smaller teams
    2. Independent deployment pipelines
    3. Isolation of bugs and releases
    4. Technology freedom across teams

    ⚠️ Challenges

    1. Complex build and deployment setup
    2. Shared dependencies must be managed carefully
    3. Inter-app communication (event bus or shared state)

    🔗 Tools & Libraries

    1. Webpack 5 Module Federation
    2. Single-SPA
    3. SystemJS
    4. qiankun (popular in China)
  • What is "differ" in ReactJS?
    In ReactJS, "differ" generally refers to the **difference calculation** process between the current UI and the updated UI. This process is known as **"diffing"** and is a core part of how React updates the DOM efficiently.
    • React uses a virtual DOM, which is a lightweight copy of the actual DOM.
    • When a component's state or props change, React creates a new virtual DOM tree.
    • It then compares (diffs) the new virtual DOM with the previous one to find what has changed.
    • This diffing process helps React to determine the minimal set of changes needed in the real DOM.
    • Only the changed elements are updated in the browser, improving performance.
    So, "differ" in ReactJS refers to the internal process of calculating and applying differences between UI states in an optimized way.
  • What is First Paint in ReactJS?
    First Paint refers to the moment when the browser renders the first pixel of content to the screen after navigating to a ReactJS application.
    • It is a key performance metric that indicates how quickly something is visually displayed.
    • In a ReactJS app, the browser initially loads a static HTML file with a root div and JavaScript bundles.
    • The First Paint typically happens when the browser displays basic HTML or loading indicators before React takes control.
    • Once the JavaScript bundle is loaded and React is initialized, the actual UI is rendered inside the root element.
    • Optimizing First Paint improves perceived performance and user experience.
    • Techniques to improve First Paint include minimizing bundle size, using code splitting, lazy loading, and server-side rendering (SSR).
    First Paint is important because it gives users a visual cue that something is happening, reducing the feeling of slowness.
  • What is the difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 in ReactJS?
    HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 are versions of the HTTP protocol used by browsers to communicate with servers. ReactJS apps benefit from the improvements in HTTP/2. Here’s how they differ:
    • HTTP/1.1:
      • Requests are sent sequentially over a single connection.
      • Only one request can be processed at a time per connection (known as head-of-line blocking).
      • Developers often use bundling (like Webpack) to reduce requests.
    • HTTP/2:
      • Supports multiplexing, allowing multiple requests in parallel over a single connection.
      • Faster page load and improved performance for ReactJS apps.
      • Enables techniques like code splitting and lazy loading without performance penalties.
      • Supports server push, where the server can preemptively send resources the client will need.
    • Impact on ReactJS:
      • React apps served over HTTP/2 load faster due to parallel asset delivery.
      • Better performance for modular JavaScript loading, especially in large applications.
    Overall, HTTP/2 provides a more efficient way to load ReactJS applications, improving speed and scalability.
  • What is ARIA in ReactJS?
    ARIA stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications. It is a set of attributes that improve accessibility for users who rely on assistive technologies, such as screen readers. In ReactJS, ARIA is used to make dynamic content and custom components more accessible.
    • ARIA attributes provide semantic information about UI elements that may not be conveyed through native HTML alone.
    • React allows you to use ARIA attributes directly in JSX by using their standard names, such as aria-label, aria-hidden, or role.
    • ARIA helps screen readers understand the purpose and state of components like modals, tabs, buttons, or custom dropdowns.
    • Common ARIA attributes include aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-hidden, aria-expanded, and role.
    • React does not modify or restrict the use of ARIA, so you can apply them just like regular HTML attributes.
    Using ARIA in ReactJS is important to build inclusive applications that work well for all users, including those with disabilities.
  • What is a Polyfill in ReactJS?
    A polyfill is a piece of JavaScript code that adds support for modern browser features in older browsers that do not natively support them. In ReactJS development, polyfills help ensure that your application works across a wide range of browser versions.
    • Polyfills simulate missing APIs or functionality in older browsers.
    • They are especially useful when using modern JavaScript features like Promises, Fetch API, or ES6 syntax.
    • React apps often use polyfills via tools like Babel or core-js to ensure compatibility.
    • Example: If an older browser doesn’t support the fetch function, a polyfill can provide an alternative implementation using XMLHttpRequest.
    • Polyfills are included during the build process and increase the browser support of your React app.
    In short, a polyfill ensures your ReactJS app can run smoothly even in environments that lack support for modern web standards.
  • What is TDZ in ReactJS?
    TDZ stands for Temporal Dead Zone. It is a behavior in JavaScript that occurs when using let or const. Although this concept is from JavaScript, it directly affects how ReactJS code behaves when using modern ES6 features.
    • TDZ is the time between when a variable is declared with let or const and when it is actually initialized.
    • Accessing the variable before initialization results in a ReferenceError.
    • TDZ prevents the use of variables before they are properly defined, improving code safety and clarity.
    • This is different from var, which gets hoisted and initialized as undefined.
    • React developers often encounter TDZ issues when using let or const inside functions, hooks, or modules and try to access them too early.
    Understanding TDZ helps ReactJS developers avoid unexpected runtime errors and encourages cleaner and more predictable code structure.
  • What is the lifecycle of a functional component in ReactJS?
    Functional components in React use Hooks to manage lifecycle events, replacing the class-based lifecycle methods. The key stages of a functional component’s lifecycle are:
    • Mounting: This happens when the component is first rendered to the DOM.
      • useEffect with an empty dependency array runs once after the initial render (similar to componentDidMount).
    • Updating: This occurs when the component re-renders due to state or prop changes.
      • useEffect with specific dependencies runs after those dependencies change (similar to componentDidUpdate).
    • Unmounting: This happens when the component is removed from the DOM.
      • useEffect can return a cleanup function that runs before unmounting (similar to componentWillUnmount).
    React functional components rely on useEffect and other hooks like useLayoutEffect, useMemo, and useCallback to handle lifecycle-related logic. This approach provides a more modular and declarative way to control side effects and updates.
  • React Functional Component: Unmount Example with Source Code
    Below is an example showing how to handle unmounting in a React functional component using useEffect cleanup:
    • Clock Component: Displays current time and updates every second.
    • Unmount Behavior: When the component is removed from the DOM, the interval is cleared to prevent memory leaks.
        function Clock() {
      const [time, setTime] = React.useState(new Date().toLocaleTimeString());
    
      React.useEffect(() => {
        const timer = setInterval(() => {
          setTime(new Date().toLocaleTimeString());
        }, 1000);
    
        // Cleanup function runs when component unmounts
        return () => {
          clearInterval(timer);
          console.log("Clock component unmounted and interval cleared");
        };
      }, []);
    
      return <h2>Current Time: {time}</h2>;
    }
    
    // Example usage with conditional rendering
    function App() {
      const [showClock, setShowClock] = React.useState(true);
    
      return (
        <div>
          <button onClick={() => setShowClock(!showClock)}>
            Toggle Clock
          </button>
          {showClock && <Clock />}
        </div>
      );
    }
    This example shows how unmounting is handled via the cleanup function inside useEffect in functional components.
  • React Functional Component: Unmount Example with API Call
    This example shows how to cancel an API call when a React functional component unmounts to prevent updating state on an unmounted component:
    • useEffect: Initiates the API call when the component mounts.
    • AbortController: Used to cancel the fetch request if the component unmounts before the response is received.
      
    // Example usage with toggle
    function App() {
      const [show, setShow] = React.useState(true);
      return (
        <div>
          <button onClick={() => setShow(!show)}>Toggle User</button>
          {show && <UserData />}
        </div>
      );
    }
  
  
    function UserData() {
      const [user, setUser] = React.useState(null);
      const [error, setError] = React.useState(null);
    
      React.useEffect(() => {
        const controller = new AbortController();
    
        fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1', {
          signal: controller.signal
        })
          .then(response => response.json())
          .then(data => setUser(data))
          .catch(err => {
            if (err.name === 'AbortError') {
              console.log('Fetch aborted');
            } else {
              setError(err.message);
            }
          });
    
        return () => {
          controller.abort(); // cancels the fetch if component unmounts
          console.log('Component unmounted, API call aborted');
        };
      }, []);
    
      if (error) return <p>Error: {error}</p>;
      if (!user) return <p>Loading...</p>;
    
      return (
        <div>
          <h3>Name: {user.name}</h3>
          <p>Email: {user.email}</p>
        </div>
      );
    }
    This pattern prevents memory leaks and warnings like "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component."
  • What happens if unmount is not handled in a React functional component?
    If you don’t handle unmounting properly in a React functional component, it can lead to performance issues and unexpected behavior. Here’s what can happen:
    • Memory Leaks: Resources like timers, intervals, event listeners, or network requests may continue running even after the component is removed from the UI.
    • Console Warnings: React may warn you with messages like “Can’t perform a React state update on an unmounted component.”
    • Unexpected State Updates: If an asynchronous operation (e.g., API call) finishes after the component is unmounted, it may try to update state that no longer exists, causing errors or ignored updates.
    • Increased CPU Usage: Unnecessary background tasks can continue to consume system resources.
    • Broken UX: Users may see stale or incorrect UI if cleanup is not done properly.
    To prevent these issues, always return a cleanup function from useEffect to stop background tasks and cancel subscriptions or requests when the component unmounts.
  • What is AbortController in ReactJS?
    AbortController is a browser API used to cancel asynchronous tasks such as fetch requests. It is especially useful in React functional components to prevent memory leaks and avoid setting state on unmounted components.
    • AbortController creates a controller object used to signal cancellation.
    • The controller's signal is passed to the fetch request via the signal property.
    • If the component unmounts before the fetch is completed, the controller's abort method can cancel the request.
    • This helps avoid React warnings like "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component."
    • In React, this is typically used inside the useEffect hook with a cleanup function.
    Example behavior:
    • Create an AbortController inside useEffect.
    • Pass controller.signal to the fetch request.
    • On component unmount, return a function that calls controller.abort to cancel the fetch.

    Using AbortController is a best practice when dealing with API calls in React to ensure safe and optimized component behavior. 
        const controller = new AbortController();
  
    fetch('https://api.example.com/data', {
      signal: controller.signal // link the controller to this fetch
    })
      .then(response => response.json())
      .then(data => console.log(data))
      .catch(error => {
        if (error.name === 'AbortError') {
          console.log('Request was aborted');
        } else {
          console.error(error);
        }
      });
  
    // Later in cleanup or unmount
    controller.abort(); // cancels the fetch
  • What is a side effect in ReactJS?
    A side effect in ReactJS refers to any operation that interacts with the outside world or affects something outside the scope of the current function. Functional components should remain pure, meaning they return the same output for the same input. Side effects break this rule and include operations such as:
    • Fetching data from an API
    • Directly manipulating the DOM
    • Setting up subscriptions or timers
    • Logging to the console
    • Changing global state or browser storage
    In React, side effects are handled using the useEffect hook. This allows you to run side-effect code after rendering, and also clean it up when the component unmounts or updates.
    Managing side effects properly helps keep components predictable, maintainable, and avoids unintended behavior.
  • Example: What is a side effect in ReactJS?
    A common example of a side effect in ReactJS is making an API call after a component is mounted. This action interacts with the outside world and does not produce the same result every time, so it is considered a side effect.
    • Scenario: A component fetches user data from an external API when it mounts.
    • Why it's a side effect: It affects things outside the component and depends on external data.
    Example behavior:
    • When the component renders, the useEffect hook triggers an API call.
    • The data is fetched and stored in the component’s state.
    • The UI updates based on the fetched data.
    Side effects like this should always be managed inside useEffect to ensure they run at the right time and do not cause issues during component lifecycle events such as unmounting or re-rendering.
  • What is debouncing in ReactJS?
    Debouncing in ReactJS is a technique used to limit how often a function is executed, especially in response to rapid user actions like typing or resizing. Instead of calling the function immediately with every change, debouncing waits for a specified time after the last event before executing the function.
    • Commonly used in input fields, search bars, or auto-complete components.
    • Improves performance by reducing the number of API calls or expensive computations.
    • Only triggers the desired function after the user stops interacting for a set delay.
    • Debouncing can be implemented using setTimeout and clearTimeout or with utility libraries like lodash.
    For example, in a search input field, debouncing ensures the API call is made only after the user stops typing, avoiding calls on every keystroke.
  • Example: How to implement debouncing in ReactJS?
    This example shows how to implement debouncing in a ReactJS functional component using setTimeout and clearTimeout. Debouncing is useful to delay a function call until the user stops typing, which reduces API requests or computations.
    • The user types in an input field.
    • The component waits 500 milliseconds after the last keystroke before triggering the search logic.
    • If the user types again before the timeout finishes, the previous timeout is cleared.
      function SearchComponent() {
    const [query, setQuery] = React.useState('');
    const [debouncedQuery, setDebouncedQuery] = React.useState('');
  
    React.useEffect(() => {
      const timer = setTimeout(() => {
        setDebouncedQuery(query);
      }, 500); // 500ms debounce delay
  
      return () => clearTimeout(timer); // Cleanup on each keystroke
    }, [query]);
  
    return (
      <div>
        <input
          type="text"
          placeholder="Search..."
          value={query}
          onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)}
        />
        <p>Debounced Output: {debouncedQuery}</p>
      </div>
    );
  }
    This implementation ensures the output updates only when the user pauses typing, helping to optimize performance in search or filter components.
  • What is React Developer Tools?
    React Developer Tools is a browser extension provided by the React team that helps developers inspect, debug, and analyze React applications more effectively.
    • It allows you to explore the component tree of your React app in real-time.
    • You can view props, state, hooks, and context for each component.
    • It helps identify unnecessary re-renders and performance issues using the Profiler tab.
    • It supports both React class components and functional components with hooks.
    • Available for Chrome, Firefox, and as a standalone app for React Native debugging.
    React Developer Tools is an essential tool for any React developer, making it easier to understand how the app behaves and how data flows between components.
  • What is Lighthouse in ReactJS?
    Lighthouse is an open-source tool developed by Google that audits web applications for performance, accessibility, SEO, best practices, and Progressive Web App standards. Although it is not specific to ReactJS, it is commonly used to test and optimize React applications.
    • It provides detailed reports with scores for Performance, Accessibility, SEO, and more.
    • Helps identify performance bottlenecks in React apps like long loading times or large bundle sizes.
    • Suggests improvements such as code splitting, lazy loading, or image optimization.
    • Can be run in Chrome DevTools, via the command line, or as a CI tool in deployment pipelines.
    • Useful for ensuring that your React application delivers a fast, accessible, and user-friendly experience.
    Lighthouse is essential for React developers who want to measure and improve the quality and user experience of their web applications.
  • What is throttling in ReactJS?
    Throttling in ReactJS is a technique used to control how frequently a function is executed over time. Unlike debouncing, which delays execution until the activity stops, throttling ensures the function is called at regular intervals, no matter how often the event occurs.
    • Throttling is useful for events that fire continuously, such as scroll, resize, or mouse movement.
    • It improves performance by limiting the number of times a function runs over a specific time frame.
    • Commonly implemented using setTimeout or utility libraries like lodash.
    • Helps prevent performance issues or UI lag in React applications.
    • Ensures that the function executes at most once every specified delay, even if the event keeps firing.
    Throttling is especially beneficial in React when tracking window resizing, scroll position, or input changes in real-time without overloading the app with too many updates.
  • What are error states in ReactJS?
    Error states in ReactJS refer to the condition of a component when something goes wrong during rendering, data fetching, or user interaction. Managing error states is crucial for providing a smooth and user-friendly experience.
    • Rendering Errors: Occur when a component fails to render due to runtime issues. These are usually handled with error boundaries in class components or libraries for functional components.
    • Network/API Errors: Happen when fetching data fails (e.g., server down, invalid response). These are handled using try-catch blocks or conditional rendering.
    • Form Validation Errors: Triggered when user input does not meet expected criteria. React stores and displays validation errors as part of component state.
    • Unexpected State Errors: When application logic fails, causing incorrect or undefined behavior.
    • UI Feedback: Error states are usually reflected in the UI with messages, alerts, or fallback components.
    React provides mechanisms like useState for storing error info, useEffect for catching side-effect errors, and error boundaries for catching errors in component trees.
  • What is Edge in ReactJS?
    In the context of ReactJS, "Edge" typically refers to Edge Computing or Edge Deployment. It means deploying React applications closer to the user's physical location using edge servers or Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) to improve performance and reduce latency.
    • Edge Deployment: Hosting parts of a React app (such as static assets or SSR content) on edge servers across the globe.
    • Faster Load Times: By serving content from servers close to users, page loads are faster and smoother.
    • React with Edge Functions: Frameworks like Next.js support running server-side logic (like API routes or SSR) at the edge using providers like Vercel or Cloudflare Workers.
    • Improved SEO and UX: Dynamic pages rendered closer to users improve perceived performance and search engine rankings.
    • Modern Architecture: Combines React's client-side rendering with edge-based server-side features for hybrid apps.
    Edge in ReactJS is a modern approach to optimizing app performance and user experience by leveraging distributed computing closer to end-users.
  • What is transpiling in ReactJS?
    Transpiling in ReactJS refers to the process of converting modern JavaScript or JSX code into an older version of JavaScript that browsers can understand. This process is handled by tools like Babel during the build step.
    • React uses JSX, which is not natively understood by browsers. Transpiling converts JSX into regular JavaScript function calls (like React.createElement).
    • Modern JavaScript features such as arrow functions, classes, optional chaining, and async/await are transpiled into compatible versions for older browsers.
    • Transpiling helps ensure cross-browser compatibility and allows developers to write cleaner, more modern code.
    • It is part of the build process in tools like Create React App, Webpack, and Vite.
    • Without transpiling, JSX and ES6+ code would cause errors in browsers that do not support them.
    Transpiling is essential in React development to bridge the gap between cutting-edge syntax and current browser capabilities.
  • What is ESM in ReactJS?
    ESM stands for ECMAScript Modules, which is the official standard for modular JavaScript code. In the context of ReactJS, ESM is commonly used to import and export components, functions, or variables across different files.
    • Syntax: Uses import and export keywords to manage dependencies and modules.
    • Browser Support: Modern browsers support ESM natively, allowing faster and more optimized delivery of JavaScript files.
    • Tree Shaking: ESM enables bundlers like Webpack or Vite to remove unused code during build, reducing bundle size.
    • React Usage: React components, hooks, and utilities are typically organized using ESM syntax for better modularity and maintainability.
    • Example: import React from 'react'; export default MyComponent;
    ESM is the preferred module system in modern JavaScript and React development due to its simplicity, efficiency, and support for static analysis by tools.
  • What is ES6 in ReactJS?
    ES6, or ECMAScript 2015, is the sixth major version of the JavaScript language standard. It introduced several new features that made JavaScript more powerful, readable, and maintainable. In ReactJS development, ES6 features are commonly used to write modern and cleaner code.
    • Let and Const: Block-scoped variable declarations that replace var.
    • Arrow Functions: Shorter function syntax and lexical this binding.
    • Classes: Class-based syntax to define React components and structure code.
    • Template Literals: Embedded expressions in strings using backticks.
    • Destructuring: Extract values from arrays or objects into variables.
    • Modules: Use of import and export to organize and reuse code across files.
    • Spread and Rest Operators: For copying and combining arrays or objects.
    • Promises: Improved handling of asynchronous operations.
    ES6 is the foundation of modern JavaScript, and ReactJS fully embraces it to build scalable, readable, and maintainable applications.

  • Explain in detail: What is SSR, SSG, ISR, and CSR in Next.js?
    Next.js is a powerful React framework that supports multiple rendering strategies to optimize performance, SEO, and user experience. Each rendering method serves a different purpose and is suitable for different types of applications:
    • SSR (Server-Side Rendering):
      The HTML of the page is generated on the server at each request. This means every time a user visits the page, Next.js executes the server-side logic (like fetching data) and returns a fully rendered HTML page.
      • Best for dynamic content like personalized dashboards or frequently changing data.
      • Improves SEO as the server sends complete HTML.
      • Slower than static generation because rendering happens on each request.
      • Implemented using getServerSideProps.
    • SSG (Static Site Generation):
      The HTML is generated at build time and reused for every request. Pages are pre-rendered into static HTML and deployed to a CDN.
      • Best for content that doesn’t change often, like blogs or documentation.
      • Super fast performance as pages are served from a CDN.
      • No server required to generate pages at runtime.
      • Implemented using getStaticProps (and optionally getStaticPaths).
    • ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration):
      ISR allows you to update static pages after deployment without rebuilding the entire site. You specify a revalidation time, and the page is regenerated in the background when needed.
      • Combines the speed of SSG with the flexibility of SSR.
      • Pages can be updated at runtime while still served statically.
      • Improves performance with controlled freshness.
      • Implemented using getStaticProps with the revalidate key.
    • CSR (Client-Side Rendering):
      In CSR, the page is rendered in the browser using JavaScript after the initial load. The server sends only a minimal HTML shell, and the React app fetches and displays the data on the client side.
      • Best for dynamic, interactive UIs like admin dashboards or user profiles.
      • Fast client-side transitions, but slower initial page load.
      • Poor SEO support since content is not rendered on the server.
      • Implemented by simply using React hooks like useEffect to fetch data on the client.
    Summary:
    Choosing between SSR, SSG, ISR, and CSR depends on your project’s requirements. SSR is great for dynamic, personalized content; SSG for static, fast-loading pages; ISR for balancing freshness with performance; and CSR for highly interactive apps with less SEO concern.
  • RxJS Required

    Is RxJS Required for ReactJS?

    No, RxJS is not required for building ReactJS applications, but it can be useful in specific use cases.

    ✅ When RxJS is NOT Required

    • Basic forms and inputs
    • Using Axios or fetch for API calls
    • State management with Redux Toolkit or Context API
    • Handling async logic with redux-thunk or redux-saga
    • Real-time features using WebSocket without Observables

    ✅ When RxJS is Useful or Recommended

    RxJS is helpful in advanced scenarios like:

    Use Case Why RxJS is Helpful
    Real-time data streams Handles async streams efficiently using Observables
    Debounced search or auto-suggestions Operators like debounceTime and distinctUntilChanged make it easy
    Multi-step async workflows Simplifies chaining and canceling requests
    Combining multiple async sources Use operators like combineLatest and merge
    Using redux-observable RxJS is required to work with Epics

    ✅ Summary

    Question Answer
    Is RxJS required for ReactJS? ❌ No
    Is RxJS useful for complex async or stream-based logic? ✅ Yes
    Common combo React + RxJS + redux-observable

    RxJS with React – Complete Guide

    RxJS (Reactive Extensions for JavaScript) is a library for reactive programming using Observables, to make it easier to work with asynchronous or callback-based code.

    🌟 RxJS?

    • RxJS provides a way to create and manage asynchronous data streams.
    • It uses Observables to emit values over time and allows operators like debounce, map, merge, filter, etc.
    • It helps manage data flow from multiple sources like WebSocket, API responses, user input, etc.

    🔗 Why Use RxJS in React?

    • Powerful control over async streams (debounce, throttle, retry, cancel requests)
    • Can handle complex interactions and side effects
    • Helps in auto-complete inputs, search bars, or WebSocket data streams
    • Works great with libraries like redux-observable

    ⚙️ Core Concepts in RxJS

    Concept Description
    Observable Represents a stream of values emitted over time
    Observer An object with next, error, and complete methods to react to emitted values
    Subscription Represents execution of Observable and is used to unsubscribe
    Operators Functions to transform or filter data (e.g., map, filter, debounceTime)
    Subject Both an Observable and Observer; can multicast values to multiple subscribers

    📌 Use Cases in React

    • Search with debounce: Prevents API calls for every keystroke
    • Auto-complete suggestions: Emits values based on input changes
    • Live updates with WebSocket: Streams real-time data to the UI
    • Handling cancelable async tasks: Abort previous API requests easily

    🧪 Example: Debounced Search Input

    1. Use RxJS Subject to collect user input events
    2. Apply debounceTime to wait for a pause in typing
    3. Subscribe to the stream and make API calls
    4. Update the component state with the search result

    📚 Libraries and Tools

    • rxjs – core reactive library
    • redux-observable – middleware for Redux using RxJS Epics
    • recompose (deprecated) – used to integrate observables into React

    ✅ When to Use RxJS

    • Advanced apps needing stream-based logic
    • Real-time dashboards and WebSocket integrations
    • Custom hooks that deal with user input and APIs
    • Replacing complex promise chains

    ❌ When Not to Use RxJS

    • Simple projects with minimal async logic
    • When Redux Toolkit or useEffect with fetch is sufficient
    • If team is not familiar with reactive programming concepts

    📌 Learning Curve

    RxJS is powerful but has a steep learning curve. It requires understanding observables, operators, subscriptions, and error handling properly. Once mastered, it’s a strong tool for managing complex side effects and data flows.

    🎯 Summary

    Feature RxJS in React
    Required for React? No
    Great for complex async workflows? Yes
    Ideal for search debounce, real-time, cancelable tasks? Yes
    Used with redux-observable? Yes
    Beginner-friendly? No, requires learning curve

    Security Vulnerable to XSS Can use HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite flags
    Accessibility Accessible via JavaScript only Accessible by both client and server
    Expiration Control Must be cleared manually Can set expiration per cookie
    Best Use Cases Theme, preferences, client cache Auth tokens, sessions, secure data

  • Why do we use Express.js?
    Express.js is a minimal and flexible Node.js web application framework that provides a robust set of features for building web and mobile applications. Key reasons for using Express.js include:
    • Simplicity and Minimalism: Express offers a clean and minimal interface to build servers and APIs quickly.
    • Routing: Built-in robust routing system to handle different HTTP methods and URLs easily.
    • Middleware Support: Enables modular code with middleware functions for handling requests, responses, logging, authentication, etc.
    • Performance: Built on top of Node.js, it is fast and non-blocking, suitable for scalable applications.
    • Community and Ecosystem: Large community support and a vast ecosystem of third-party middleware and plugins.
    • Integration: Easily integrates with databases like MongoDB, MySQL, and tools like Socket.IO or templating engines.
    • RESTful API Support: Ideal for creating RESTful APIs and microservices architectures.
  • How is error handling done in React.js?
    Error handling in React.js can be done using several approaches to ensure robust UI and graceful error recovery:
    • Error Boundaries: React components that catch JavaScript errors in their child component tree, log them, and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the app. 
      
class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
  constructor(props) {
    super(props);
    this.state = { hasError: false };
  }
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) {
    return { hasError: true };
  }
  componentDidCatch(error, info) {
    console.error("Error caught:", error, info);
  }
  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return <h1>Something went wrong.</h1>;
    }
    return this.props.children;
  }
}
    • Try-Catch Blocks: Use inside event handlers or async functions to catch runtime errors. 
      
try {
  const response = await fetch("/api/data");
  const data = await response.json();
  setData(data);
} catch (error) {
  console.error("Fetch error:", error);
}
    • React Hook Error Handling: Handle errors in custom hooks or `useEffect` using try-catch patterns.
    • Global Error Logging: Use tools like Sentry, LogRocket, or custom logging to capture and report runtime exceptions.
    • Form Error Handling: Use libraries like Formik or React Hook Form to validate input and show errors to users.
  • How is error handling done in Node.js?
    Error handling in Node.js is crucial for building reliable applications and involves managing synchronous and asynchronous errors effectively. Common techniques include:
    • Try-Catch Blocks (Synchronous Code): Used to catch errors in synchronous code blocks. 
      
try {
  let result = riskyFunction();
  console.log(result);
} catch (error) {
  console.error("Caught error:", error);
}
    • Callback Pattern (Asynchronous): Traditional Node.js style using error-first callbacks. 
      
fs.readFile('file.txt', (err, data) => {
  if (err) {
    return console.error("Read error:", err);
  }
  console.log(data.toString());
});
    • Promises & Async/Await: Handle asynchronous code with try-catch and `.catch()`. 
      
async function fetchData() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com");
    const data = await res.json();
    console.log(data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Async error:", error);
  }
}
    • Global Error Handlers: Catch uncaught exceptions and unhandled promise rejections. 
      
process.on("uncaughtException", (err) => {
  console.error("Uncaught Exception:", err);
});
process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason, promise) => {
  console.error("Unhandled Rejection:", reason);
});
    • Express Error Middleware: Centralized error handling in Express.js. 
      
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.error("Error:", err.message);
  res.status(500).json({ error: "Something went wrong!" });
});
  • How is data sharing handled in Next.js?
    In Next.js, data sharing between components and pages can be achieved using various methods depending on the context and requirements:
    • Props: The most basic method. Data is passed from parent to child components using props. 
      
export default function Parent() {
  return <Child message="Hello from parent!" />;
}
    • Context API: For sharing global state across multiple components without prop drilling. 
      
const MyContext = React.createContext();
export function MyProvider({ children }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  return (
    <MyContext.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>
      {children}
    </MyContext.Provider>
  );
}
    • Custom Hooks: Encapsulate logic and shared state in reusable hooks. 
      
function useAuth() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  return { user, login: () => setUser({ name: "Dev" }) };
}
    • Server-side Sharing (getServerSideProps / getStaticProps): Share fetched data with pages at request/build time. 
      
export async function getServerSideProps() {
  const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/data");
  const data = await res.json();
  return { props: { data } };
}
    • URL Query Parameters: Pass and share lightweight data via the query string. 
      
const router = useRouter();
console.log(router.query.id);
    • State Management Libraries: Use tools like Redux, Zustand, or Recoil for complex or large-scale data sharing across the app.
  • Is Redux usable in Next.js?
    Yes, Redux can be used in Next.js to manage global state across components and pages. It is especially useful for large applications where complex state logic needs to be shared. Here's how Redux works with Next.js:
    • Integration with SSR: Next.js supports server-side rendering (SSR), and Redux can be integrated with SSR using libraries like next-redux-wrapper to ensure state hydration across client and server.
    • Installation: 
      
npm install redux react-redux next-redux-wrapper
    • Store Configuration: Create a Redux store and wrap the app using Provider and createWrapper. 
      
// store.js
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
import counterReducer from './counterSlice';

export const store = () => configureStore({ reducer: { counter: counterReducer } });
        
      
// _app.js
import { Provider } from 'react-redux';
import { wrapper } from './store';

function MyApp({ Component, ...rest }) {
  const { store, props } = wrapper.useWrappedStore(rest);
  return (
    <Provider store={store}>
      <Component {...props.pageProps} />
    </Provider>
  );
}

export default MyApp;
    • Accessing State: Use Redux hooks like useSelector and useDispatch inside components. 
      
import { useSelector, useDispatch } from 'react-redux';
const count = useSelector(state => state.counter.value);
const dispatch = useDispatch();
    • SSR Compatibility: Redux state can be preloaded in getServerSideProps or getStaticProps using store.dispatch().
    Conclusion: Redux works very well in Next.js, especially when using next-redux-wrapper to support SSR and CSR (Client-Side Rendering).

  • Redux Toolkit?

    Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official, recommended way to write Redux logic. It provides a set of tools and abstractions to simplify Redux development and eliminate boilerplate code.

    🔧 Features:

    • createSlice: Combines reducers and actions into a single slice.
    • configureStore: Sets up the Redux store with sensible defaults like middleware and DevTools support.
    • createAsyncThunk: Simplifies async logic and data fetching (e.g. API calls).
    • createReducer: Reduces boilerplate when writing reducers with immutability handled internally.
    • Immer.js integration: Allows writing “mutating” code that is internally converted to immutable updates.

    ✅ Benefits:

    • Less boilerplate code
    • Built-in DevTools setup
    • Standardized Redux patterns
    • Improved developer experience

    📦 Example:

    // counterSlice.js
import { createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

const counterSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'counter',
  initialState: { value: 0 },
  reducers: {
    increment: state => { state.value += 1 },
    decrement: state => { state.value -= 1 },
    reset: state => { state.value = 0 },
  }
});

export const { increment, decrement, reset } = counterSlice.actions;
export default counterSlice.reducer;

    Use this slice in your Redux configureStore():

    // store.js
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
import counterReducer from './counterSlice';

export const store = configureStore({
  reducer: {
    counter: counterReducer,
  }
});

    📚 Documentation:

    https://redux-toolkit.js.org
  • Redux vs Redux Toolkit

    Redux is a state management library, and Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official, recommended way to use Redux efficiently.

    🔍 Comparison:

    Feature Redux Redux Toolkit (RTK)
    Boilerplate Verbose and repetitive code Minimal code using helpers like createSlice
    Setup Manual store, middleware, DevTools setup configureStore auto-configures everything
    Reducers Written manually with switch-case Created using createSlice and Immer
    Async Actions Manual thunk creation and boilerplate createAsyncThunk simplifies async logic
    Best Practices Optional Built-in by design
    Learning Curve Steeper Beginner-friendly

    ✅ Conclusion:

    • Redux: Good for learning concepts, but verbose and error-prone.
    • Redux Toolkit: The modern, recommended way to write Redux apps with less code and better defaults.

    📘 Official Docs:

    • https://redux.js.org (Redux)
    • https://redux-toolkit.js.org (Redux Toolkit)

export const decrement = () => ({ type: 'DECREMENT' });

    2️⃣ redux/reducer.js
const initialState = { value: 0 };

export const counterReducer = (state = initialState, action) => {
switch (action.type) {
case 'INCREMENT':
return { value: state.value + 1 };
case 'DECREMENT':
return { value: state.value - 1 };
case 'RESET':
return { value: 0 };
default:
return state;
}
};

    📁 Folder Structure (app router):

├── useCounterStore.js

    1️⃣ store/useCounterStore.js

'use client';
import { create } from 'zustand';

export const useCounterStore = create((set) => ({
count: 0,
increment: () => set((state) => ({ count: state.count + 1 })),
decrement: () => set((state) => ({ count: state.count - 1 })),
reset: () => set({ count: 0 }),
}));

    2️⃣ app/components/CompA.js      
'use client';
import { useCounterStore } from '../../store/useCounterStore';

'use client';
import { createContext, useContext, useState } from 'react';

const CounterContext = createContext();
export const useCounter = () => useContext(CounterContext);

export function CounterProvider({ children }) {
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

const increment = () => setCount((c) => c + 1);
const decrement = () => setCount((c) => c - 1);
const reset = () => setCount(0);

return (
<CounterContext.Provider value={{ count, increment, decrement, reset }}>
{children}
</CounterContext.Provider>
);
}

  • What happens if we don't use Redux Thunk to call an API?

    🚫 Without Redux Thunk (or middleware):

    Redux only supports synchronous actions by default. This means:

    • You can only dispatch plain JavaScript objects — not functions or Promises.
    • If you try to dispatch an async function (like a fetch call), Redux will throw an error because it doesn't know how to handle it.

    🧪 Example (Invalid without Thunk):

    
// ❌ This won't work without Redux Thunk
dispatch(async (dispatch) => {
const response = await fetch('/api/data');
const data = await response.json();
dispatch({ type: 'SET_DATA', payload: data });
});

    Redux will throw: Actions must be plain objects. Use custom middleware for async actions.

    ✅ What Redux Thunk Enables:

    • Lets you return functions (not just plain objects) from your action creators.
    • Allows you to delay the dispatch of an action, or to dispatch only if a certain condition is met.
    • Gives access to dispatch and getState inside the thunk.

    🛠️ Alternative Solutions:

    • Redux Toolkit Query (RTK Query) – Modern approach, handles API requests and caching.
    • Redux Saga – Generator-based middleware for complex flows.
    • Use useEffect + Context or Zustand – Simpler state management without Redux at all.

    📝 Summary:

    • Redux cannot handle async logic on its own.
    • Using Redux Thunk or other middleware is essential if you want to perform side effects like API calls in Redux actions.
  • difference between process.nextTick() and setImmediate() in Node.js?

    🔍 Summary:

    • process.nextTick() queues a callback to be invoked immediately after the current operation, before any I/O or timers.
    • setImmediate() queues a callback to be run on the next iteration of the event loop, after I/O events.

    📌 Execution Order Example:

    
console.log('Start');

process.nextTick(() => {
console.log('nextTick callback');
});

setImmediate(() => {
console.log('setImmediate callback');
});

console.log('End');

    🧾 Output:

    
Start
End
nextTick callback
setImmediate callback

    📘 Explanation:

    • process.nextTick() callbacks are executed after the current function but before the event loop continues.
    • setImmediate() callbacks are scheduled to run on the next tick of the event loop, after I/O events like timers or network requests.

    ⛔ Warning:

    Overusing process.nextTick() (e.g., recursively) can block the event loop and cause starvation of I/O operations.

    ✅ Use When:

    • Use process.nextTick() to delay execution until after the current function but before I/O.
    • Use setImmediate() when you want to execute code after I/O events or to yield the event loop.
  • React.memo?
    React.memo is a higher-order component (HOC) in React that memoizes a functional component.
    It prevents unnecessary re-renders by caching the component’s output unless its props change. 
      const MyComponent = React.memo((props) => {
    // ...
  });

    React.memo can cause unnecessary complexity, stale UI bugs due to shallow prop comparison, and increased memory usage.
    It adds overhead if the component is simple or props don’t change often.

    Overusing it without profiling may degrade performance rather than improve it, especially in large or dynamic component trees.


    • Extra work on every render due to shallow comparison
    • False sense of performance improvement
    • Stale or mutated props causing bugs
    • Over-optimizing the wrong layer
    • Blocks intentional re-renders (e.g., animations)
    • Increased memory overhead
    • Hurts concurrent rendering in React 18
    • Makes debugging more difficult

  • Reconciliation?
    Reconciliation is the process React uses to update the DOM efficiently when the state or props of a component change. Instead of re-rendering the entire UI, React:
    1. Uses the Virtual DOM to represent the current state of the UI.
    2. Compares the new Virtual DOM with the previous one using a diffing algorithm.
    3. Calculates the minimal number of changes needed.
    4. Updates only the changed parts in the real DOM.
    Example: If only one item in a list changes, React will update that item instead of re-rendering the entire list.
    Benefits: - Improves performance. - Avoids full page refresh. - Provides smooth user experiences by minimizing DOM operations. This efficient update process is what makes React fast and responsive.
  • React?
    1. React is a JavaScript library developed by Facebook for building user interfaces, especially for single-page applications. It allows developers to create reusable UI components.
    2. Components are the building blocks of a React application. They can be functional or class-based, and each component represents a part of the UI.
    3. JSX (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension that allows writing HTML inside JavaScript. It makes the code more readable and easier to write React elements.
    4. Reconciliation React compares the new virtual DOM with the previous one using a diffing algorithm and updates only the parts of the DOM that changed (this process is called reconciliation).
    5. Controlled Components : form elements whose values are controlled by React state.
    6. Uncontrolled components : form elements that maintain their state using the DOM (accessed via refs).
    7. useState() : The useState() hook is used in React functional components to manage local state. It allows you to store, read, and update values across re-renders.
      This enables your component to reactively update the UI based on user interactions or other changes.
    8. Prop Drilling : Prop Drilling refers to the process of passing data from a parent component down to child components, and then further down to deeply nested components, even if intermediate components don’t need that data. It becomes problematic when the component tree is large, leading to tight coupling and making components harder to manage and maintain.
    9. defaultProps : is a feature in React that allows you to define default values for a component’s props. If a parent component does not provide a specific prop, the default value will be used instead. It helps prevent bugs and ensures components behave as expected even if some props are not passed.
      Usage (for functional components):
      
    const Greeting = ({ name = "Guest" }) => (
    <h1>Hello, {name}</h1>
    );

  • useReducer Example. 
      🔧 🧪 Counter Component
  import React, { useReducer } from 'react';
  const initialState = { count: 0 };
  
  function myreducer(state, action) {
    switch (action.type) {
      case 'increment':
        return { count: state.count + 1 };
      case 'decrement':
        return { count: state.count - 1 };
      case 'reset':
        return initialState;
      default:
        throw new Error('Unknown action type');
    }
  }
  
  function Counter() {
    const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(myreducer, initialState);
  
    return (
      <div>
        <h2>Count: {state.count}</h2>
        <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'decrement' })}>-</button>
        <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'reset' })}>Reset</button>
        <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'increment' })}>+</button>
      </div>
    );
  }

  export default Counter;

      📌 Explanation
  1. useReducer(reducer, initialState): Initializes state and gives you a dispatch method.
  2. reducer: A pure function to calculate new state based on the action type.
  3. dispatch({ type: 'increment' }): Triggers a state update through the reducer.

  ✅ When to Use useReducer
  1. For complex state logic (e.g., multiple related values)
  2. When state changes are triggered by many different actions
  3. When the same logic must be reused across components

  • What is a Higher Order Component (HOC) in React? Explain with example.

    Higher Order Component (HOC) is a function that takes a component and returns a new component with additional functionality.

    Definition:

    HOC = Function that receives a component → returns a new enhanced component

    Common Use Cases:

    • Authentication
    • Logging
    • Data fetching
    • Permission control
    • Performance optimization

    Example: Authentication HOC

    import React from "react";
import { useNavigate } from "react-router-dom";

const withAuth = (WrappedComponent) => {

  const AuthComponent = (props) => {

    const navigate = useNavigate();
    const isAuthenticated = localStorage.getItem("token");

    if (!isAuthenticated) {
      navigate("/login");
      return null;
    }

    return <WrappedComponent {...props} />;

  };

  return AuthComponent;
};

export default withAuth;

    Protected Component Example:

    import React from "react";
import withAuth from "./withAuth";

const Dashboard = () => {

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Dashboard Page</h2>
      <p>Only logged in users can see this</p>
    </div>
  );

};

export default withAuth(Dashboard);

    Reusable Loader HOC:

    const withLoader = (WrappedComponent) => {

  return function EnhancedComponent({ isLoading, ...props }) {

    if (isLoading) {
      return <h3>Loading...</h3>;
    }

    return <WrappedComponent {...props} />;

  };

};

export default withLoader;

    Best Practices:

    • Do not modify the original component
    • Always pass props using {...props}
    • Use naming convention like withAuth, withLoader
    • Keep HOC reusable

    Modern Alternative: Many developers now prefer React Hooks instead of HOCs.

    function useAuth() {

  const token = localStorage.getItem("token");

  return !!token;

}
  • HOC?
    A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is an advanced pattern in React used to reuse component logic. It’s a function that takes a component and returns a new component with added functionality.

    Syntax:
    
    const withExtraProps = (WrappedComponent) => {
    return (props) => <WrappedComponent {...props} extra="value" />;
    };

    Use Cases:
    • Authentication
    • Logging
    • Theming or Localization
    • Permission Checks

    Example:
    
    const withLogger = (WrappedComponent) => {
    return (props) => {
    console.log('Props:', props);
    return <WrappedComponent {...props} />;
    };
    };
    
    const MyComponent = (props) => <div>{props.message}</div>;
    
    export default withLogger(MyComponent);

    Main Use:
    To reuse logic across multiple components without duplicating code.

    HOC vs Alternatives:
    • HOC: Wraps and returns enhanced component.
    • Render Props: Uses a function to determine what to render.
    • Custom Hooks: Encapsulates reusable logic using useXYZ.

  • React Vs ReactDOM?
    React and ReactDOM are two separate libraries in the React ecosystem, each with a distinct purpose:

    React : - React is the core library for building component-based user interfaces. - It provides methods like React.createElement(), useState(), and useEffect() for component logic. - It’s platform-agnostic, meaning it doesn’t assume the environment (browser, mobile, etc.).

    ReactDOM : - ReactDOM is the library that specifically handles rendering React components to the DOM (i.e., web browsers). - It includes methods like ReactDOM.createRoot() and ReactDOM.render(). - It bridges React with the actual DOM for web applications.

    In Summary:
    - Use React for building components and managing logic. - Use ReactDOM for mounting React components to the web page.
  • improve performance in a React application?
    Improving performance in a React application involves multiple strategies to minimize re-renders, optimize rendering behavior, and reduce resource usage.

    Key Techniques:
    1. Memoization: Use React.memo for components and useMemo for values to avoid unnecessary recalculations.
    2. useCallback: Prevents re-creation of functions during re-renders.
    3. Code Splitting: Use React.lazy and Suspense to load components on demand.
    4. Virtualization: Libraries like react-window or react-virtualized render only visible items in long lists.
    5. Efficient State Management: Keep state local where possible and avoid lifting state unnecessarily.
    6. Avoid Inline Functions: Especially in props of frequently updating components.
    7. Debounce Input Handlers: Reduces update frequency in response to user typing or scroll events.
    8. Use Production Builds: Always deploy with optimized production build using npm run build.

    Tools: Use tools like React DevTools, Lighthouse, and Chrome Performance tab to identify performance bottlenecks.
