    The _document.js file is used to augment the HTML document structure. It's rendered only on the server side and allows you to modify the <html> and <body> tags, include meta tags, preload fonts, and more.
  • difference between _app.js and _document.js?
    • _app.js: Controls how pages are rendered and wraps page components.
    • _document.js: Controls the structure of the HTML document and is rendered on the server only.
    Use _app.js for layouts, context, and global styles. Use _document.js for customizing the HTML document shell.
  • next.config.js?
    next.config.js is a configuration file used to customize and extend the default behavior of a Next.js app. It allows you to configure features such as custom Webpack settings, image optimization, environment variables, internationalization, redirects, rewrites, and more. This file must be placed in the root of the project.
  • enable custom environment variables in Next.js?
    To use custom environment variables in Next.js:
    • Create a .env.local file in the root directory.
    • Prefix your variables with NEXT_PUBLIC_ to expose them to the browser.
    • Example:
      NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.example.com
    • Then, access it using process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL in your code.
    Variables without the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix will only be available on the server side.
  • add a custom Webpack configuration?
    You can extend the default Webpack configuration in next.config.js like this: 
    module.exports = {
webpack: (config, { isServer }) => {
  // Modify the config
  config.module.rules.push({
    test: /\.txt$/,
    use: 'raw-loader',
  });
  return config;
},
};
    This allows you to add loaders, plugins, aliases, or modify behavior for both server and client builds.
  • serve static files in Next.js?
    In Next.js, static files can be served by placing them inside the public/ directory. Any file in the public/ folder can be accessed via a URL path relative to the base URL of your site.

    For example, if you add an image to public/images/logo.png, it can be accessed in the browser at /images/logo.png.

    You can reference static assets in your components like:
    <img src="/images/logo.png" alt="Logo" />
  • x difference between public/ and static/?
    • public/: This is the recommended folder in modern Next.js apps for serving static assets. Files here are served as-is and can be directly accessed from the root URL. It supports all asset types (images, fonts, etc.).
    • static/: This folder was used in older versions of Next.js (prior to version 9). It's now deprecated. Use public/ instead.
    Recommendation: Always use the public/ directory for serving static files in current versions of Next.js.
  • navigate between pages in Next.js?
    In Next.js, you navigate between pages using the built-in Link component from next/link. It enables client-side transitions between routes without a full page reload.

    Example usage:
    <Link href="/about">Go to About</Link>
    Alternatively, you can use the useRouter() hook from next/router for programmatic navigation:
    router.push('/about')
  • Link component in Next.js?
    The Link component is a wrapper around anchor tags that enables seamless client-side navigation in Next.js. It improves performance by prefetching linked pages in the background and avoids full reloads.

    Example:
    <Link href="/contact">
      <a>Contact Us</a>
    </Link>
    In modern versions, wrapping with <a> is optional if no custom styles or behaviors are needed.
  • shallow routing?
    Shallow routing allows you to change the URL without running data fetching methods like getServerSideProps, getStaticProps, or reloading the page.

    Example:
    router.push('/dashboard?tab=profile', undefined, { shallow: true })
    This is useful for updating query parameters, tabs, or filters without triggering a full re-render or page reload.
  • getStaticProps()?
    getStaticProps is a Next.js function used for Static Site Generation (SSG). It runs at build time and allows you to fetch data that will be rendered as static HTML. It is typically used for pages that can be pre-rendered ahead of time and do not need to update often.

    Example use case: blog posts, documentation pages, product listings.
  • getServerSideProps()?
    getServerSideProps is used for Server-Side Rendering (SSR). It runs on every request and fetches data on the server before rendering the page. This is ideal for pages that need up-to-date data on each request, such as user dashboards or real-time content.

    Example use case: authenticated pages, dashboards, search results.
  • getStaticPaths()?
    getStaticPaths is used with getStaticProps to generate dynamic static pages at build time. It tells Next.js which dynamic routes to pre-render based on external data.

    Example use case: generating static pages for each blog post using its slug or ID.
  • Can you use getStaticProps and getServerSideProps together?
    No, you cannot use both getStaticProps and getServerSideProps in the same page. A page can use only one data-fetching method. You must choose based on whether you want static generation (faster, cached at build) or server-side rendering (fresh on every request).
  • use of revalidation in getStaticProps?
    Revalidation allows you to update static pages after they’ve been built, without needing to rebuild the entire site. In getStaticProps, you can return a revalidate key (in seconds), which tells Next.js to regenerate the page in the background when a request comes in after the revalidate time has passed.

    Example:
    return { props: { data }, revalidate: 60 }
    This ensures your content stays fresh while keeping the performance benefits of static generation.
  • Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)?
    ISR allows Next.js to create or update static pages after the site has been built and deployed. It combines the benefits of static generation with the flexibility of server-rendered content. ISR uses the revalidate option in getStaticProps to automatically regenerate the page behind the scenes after a specified time interval.

    It supports scalable and dynamic static pages, making it ideal for eCommerce, blogs, and news sites.
  • fallback in getStaticPaths()?
    The fallback key in getStaticPaths() defines how Next.js handles dynamic routes not returned by getStaticPaths at build time. It has three options:
    • false: Only paths returned by getStaticPaths will be statically generated; others will return 404.
    • true: Paths not returned at build time will be rendered on-demand and cached.
    • 'blocking': Similar to true, but the user waits for the HTML to be generated on the server before receiving the response.
    This makes your app more scalable by allowing on-demand static page generation.
  • fetch data on the client side?
    In Next.js, you can fetch data on the client side using standard React hooks like useEffect along with the Fetch API, Axios, or other libraries. This method runs in the browser after the initial render.

    Example: 
    useEffect(() => {
fetch('/api/data')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(data => setData(data));
}, []);
    This is commonly used when the data is dynamic, user-specific, or should not be statically or server-rendered.
  • some recommended libraries for data fetching in Next.js?
    Popular libraries used for client-side data fetching in Next.js include:
    • Axios – Promise-based HTTP client for easy API calls.
    • SWR (stale-while-revalidate) – A React Hooks library by Vercel for efficient caching, revalidation, and pagination.
    • React Query – A powerful data-fetching and caching library that supports mutations, background refetching, and more.
    • GraphQL Clients – Such as Apollo Client or URQL for querying GraphQL APIs.
    These libraries enhance performance, reduce boilerplate, and manage data fetching state intelligently.
  • add meta tags in Next.js?
    Meta tags in Next.js are added using the built-in Head component from next/head. You include this component in your page or layout and insert your meta tags inside it.

    Example: 
    import Head from 'next/head';

<Head>
<title>My Page Title</title>
<meta name="description" content="This is a description for SEO." />
<meta property="og:title" content="My Page Title" />
</Head>
    This allows you to set page titles, descriptions, Open Graph tags, and other SEO-related metadata.
  • Head component?
    The Head component in Next.js is a special component imported from next/head that lets you modify the <head> section of the HTML document. You can use it to dynamically add meta tags, title, favicon links, scripts, and more on a per-page basis.
  • make a page SEO-friendly in Next.js?
    To make a page SEO-friendly in Next.js, follow these best practices:
    • Use the Head component to set a unique title and meta description for each page.
    • Use semantic HTML (e.g., <main>, <article>, <header>, <footer>).
    • Implement structured data using JSON-LD inside Head.
    • Use getStaticProps or getServerSideProps to serve crawlable content.
    • Ensure fast load time by optimizing images and reducing bundle size.
    • Use accessible tags and attributes for screen readers (ARIA roles, alt text).
    These techniques help improve your page's visibility in search engines and enhance user experience.
  • implement authentication in Next.js?
    Authentication in Next.js can be implemented using several approaches:
    • NextAuth.js: A powerful library that supports OAuth, credentials, JWT, and social providers like Google or GitHub.
    • Custom JWT-based Auth: Use getServerSideProps or middleware to verify JWT tokens on server-side rendered pages.
    • Session Cookies: Store session tokens in HTTP-only cookies and validate them via API routes or middleware.
    You can protect routes and APIs by checking tokens or session state on each request.
  • handle protected routes?
    Protected routes in Next.js can be handled by:
    • Using getServerSideProps to check authentication before rendering the page.
    • Redirecting unauthenticated users to a login page using context.res.writeHead() or return { redirect }.
    • Using middleware (in middleware.js) to inspect cookies or headers and block/redirect unauthorized access before a route loads.
    • Client-side checks using hooks like useEffect() to redirect if session is missing (for CSR pages).
  • What tools does Next.js provide for performance optimization?
    Next.js offers several built-in performance optimizations:
    • Automatic code splitting – Loads only the JavaScript required for the current page.
    • Image optimization – Automatic resizing, compression, and lazy loading of images.
    • Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) – Updates static pages on-demand without full rebuilds.
    • Prefetching – Prefetches linked pages in the background to improve navigation speed.
    • Fast refresh – Fast reload during development for better DX.
    • Middleware & Edge Functions – Minimize backend latency and route-specific logic.
  • automatic code splitting?
    Automatic code splitting means that Next.js only sends the JavaScript required for the page being viewed. It splits the bundle by route so that each page loads faster, reducing initial load time and improving performance. Shared components and dependencies are also chunked efficiently.
  • Image Optimization in Next.js?
    Next.js provides an advanced next/image component that optimizes images on the fly. Key features include:
    • Automatic resizing based on device size and resolution
    • Built-in lazy loading
    • WebP support and format selection
    • On-demand server-side optimization
    Example usage:
    <Image src="/hero.png" width={800} height={400} alt="Hero" />
    It helps improve performance and Core Web Vitals by reducing image payload.
  • test Next.js components?
    You can test Next.js components using popular React testing tools like:
    • Jest: A testing framework by Meta used for unit and integration testing.
    • React Testing Library (RTL): A lightweight library that encourages testing from the user’s perspective.
    Example setup:
    • Install dependencies: npm install --save-dev jest @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom
    • Create test files with .test.js or .spec.js extensions
    Example test: 
    import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import Home from '../pages/index';

test('renders home page', () => {
render(<Home />);
expect(screen.getByText('Welcome')).toBeInTheDocument();
});
  • What tools can be used for end-to-end testing?
    Popular tools for end-to-end (E2E) testing in Next.js include:
    • Playwright: A fast, reliable framework that supports multiple browsers and advanced features.
    • Cypress: A developer-friendly E2E testing tool that runs tests directly in the browser.
    • Selenium: A more traditional tool for automated browser testing (less common in modern React workflows).
    These tools simulate user behavior and test full workflows like login, navigation, and form submission.
  • deploy a Next.js app?
    You can deploy a Next.js app by:
    • Vercel: One-click deploy and automatic integration with GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket
    • Netlify: Great for static and hybrid sites (requires next export or custom functions)
    • Render, Railway, or Fly.io: Modern PaaS with container support
    • AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud: For advanced custom deployments
    • Docker: Package and deploy as a container anywhere
    For static export, use:
    next export
    For full SSR features, choose platforms with Node.js support.
  • What platforms support Next.js deployment?
    Supported platforms include:
    • Vercel (official)
    • Netlify
    • Render
    • Railway
    • AWS Amplify / Lambda
    • Heroku (with custom Node server)
    • DigitalOcean (via droplet or App Platform)
  • Vercel and how is it related to Next.js?
    Vercel is a cloud platform for frontend developers, designed by the creators of Next.js. It offers seamless deployment for Next.js apps with zero configuration. It supports features like:
    • Automatic deployments from Git
    • Built-in CDN
    • Incremental Static Regeneration
    • Serverless functions
    Vercel is considered the best platform for deploying full-featured Next.js applications.
  • create nested routes in Next.js?
    In Next.js, you create nested routes by organizing files into subfolders inside the pages directory. Each folder represents a segment of the URL path.

    Example structure: 
    pages/
blog/
  index.js         → /blog
  post.js          → /blog/post
  comments/
    index.js       → /blog/comments
    This structure automatically creates nested routes without any manual routing configuration.
  • API routes in Next.js?
    API routes in Next.js allow you to build server-side functions as RESTful endpoints. You can place JavaScript or TypeScript files inside the pages/api directory.

    Example: 
    pages/api/hello.js
    Will be available at: 
    /api/hello
    These routes run on the server only and can be used to handle form submissions, database queries, authentication, etc.
  • secure API routes?
    To secure API routes in Next.js, you can:
    • Check for an authenticated session (e.g., using next-auth)
    • Verify JWT tokens passed via headers or cookies
    • Validate API keys or custom headers
    • Use rate limiting and CORS policies to restrict access
    Example check: 
    export default function handler(req, res) {
const token = req.headers.authorization;
if (!token || token !== 'expected_token') {
  return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Unauthorized' });
}
res.status(200).json({ message: 'Secure data' });
}
  • use dynamic API routes?
    Dynamic API routes are created by adding square brackets in the filename under pages/api.

    Example: 
    pages/api/user/[id].js
    This route matches /api/user/123. You can access the dynamic parameter from req.query: 
    export default function handler(req, res) {
const { id } = req.query;
res.status(200).json({ userId: id });
}
    This allows you to create RESTful API endpoints that respond based on dynamic values.
  • Next.js middleware?
    Middleware in Next.js runs before a request is completed and allows you to execute code, redirect, rewrite, or modify the request/response. It runs at the edge, close to the user, improving performance and latency for logic like auth, geo-targeting, and A/B testing.

    Middleware is defined in a middleware.js (or .ts) file at the root or in specific folders.
  • implement and use middleware?
    To create middleware, add a middleware.js file in the root or inside a folder for route-specific logic.

    Example: 
    export function middleware(request) {
const loggedIn = Boolean(request.cookies.get('token'));
if (!loggedIn) {
  return Response.redirect(new URL('/login', request.url));
}
return NextResponse.next();
}
    You must export a config if you want to restrict which routes the middleware applies to: 
    export const config = {
matcher: ['/dashboard/:path*'],
};
  • use cases for middleware in Next.js?
    Common use cases include:
    • Authentication and authorization checks
    • Locale-based redirection
    • Bot detection and blocking
    • Geo-targeting and country-based content
    • Custom headers or rewrites
    • A/B testing or feature flag logic
    Middleware runs before rendering and can modify or redirect the request without changing the route file.
  • app directory in Next.js 13+?
    The app/ directory is a new routing and file structure introduced in Next.js 13 as part of the App Router. It replaces pages/ and allows better flexibility, layouts, loading states, and server components.

    Each folder in app/ represents a route and can contain:
    • page.js – Main route component
    • layout.js – Shared layout wrapper
    • loading.js – Loading UI for async content
    • error.js – Error boundary for route
    It supports server-first rendering and streaming by default.
  • use layout.js in the new app directory?
    In the App Router, layout.js is used to wrap multiple pages with shared UI (like headers or sidebars). It persists across nested routes without reloading.

    Example: 
    export default function Layout({ children }) {
return (
  <html>
    <body>
      <Header />
      {children}
    </body>
  </html>
);
}
    Place this inside a folder like app/dashboard/layout.js to apply it to all nested routes under /dashboard.
  • How does routing differ in the app vs pages directory?
    Feature pages/ Directory app/ Directory
    Routing File-based (each file = route) Folder-based (folder + page.js = route)
    Layouts Custom via _app.js or manual composition Built-in via layout.js
    Streaming / Server Components No Yes (Server-first by default)
    Error Handling Global via _error.js Per route via error.js
    Loading UI Manual with state Built-in via loading.js
    Status Stable Stable (from Next.js 14+)
  • cache SSR pages?
    In Next.js, SSR pages (using getServerSideProps) are rendered on each request by default. To cache them:
    • Use external caching (e.g., CDN like Cloudflare, or Varnish)
    • Set cache headers manually in the API or SSR response
    • Example with header: 
      export async function getServerSideProps({ res }) {
res.setHeader(
  'Cache-Control',
  'public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=30'
);
return { props: { time: Date.now() } };
}
    This enables caching at the CDN level while allowing background revalidation.
  • How does ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration) work under the hood?
    ISR allows static pages to be updated after the site is built and deployed. When a request is made:
    • If the page is fresh (within revalidate time), it is served from cache.
    • If the page is stale, Next.js shows the cached version and triggers a background regeneration.
    • The new static version replaces the old one once built.
    ISR uses a combination of getStaticProps and a revalidate value to make this work automatically.
  • use of revalidate in ISR?
    The revalidate key (in seconds) tells Next.js how often to regenerate the static page in the background. It ensures that content stays up-to-date while benefiting from the speed of static pages.

    Example: 
    export async function getStaticProps() {
const data = await fetchData();
return {
  props: { data },
  revalidate: 60 // page regenerates at most every 60 seconds
};
}
    With this, your content updates in near real-time without full redeployments.
  • integrate TypeScript into a Next.js project?
    To use TypeScript in Next.js:
    • Rename files from .js to .ts or .tsx
    • Run: npx create-next-app@latest --typescript or add manually
    • Or install manually: 
      npm install --save-dev typescript @types/react @types/node
    • Start the dev server: npm run dev
    • Next.js will auto-generate tsconfig.json
  • type getStaticProps and getServerSideProps?
    You can use Next.js types from next for accurate typings.

    Example with getStaticProps: 
    import { GetStaticProps } from 'next';

export const getStaticProps: GetStaticProps = async (context) => {
return {
  props: { data: 'hello' },
};
};
    Example with getServerSideProps: 
    import { GetServerSideProps } from 'next';

export const getServerSideProps: GetServerSideProps = async (context) => {
return {
  props: { data: 'hello from SSR' },
};
};
    You can also define custom prop types for better IntelliSense and type safety.
  • Next.js Image component?
    The Image component in Next.js is a built-in component from next/image used for optimized image rendering. It automatically provides lazy loading, resizing, format selection (like WebP), and responsive behavior out of the box.

    Example: 
    import Image from 'next/image';

<Image
src="/profile.jpg"
alt="Profile"
width={200}
height={200}
/>
    This helps improve performance and Core Web Vitals by reducing image size and load time.
  • How does image optimization work in Next.js?
    Next.js automatically optimizes images with the Image component by:
    • Serving the appropriate size based on the device screen size
    • Using modern formats like WebP when supported
    • Applying lazy loading by default
    • Serving images through a built-in server or custom CDN (e.g., Vercel Image Optimization API)
    This eliminates the need for manual image resizing or performance tuning.
  • add custom fonts in Next.js?
    There are two common methods to add custom fonts:
    • Using Google Fonts (recommended in Next.js 13+): 
      import { Inter } from 'next/font/google';

const inter = Inter({ subsets: ['latin'] });

export default function Page() {
return (
  <main className={inter.className}>
    Hello World
  </main>
);
}
      This uses built-in font optimization with automatic preload and fallback.
    • Using self-hosted fonts:
      • Place your font files (e.g., .woff, .woff2) inside /public/fonts
      • Add @font-face in a global CSS file (e.g., globals.css)
      • Example: 
        @font-face {
font-family: 'MyFont';
src: url('/fonts/MyFont.woff2') format('woff2');
font-weight: normal;
font-style: normal;
}
        Then use font-family: 'MyFont' in your styles.
  • What styling options are supported in Next.js?
    Next.js supports various styling methods out of the box:
    • CSS Modules – Component-scoped styles using .module.css
    • Global CSS – Imported in _app.js for global use
    • Tailwind CSS – Utility-first framework, easily integrated
    • Styled-components – CSS-in-JS styling
    • Emotion – CSS-in-JS with powerful theming
    • SASS/SCSS – With next-sass or built-in support
    Next.js allows developers to mix and match based on project needs.
  • use CSS Modules in Next.js?
    CSS Modules are scoped locally to the component where they are imported. To use them:
    • Create a CSS file named with .module.css (e.g., Button.module.css)
    • Import it into your component: 
      import styles from './Button.module.css';

export default function Button() {
return <button className={styles.primary}>Click</button>;
}
    This ensures no class name collisions.
  • Can you use Tailwind CSS in Next.js?
    Yes, Tailwind CSS integrates seamlessly with Next.js. Steps to install:
    • Run: 
      npx create-next-app my-app
cd my-app
npm install -D tailwindcss postcss autoprefixer
npx tailwindcss init -p
    • Edit tailwind.config.js: 
      content: ["./pages/**/*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}", "./components/**/*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}"],
    • Add Tailwind to globals.css: 
      @tailwind base;
@tailwind components;
@tailwind utilities;
  • use next-auth?
    next-auth is a complete authentication solution for Next.js.
    • Install: npm install next-auth
    • Create a file at pages/api/auth/[...nextauth].js
    • Configure providers (e.g., GitHub, Google, Credentials)
    • Use hooks: 
      import { useSession, signIn, signOut } from 'next-auth/react';
    • Wrap your app in SessionProvider inside _app.js
  • store JWT tokens securely in Next.js?
    JWT tokens can be stored securely by:
    • Using HTTP-only cookies to prevent access from JavaScript (XSS protection)
    • Avoiding localStorage or sessionStorage for sensitive tokens
    • Setting secure, SameSite, and HttpOnly flags in cookies
    Example with next-auth using JWT: 
    jwt: {
secret: process.env.JWT_SECRET,
},
session: {
strategy: 'jwt',
},
  • protect SSR/SSG routes?
    To protect SSR or SSG pages:
    • Use getServerSideProps to check session/token and redirect if unauthorized
    • Use getStaticProps with revalidate only if content is public or secured via another layer
    • Example SSR protection: 
      import { getSession } from 'next-auth/react';

export async function getServerSideProps(context) {
const session = await getSession(context);
if (!session) {
  return {
    redirect: {
      destination: '/login',
      permanent: false,
    },
  };
}
return { props: { user: session.user } };
}
  • Next.js i18n, Forms, and File Upload Questions and Answers
  • i18n in Next.js?
    i18n (internationalization) in Next.js allows you to build multilingual applications with locale-based routing and content translation. Next.js provides built-in support via the i18n config in next.config.js.

    Example configuration: 
    module.exports = {
i18n: {
  locales: ['en', 'fr', 'de'],
  defaultLocale: 'en',
},
};
    This enables routing like /en/about, /fr/about, etc., and automatically handles locale detection.
  • configure locale-specific routing?
    Locale-specific routing is handled by enabling i18n in next.config.js. Next.js will prefix routes with locale codes and provide automatic redirection based on the user’s language settings.

    Example usage in a link: 
    import Link from 'next/link';

<Link href="/" locale="fr">French Home</Link>
    To get the current locale inside a page: 
    import { useRouter } from 'next/router';
const { locale, locales, defaultLocale } = useRouter();
  • handle forms in Next.js?
    Form handling in Next.js works the same as in React. You can use:
    • React state for controlled inputs
    • Refs for uncontrolled inputs
    • Libraries like React Hook Form for complex forms
    Example: 
    function ContactForm() {
const [name, setName] = useState('');
const handleSubmit = (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  fetch('/api/contact', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify({ name }),
  });
};

return (
  <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
    <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />
    <button type="submit">Send</button>
  </form>
);
}
  • upload a file using Next.js?
    File uploads in Next.js can be handled using a form with enctype="multipart/form-data" and an API route.

    Example frontend: 
    <form method="POST" action="/api/upload" encType="multipart/form-data">
<input type="file" name="file" />
<button type="submit">Upload</button>
</form>
    Example backend (API route using formidable): 
    import formidable from 'formidable';
export const config = {
api: {
  bodyParser: false,
},
};

export default function handler(req, res) {
const form = new formidable.IncomingForm();
form.parse(req, (err, fields, files) => {
  if (err) return res.status(500).json({ error: err });
  res.status(200).json({ uploaded: files });
});
}
    You must install formidable with: npm install formidable
  • Next.js Client vs Server Components, Logging, and Monitoring
  • difference between client and server components?
    In Next.js (v13+ with the App Router), components can be rendered either on the server or the client:
    • Server Components (default):
      • Rendered on the server
      • Do not include JavaScript in the browser
      • Cannot use React state, effects, or browser-only APIs
      • Great for performance and SEO
    • Client Components:
      • Rendered on the client (browser)
      • Can use useState, useEffect, and other hooks
      • Required for interactive UI
  • mark a component as a client component?
    To mark a component as a client component in the Next.js App Router, add the directive: 
    'use client';
    at the top of the file.

    Example: 
    'use client';

import { useState } from 'react';

export default function Counter() {
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}
    Without this directive, the component is treated as a server component by default.
  • add logging in a Next.js app?
    You can add logging in both client-side and server-side code:
    • Client-side logging: Use console.log() or libraries like loglevel
    • Server-side logging (e.g. in getServerSideProps, API routes): 
      console.info('Fetching data...');
console.error('Error occurred:', error);
    • For advanced logging:
      • Use winston or pino for structured logs
      • Send logs to a centralized service like Logtail, AWS CloudWatch, or Elasticsearch
  • What tools can be used for error monitoring in production?
    Common tools for real-time error monitoring in production Next.js apps include:
    • Sentry – Tracks frontend and backend errors with stack traces
    • Bugsnag – Offers stability insights and error alerting
    • LogRocket – Combines session replay with error tracking
    • Datadog – Full observability platform with logging and APM
    • New Relic – Performance monitoring with alerting and diagnostics
    These tools help identify runtime issues, user impact, and performance bottlenecks in production environments.
  • Next.js Monorepos, Code Sharing, and Custom Server Integration
  • Can you use Next.js in a monorepo?
    Yes, Next.js works well in monorepos using tools like:
    • Turborepo (from Vercel) – Optimized for monorepos with caching and dependency graph
    • Yarn Workspaces or npm workspaces – For managing multiple packages
    Monorepos allow managing multiple apps and packages (e.g., design systems, shared utils) in one repository.

    Example structure: 
    my-monorepo/
apps/
  web/
  admin/
packages/
  ui/
  utils/
  config/
    Each app (like `web` or `admin`) can be a separate Next.js application.
  • share code between multiple Next.js apps?
    You can share code across apps in a monorepo using:
    • Creating shared packages inside a packages/ folder
    • Using yarn workspaces or npm workspaces to manage dependencies
    • Importing shared code like: 
      import { formatDate } from '@myorg/utils';
    • Using TypeScript path aliases or symlinks (configured in tsconfig.json and next.config.js)
  • a custom server in Next.js?
    A custom server in Next.js replaces the default Next.js server with your own Node.js server using frameworks like Express or Fastify.

    Use cases:
    • Custom routing or middleware
    • Integrating with existing backend logic
    • Serving dynamic content or APIs not handled via pages/api
    Note: Using a custom server disables automatic static optimization and edge functions. Vercel does not support custom servers.
  • use Express or Fastify with Next.js?
    Example with Express: 
    // server.js
const express = require('express');
const next = require('next');

const app = next({ dev: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' });
const handle = app.getRequestHandler();

app.prepare().then(() => {
const server = express();

server.get('/custom', (req, res) => {
  return res.send('Custom route');
});

server.all('*', (req, res) => {
  return handle(req, res);
});

server.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log('> Ready on http://localhost:3000');
});
});
    Example with Fastify: 
    // server.js
const next = require('next');
const fastify = require('fastify')();

const app = next({ dev: true });
const handle = app.getRequestHandler();

app.prepare().then(() => {
fastify.get('/custom', (req, reply) => {
  reply.send('Custom Fastify route');
});

fastify.all('/*', (req, reply) => {
  handle(req.raw, reply.raw).then(() => {
    reply.sent = true;
  });
});

fastify.listen({ port: 3000 }, () => {
  console.log('> Ready on http://localhost:3000');
});
});
  • Next.js Error Pages, GitHub Actions, and Deployment
  • Can you customize the 404 and 500 error pages?
    Yes, Next.js allows full customization of:
    • 404.js – for "Page Not Found" errors
    • 500.js – for internal server errors (SSR failures)
    Example for pages/404.js: 
    export default function Custom404() {
return <h1>404 - Page Not Found</h1>;
}
    Example for pages/500.js: 
    export default function Custom500() {
return <h1>500 - Server-side Error</h1>;
}
  • purpose of _error.js?
    The file pages/_error.js is used to customize error handling for both client-side and server-side rendering. It is only used in the **Pages Router** (not App Router).
    • Handles 404, 500, and other HTTP errors
    • Can access the error object and customize UI or log errors
    Example: 
    function Error({ statusCode }) {
return (
  <p>
    {statusCode
      ? `An error ${statusCode} occurred on server`
      : 'An error occurred on client'}
  </p>
);
}

Error.getInitialProps = ({ res, err }) => {
const statusCode = res ? res.statusCode : err ? err.statusCode : 404;
return { statusCode };
};

export default Error;
  • use GitHub Actions with Next.js?
    GitHub Actions can build, test, and deploy your Next.js app automatically.

    Example workflow: .github/workflows/deploy.yml 
    name: Deploy Next.js

on:
push:
  branches: [main]

jobs:
build:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest

  steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v3
  - uses: actions/setup-node@v3
    with:
      node-version: 18

  - run: npm install
  - run: npm run build
  - run: npm run export # for static export
    You can also add deployment steps for platforms like Vercel, S3, or Netlify CLI.
  • deploy a Next.js app to AWS, Netlify, or Heroku?
    • ✅ AWS (S3 + CloudFront):
      • Run next export to generate static files
      • Upload out/ directory to S3
      • Serve via CloudFront for CDN performance
    • ✅ Netlify:
      • Install plugin: @netlify/plugin-nextjs
      • Deploy via GitHub or CLI
      • No need to export – full support for SSR/ISR
    • ✅ Heroku:
      • Create Procfile: web: next start
      • Set NODE_ENV=production
      • Use heroku buildpacks:add heroku/nodejs
      • Push to Heroku via Git
  • Next.js Optimization and Testing Questions and Answers
  • tree-shaking?
    Tree-shaking is a technique used during the JavaScript bundling process to remove unused code (also called "dead code").

    Next.js (via Webpack or Turbopack) automatically tree-shakes ES6 modules during the build to reduce the final bundle size.

    ✅ Tip: Use ES module syntax (import { something } from 'library') instead of require to ensure tree-shaking works.
  • reduce bundle size in Next.js?
    Several strategies help reduce bundle size in a Next.js app:
    • Use dynamic imports with next/dynamic for large components or libraries
    • Enable modular imports (e.g., import Button from 'antd/lib/button')
    • Remove unused dependencies and dead code
    • Split third-party code using dynamic()
    • Use analyze plugin to visualize bundle size: 
      npm install @next/bundle-analyzer
// next.config.js
const withBundleAnalyzer = require('@next/bundle-analyzer')({ enabled: true });
module.exports = withBundleAnalyzer({});
    • Tree-shake utility libraries like lodash using lodash-es
  • best way to unit test pages and API routes?
    For unit testing in Next.js, the best practices include:
    • Pages and Components: Use Jest with React Testing Library
    • API Routes: Use Jest to test handlers directly by mocking req and res objects
    • Setup: 
      npm install --save-dev jest @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom
    Example test for a component: 
    // __tests__/Home.test.tsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import Home from '../pages/index';

test('renders home page', () => {
render(<Home />);
expect(screen.getByText('Welcome')).toBeInTheDocument();
});
    Example test for an API route: 
    // __tests__/api/hello.test.ts
import handler from '../../pages/api/hello';

test('returns hello response', async () => {
const req = {};
const res = {
  status: jest.fn().mockReturnThis(),
  json: jest.fn()
};

await handler(req, res);
expect(res.status).toHaveBeenCalledWith(200);
expect(res.json).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ name: 'John Doe' });
});
  • mock getStaticProps in tests?
    You can mock getStaticProps using Jest by isolating it from the page or mocking it directly in your tests.

    Example of mocking getStaticProps: 
    jest.mock('../pages/index', () => {
const original = jest.requireActual('../pages/index');
return {
  __esModule: true,
  ...original,
  getStaticProps: jest.fn(() => ({
    props: { title: 'Mocked Title' },
  })),
};
});
    Or test it directly: 
    import { getStaticProps } from '../pages/index';

test('getStaticProps returns expected data', async () => {
const response = await getStaticProps();
expect(response).toEqual({
  props: { title: 'Expected Title' }
});
});
    ✅ Tip: Place `getStaticProps` in a separate file (e.g., `lib/data.ts`) for easier mocking and unit testing.
  • Next.js CMS Integration, GraphQL Support, and Static Export
  • connect a CMS (e.g., Strapi, Contentful) with Next.js?
    You can connect any headless CMS by fetching data from its REST or GraphQL API during build or runtime.

    Example with REST API (e.g., Strapi in getStaticProps): 
    export async function getStaticProps() {
const res = await fetch('https://cms.example.com/posts');
const posts = await res.json();

return {
  props: { posts },
  revalidate: 10
};
}
    Example with Contentful (using official SDK): 
    import { createClient } from 'contentful';

const client = createClient({
space: process.env.CONTENTFUL_SPACE_ID,
accessToken: process.env.CONTENTFUL_ACCESS_TOKEN
});

export async function getStaticProps() {
const entries = await client.getEntries({ content_type: 'blogPost' });

return {
  props: { posts: entries.items }
};
}
  • Can you use GraphQL with Next.js?
    Yes, you can integrate GraphQL in both client and server parts of a Next.js app. Common tools include:
    • graphql-request – Lightweight GraphQL client for server-side fetching
    • @apollo/client – Full-featured client for browser and SSR support
    Example using graphql-request in getStaticProps: 
    import { request, gql } from 'graphql-request';

export async function getStaticProps() {
const query = gql`
  {
    posts {
      id
      title
    }
  }
`;

const data = await request('https://api.example.com/graphql', query);
return {
  props: { posts: data.posts }
};
}
  • export a fully static Next.js site?
    To export a static site, use the next export command. This works only with **Static Site Generation (SSG)** – no SSR or API routes.

    Steps:
    • Ensure all pages use getStaticProps or are purely static
    • Set output: 'export' in next.config.js (Next.js 13+)
    • Run: 
      npm run build
npm run export
    • Static files will be in the out/ directory, ready to deploy to S3, GitHub Pages, etc.
  • limitations of static export?
    Static export has several limitations:
    • ❌ No support for getServerSideProps or API routes
    • ❌ No server-side rendering or runtime logic
    • ❌ No dynamic routes unless all paths are known at build time via getStaticPaths
    • ✅ Works well only for purely static content (e.g., blogs, documentation)
    • ✅ Cannot use incremental static regeneration (ISR)
    It’s ideal for JAMstack-style deployments but not suitable for highly dynamic apps.
  • Next.js Routing Hooks and Navigation Methods
  • use the new useRouter and usePathname hooks?
    In the **App Router** (Next.js 13+), routing has been split into separate, focused hooks:
    • useRouter is available in the **Pages Router** and was used to access pathname, query, and push/replace functions.
    • In the **App Router**, you now use more specific hooks:
      • usePathname() – returns the current URL path (string)
      • useSearchParams() – returns a URLSearchParams object
      • useRouter() – from next/navigation, used for navigation

    Example: 
    'use client';

import { usePathname, useSearchParams, useRouter } from 'next/navigation';

export default function MyComponent() {
const pathname = usePathname();
const searchParams = useSearchParams();
const router = useRouter();

const handleClick = () => {
  router.push('/about');
};

return (
  <div>
    <p>Path: {pathname}</p>
    <button onClick={handleClick}>Go to About</button>
  </div>
);
}
  • React difference between next/link and next/navigation?
    • next/link:
      • Used to create clickable links in JSX
      • Preloads pages in the background for fast transitions
      • Syntax is declarative
      • Used like: 
        import Link from 'next/link';

<Link href="/about">About</Link>
    • next/navigation:
      • Programmatic navigation using useRouter() hook
      • Useful inside event handlers, conditions, etc.
      • Syntax is imperative
      • Example: 
        'use client';
import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation';

const router = useRouter();
router.push('/about');
    ✅ Use next/link for links in the UI
    ✅ Use next/navigation for actions, redirects, or conditional routing
  • differences between Pages Router and App Router?
    The Pages Router is the traditional routing method in Next.js, where each file inside the pages/ directory automatically becomes a route. The App Router, introduced in Next.js 13, uses the app/ directory and enables a more flexible and powerful routing system. Key differences:
    • Pages Router uses file-based routing with React components.
    • App Router introduces layouts, templates, and nested routing using React Server Components.
    • App Router supports advanced features like loading and error UI, route groups, and partial rendering.
    • Pages Router supports only Client Components, while App Router supports both Client and Server Components.
  • a Server Component in Next.js 13+?
    A Server Component is a React component that runs only on the server. It can fetch data directly from the database or APIs without sending any extra JavaScript to the browser. Benefits include:
    • Improved performance due to reduced JavaScript bundle size.
    • Better security since sensitive logic stays on the server.
    • No client-side hydration required.
    Server Components are the default in the App Router and help deliver faster and more scalable applications.
  • How do Client and Server Components interact?
    Client and Server Components interact by allowing Server Components to render Client Components, but not the other way around. This enables the following:
    • Server Components fetch data and pass it as props to Client Components.
    • Client Components handle interactivity like click events and local state.
    • Server Components can include multiple Client Components as children, but Client Components cannot include Server Components.
    • To mark a component as Client, use the "use client" directive at the top of the file.
  • limitations of Server Components?
    Server Components in Next.js come with several limitations because they are rendered on the server and do not include client-side interactivity. Key limitations include:
    • They cannot use React state or lifecycle hooks like useState or useEffect.
    • They cannot access browser-specific APIs like window or document.
    • They cannot respond to user interactions (e.g., onClick) directly.
    • They cannot import client-only libraries such as charting or animation libraries.
    • They must only render other Server Components or Client Components marked with "use client".
    Server Components are ideal for static content, data fetching, and layout rendering, but not for interactive UI elements.
  • How does hydration work in Next.js?
    Hydration in Next.js is the process of attaching event listeners and restoring interactivity on the client side after the initial HTML is rendered by the server. This allows React to take over the static HTML and make it dynamic. Key points:
    • The server sends pre-rendered HTML to the browser for fast initial load.
    • React then loads the JavaScript bundle and reuses the static content to attach interactivity.
    • This process is called "hydration", and it's essential for seamless transitions and interactive behavior.
    • Hydration is only necessary for Client Components, as Server Components do not include interactivity.
  • use the use client directive?
    The "use client" directive is used at the top of a React component file in Next.js to mark it as a Client Component. This allows the component to use browser features and interactivity. Usage guidelines:
    • Add "use client" as the first line in the component file.
    • Only Client Components can use hooks like useState, useEffect, and event handlers.
    • Client Components can import other Client Components but not Server Components.
    • Use "use client" only when necessary to keep the JavaScript bundle size small.
    This directive helps Next.js optimize performance by separating static content from interactive parts.
  • pass data from Server to Client Components?
    In Next.js, you can pass data from Server Components to Client Components using props. Server Components can fetch data on the server and then render Client Components by passing the fetched data as props. This approach allows you to separate data fetching logic from interactive UI logic while maintaining performance and scalability.
    • Fetch data inside a Server Component using async/await or fetch.
    • Render a Client Component and pass the data as a prop.
    • The Client Component receives the data and can use it normally with hooks and events.
  • How are layouts different in App Router?
    In the App Router of Next.js 13+, layouts are persistent UI wrappers defined using a special layout.js file in each route segment. They differ from traditional layouts because:
    • They remain mounted between route changes, which preserves state and improves performance.
    • They support nested and shared layouts across the route hierarchy.
    • You can define multiple layouts at different route levels (e.g., dashboard, admin).
    • They can include both Server and Client Components.
    This new layout model provides better flexibility and control over application structure and rendering.
  • parallel routes?
    Parallel routes in Next.js 13+ allow you to render multiple pages or components side-by-side within a single layout. This is useful for dashboards, tabbed views, or modals. Instead of a single default route, you define multiple route slots using the @ symbol in the folder name.
    • Each slot acts like an independent sub-route.
    • You can render them concurrently within the same layout.
    • Useful for scenarios like rendering a sidebar and main content at the same time.
    Parallel routes improve UX by allowing simultaneous rendering of independent parts of a page.
  • implement intercepting routes?
    Intercepting routes in Next.js allow you to override the default navigation behavior and show a different page in a specific layout, like a modal on top of a previous page. This is implemented using the (.) folder naming convention.
    • Create a folder with (.) to define an intercepting route.
    • Use it to display content like modals or drawers without leaving the current page.
    • This allows partial route changes and preserves background state.
    Intercepting routes are useful for creating smooth and non-disruptive UI experiences, such as modal previews or side panels.
  • How does Next.js handle nested routing in the App Router?
    In Next.js App Router, nested routing is handled by organizing folders inside the app/ directory to represent route segments. Each folder corresponds to a path, and nested folders define nested routes. You can use layout.js files to persist layout components across nested routes.
    • Each folder inside app/ becomes a route segment (e.g., app/dashboard/settings becomes /dashboard/settings).
    • layout.js defines shared UI (like sidebars or headers) for nested routes.
    • page.js inside each segment defines the content of that route.
    Nested routing allows building complex hierarchies of pages with shared UI and consistent structure.
  • dynamic segments and how do they work in app/?
    Dynamic segments in Next.js App Router allow you to create routes with variable parameters by using square brackets in folder names. These segments are resolved at runtime based on the URL.
    • Create a folder like [id] inside app/ to match dynamic parts of the URL (e.g., app/products/[id] matches /products/123).
    • Inside the page or layout file, use params in server functions (like generateMetadata or Page) to access the dynamic value.
    • Supports nested dynamic segments (e.g., app/blog/[slug]/comments/[commentId]).
    Dynamic segments allow you to build dynamic pages such as product details, user profiles, or blog posts with clean URLs.
  • implement modal routes?
    Modal routes in Next.js App Router are implemented using intercepting routes. This technique allows you to show modals over an existing page without fully navigating away from the background route.
    • Create a folder named with parentheses like (modals) to define modal content.
    • Use @ to create parallel routes (e.g., @modal) that render both background and modal content simultaneously.
    • The modal route can be triggered using navigation and rendered within the existing layout while the background remains intact.
    This approach provides a smooth user experience by keeping the current view visible while displaying additional content in a modal overlay.
  • How does usePathname() differ from useRouter()?
    In Next.js App Router, both usePathname() and useRouter() are React hooks used for accessing routing information, but they serve different purposes:
    • usePathname() returns the current URL path as a string. It is useful when you just need to read the pathname (e.g., to highlight active links).
    • useRouter() provides more comprehensive navigation control, including functions like push(), replace(), and back() to programmatically navigate between routes.
    usePathname() is lightweight and read-only, while useRouter() is more powerful for handling dynamic navigation in client components.
  • How does redirect() and notFound() work in App Router?
    In Next.js App Router, redirect() and notFound() are functions used for server-side navigation control inside Server Components, Layouts, and Route Handlers:
    • redirect(url): Immediately sends a redirect response to the client, navigating to the specified URL. It’s commonly used in server actions or loaders when conditional logic is met (e.g., unauthenticated access).
    • notFound(): Triggers Next.js’s built-in 404 page. It is used when the requested content doesn’t exist or access is denied.
    These functions work only in the server layer and replace client-side hooks like useRouter().push() in traditional navigation logic.
  • new fetch() caching behavior in Next.js?
    In the App Router of Next.js, the fetch() function is enhanced with built-in caching for improved performance. By default, fetch requests are cached on the server and reused between requests when possible. This behavior allows:
    • Automatic caching of GET requests.
    • Reusability across requests in the same session.
    • Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) support using revalidate options.
    You can customize caching using options like cache, next.revalidate, and next.tags in the fetch config.
  • disable caching for a particular request?
    To disable caching for a specific fetch request in Next.js, use the cache: "no-store" option. This ensures the request always fetches fresh data from the server:
    • Pass it like this: fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" })
    • Useful for real-time data like dashboards, logs, or admin panels.
    This disables Next.js's automatic request caching for that fetch call.
  • revalidate data using revalidatePath() and revalidateTag()?
    In Next.js, revalidatePath() and revalidateTag() are used to manually trigger regeneration of cached data for specific paths or tags. These functions are typically called in Server Actions or Route Handlers:
    • revalidatePath('/dashboard'): Revalidates all cached fetches associated with that path.
    • revalidateTag('user-data'): Revalidates all fetch calls that were tagged with next: { tags: ['user-data'] }.
    • They allow cache to be updated manually when a mutation occurs (e.g., form submission, data update).
    These functions give developers fine-grained control over incremental data refreshing in Next.js applications.
  • cache tags in Next.js?
    Cache tags in Next.js are custom labels you can assign to fetch requests in Server Components to manage and invalidate cached data precisely. These tags allow you to group cached responses and later revalidate them selectively using revalidateTag().
    • Tags are assigned using the next: { tags: ['tag-name'] } option in fetch.
    • You can assign the same tag to multiple fetch calls.
    • When you call revalidateTag('tag-name'), all data with that tag is refreshed.
    • This gives you control over cache updates after mutations without needing full page revalidation.
    Cache tags are useful for complex apps where data needs to stay fresh but without over-fetching.
  • fetch data conditionally in a Server Component?
    In Server Components, you can conditionally fetch data based on props, context, or logic before rendering. Since Server Components run only on the server, you can use async/await directly and check conditions before calling fetch.
    • Use if statements to skip unnecessary requests.
    • Fetch different endpoints based on props (e.g., user roles or route params).
    • You can return early if conditions aren't met, such as rendering a message or null.
    • Fetch results are then passed to child components as props, including Client Components.
    Conditional fetching helps optimize performance and ensures components render only the necessary data for the current context.
  • generate dynamic metadata in the App Router?
    In the App Router of Next.js, dynamic metadata is generated using the generateMetadata() function in a page.js or layout.js file. This function runs on the server and allows you to generate metadata based on dynamic content such as route parameters or fetched data.
    • Create an async generateMetadata() function and export it from your page or layout file.
    • Use params to access dynamic segments of the URL.
    • Fetch necessary data inside this function and return metadata like title, description, etc.
    This ensures each page has unique SEO-optimized metadata.
  • generateMetadata() function?
    The generateMetadata() function in Next.js App Router is a special server-only function used to define page-specific metadata. It replaces the older Head component approach from the Pages Router.
    • It runs before the page is rendered and can include async logic like API calls or database queries.
    • It returns an object with metadata fields like title, description, robots, openGraph, and twitter.
    • Supports dynamic metadata for each route or slug using params.
    It allows for better SEO and social media optimization by customizing page metadata dynamically.
  • set OG (Open Graph) and Twitter metadata?
    You can define Open Graph and Twitter metadata inside the generateMetadata() function using the openGraph and twitter properties in the returned object.
    • openGraph includes properties like title, description, images, url, and siteName.
    • twitter includes card, title, description, images, and creator.
    • These metadata tags are used by social platforms like Facebook and Twitter to display rich previews when your page is shared.
    This structured metadata enhances link previews and boosts social media engagement.
  • integrate structured data (JSON-LD)?
    To integrate structured data using JSON-LD in Next.js, you embed a script tag containing JSON-LD inside a Client Component or the <head> of a page. This helps search engines better understand your content.
    • Create a JavaScript object with your structured data (e.g., type Article, Product, FAQ).
    • Render a script tag with type="application/ld+json" inside your component.
    • Use dangerouslySetInnerHTML to inject the JSON string into the script tag.
    • This is best done inside a Client Component or in a custom <Head> block using next/head.
    JSON-LD structured data improves SEO by enabling enhanced search features like rich snippets, FAQs, and breadcrumbs.
  • implement custom robots.txt and sitemap.xml?
    In Next.js, custom robots.txt and sitemap.xml can be implemented in the app/ or pages/ directory using API routes or static file generation:
    • robots.txt:
      • Create app/robots.txt/route.js (App Router) or pages/api/robots.txt.js (Pages Router).
      • Return plain text content using Content-Type: text/plain.
    • sitemap.xml:
      • Generate dynamically using route.js in app/sitemap.xml.
      • Include all public URLs with optional last modified dates.
    • Alternatively, you can place static files directly in the public/ directory (e.g., public/robots.txt and public/sitemap.xml).
    This ensures proper crawling by search engines and improves site discoverability.
  • How does middleware help in route protection?
    Middleware in Next.js runs before a request reaches a route or page. It helps protect routes by intercepting requests and redirecting users based on conditions like authentication or role checks.
    • Placed in the root middleware.js file or inside the app/ directory.
    • Executes on the Edge runtime and allows modifying request/response headers, rewriting, or redirecting.
    • Use it to check cookies, tokens, or session headers to protect routes without loading full page code.
    Middleware is ideal for global route protection, tenant-based routing, or enforcing locale and device checks.
  • implement session-based auth in Next.js?
    Session-based authentication in Next.js can be implemented using cookies to store session tokens. Common steps include:
    • Authenticate the user and create a signed JWT or session token on the server.
    • Store the token in a secure, HTTP-only cookie.
    • Use middleware or server components to read and verify the token from the cookie for each request.
    • Protect routes by checking if a valid session exists.
    • Use libraries like iron-session or cookie to simplify session handling.
    This approach keeps sensitive tokens on the server side and works well with SSR and API routes.
  • use NextAuth.js with Server Components?
    NextAuth.js integrates with Server Components in Next.js App Router using the getServerSession() method. This enables secure access to user data inside Server Components and Layouts.
    • Configure NextAuth with providers (like GitHub, Google) in app/api/auth/[...nextauth]/route.js.
    • In any Server Component or layout, call getServerSession(authOptions) to retrieve the session.
    • Conditionally render UI based on whether the session exists or not.
    • Combine with middleware to restrict routes based on authentication status.
    This provides a secure and SSR-compatible way to manage authentication in modern Next.js apps.
  • protect dynamic routes from unauthorized access?
    To protect dynamic routes in Next.js, especially in the App Router, you can use a combination of middleware and Server Components to validate user sessions or tokens before rendering content.
    • Use middleware.js to intercept all route requests and check authentication status using cookies or headers.
    • Redirect users to a login page if they are not authenticated.
    • Inside dynamic page.js files, use getServerSession() or token validation to verify access.
    • Render a 401 error, a custom message, or redirect unauthorized users.
    This ensures users cannot access routes like /dashboard/[id] unless properly authenticated.
  • handle role-based access control (RBAC)?
    Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) in Next.js is implemented by assigning roles to users (e.g., admin, editor, viewer) and restricting content or routes based on those roles.
    • Store the user's role in their session or JWT token.
    • Use middleware.js or getServerSession() to read the role and conditionally allow access.
    • Render different UI or block access based on role inside Server Components or Client Components.
    • Protect admin routes or dashboards by validating the user's role server-side before rendering.
    RBAC helps ensure that users only access the resources and actions they’re authorized to use, improving both security and UX.
  • test Server Components?
    Server Components in Next.js can be tested using testing libraries like React Testing Library and Jest. Since they are server-only, you test them by rendering the component with mock props and checking the returned HTML output.
    • Use @testing-library/react with Node.js environment or render-to-string tools.
    • Call the async Server Component and wait for the resolved JSX.
    • Use screen.getByText() or snapshot testing to verify the content.
    • Ensure that mock data or props are passed properly for isolated tests.
    Server Components are typically tested by asserting their static output and checking conditional rendering based on server logic.
  • mock fetch in Server Components?
    To mock fetch in Server Components, you can use jest.mock() or override the global fetch in your test file. Since fetch runs on the server in these components, mocking is important for unit tests.
    • Use global.fetch = jest.fn() to override the fetch behavior before rendering the component.
    • Return mock responses using Promise.resolve({ json: () => ... }).
    • Clean up and restore the fetch mock after each test using afterEach().
    • Mocking enables you to test how your component behaves with different data without making actual HTTP requests.
    This method allows you to simulate server-side data fetching within isolated test cases.
  • test generateMetadata()?
    The generateMetadata() function in Next.js App Router is a server-only export used to provide dynamic metadata. You can test it by importing the function and calling it directly with mock params or props.
    • Import the generateMetadata function in your test file.
    • Pass mock route parameters or fetch responses as inputs.
    • Assert the returned metadata object contains expected title, description, or openGraph fields.
    • Mock any internal fetch or database calls used inside the function.
    Testing generateMetadata() ensures SEO-relevant content is generated properly for dynamic pages like blogs or product details.
  • write integration tests with Playwright or Cypress?
    Integration tests with Playwright or Cypress are used to simulate real user interactions and validate how components, pages, and routing behave together in a Next.js application.
    • Playwright is a powerful tool for E2E tests with cross-browser support. Use page.goto(), page.click(), and page.locator() to test navigation, forms, and modal rendering.
    • Cypress runs directly in the browser and provides a developer-friendly UI. Use cy.visit(), cy.get(), and cy.contains() for interaction testing.
    • Test full page navigation in the App Router, such as loading nested routes, server components, and modals.
    • Mock network responses or test against a real dev server using npm run dev and a base URL.
    • Use CI/CD tools to run Playwright/Cypress on pull requests for regression testing.
    These tools validate the behavior of the full stack (routing, layout, server/client interaction), ensuring the app works as expected from a user’s perspective.
  • best practices for unit testing in App Router?
    Best practices for unit testing in the App Router focus on testing individual components and functions, including both Client and Server Components.
    • Use Jest with @testing-library/react for rendering and querying components.
    • Mock fetch(), getServerSession(), and next/navigation for isolated testing.
    • Test Server Components by calling the component function and asserting on the returned JSX.
    • For Client Components, test interactivity using fireEvent or userEvent.
    • Group tests by file or feature and maintain clear test descriptions.
    • Use snapshot testing selectively to avoid brittle tests.
    • Mock dynamic segments and metadata functions using dummy params and responses.
    These practices help you confidently test the modern routing and rendering features of Next.js 13+ with maintainable and reliable tests.
  • How does next.config.js control routing and output?
    The next.config.js file in Next.js is used to customize routing behavior and control how your application is built and served. It allows developers to configure rewrites, redirects, base paths, and output strategies.
    • rewrites map incoming request paths to different destination paths without changing the URL in the browser.
    • redirects perform client- or server-side redirects based on specific conditions.
    • basePath sets a subdirectory as the root of the application (e.g., /dashboard).
    • trailingSlash determines whether URLs should end with a slash.
    • output specifies whether the build is for static export or a standalone Node.js server.
    These options give you fine-grained control over route handling, deployment behavior, and the output format of your app.
  • output: export vs output: standalone?
    The output setting in next.config.js controls how Next.js builds your project. The two common options are:
    • output: "export": Generates a fully static version of your site with HTML and assets. No server is required. Used for static hosting like GitHub Pages or S3.
    • output: "standalone": Builds a minimal production-ready Node.js app with all required files in the .next/standalone directory. Ideal for serverless or containerized deployments.
    Use export when your app has no server-side logic, and standalone when deploying dynamic routes or server-rendered pages.
  • enable experimental features in Next.js?
    Next.js allows developers to opt into experimental features by using the experimental field in next.config.js. This enables access to upcoming or unstable features.
    • Add an experimental object in your config file with feature flags as keys.
    • Common flags include:
      • serverActions: Enable Server Actions support.
      • turbopack: Enable the new Rust-based bundler.
      • appDir: Enable the App Router features (enabled by default in latest versions).
    • These features are not guaranteed to be stable and may change in future releases.
    Use experimental flags cautiously in production and stay updated with release notes and changelogs.
  • modularizeImports setting?
    The modularizeImports setting in next.config.js allows you to automatically rewrite imports to reduce bundle size by enabling tree-shaking for libraries that don't support it well by default.
    • It transforms full imports into per-module imports (e.g., import { Button } from "ui-lib" → import Button from "ui-lib/Button").
    • This improves performance by including only the components you use instead of the entire library.
    • Commonly used for libraries like lodash, date-fns, or large UI kits like Material UI.
    • You define a map of modules to rewrite under modularizeImports in next.config.js.
    It's a powerful optimization tool for large projects with many third-party libraries.
  • reduce bundle size in large Next.js projects?
    To reduce bundle size in large Next.js projects, use a combination of code splitting, optimized imports, and caching strategies:
    • Use dynamic imports to load components only when needed.
    • Enable modularizeImports to avoid full-package imports.
    • Tree-shake unused code by using modern libraries and avoiding default imports from large packages.
    • Use Server Components to move non-interactive logic to the server.
    • Analyze the bundle with next build && next export && npx next-bundle-analyzer.
    • Avoid large images and fonts directly in your bundle — use CDN and lazy loading instead.
    • Remove unnecessary polyfills and console logs in production.
    These strategies help maintain fast performance and reduce load times for end users.
  • Flight and how does it optimize rendering?
    Flight is the underlying protocol used by React Server Components (RSC) in Next.js to send component tree information from the server to the client. Instead of sending fully rendered HTML, Flight sends a lightweight representation of the component structure.
    • Flight serializes component payloads from the server and transmits them to the browser efficiently.
    • Client receives only what it needs for hydration or interactivity, reducing bandwidth.
    • This model avoids sending duplicate JavaScript and accelerates time-to-interactive.
    • It enables partial rendering on the server and seamless merging with interactive components on the client.
    Flight improves performance by allowing components to render on the server without forcing full hydration or bundling all logic to the client.
  • How does React Server Components improve performance?
    React Server Components (RSC), supported in Next.js App Router, improve performance by shifting rendering responsibility to the server, reducing the amount of JavaScript sent to the client.
    • Non-interactive components are rendered entirely on the server — no client-side JS is needed.
    • Allows sending only minimal data to the client through the Flight protocol.
    • Fewer bundle sizes lead to faster load times and better Core Web Vitals.
    • Reduces the time-to-hydration by offloading logic to the server, especially useful for dashboards or data-heavy UIs.
    RSC enables a hybrid rendering model where only interactive components are hydrated on the client, dramatically reducing unnecessary computation.
  • use Lighthouse to audit a Next.js app?
    Lighthouse is a performance auditing tool built into Chrome DevTools and available via CLI or CI integration. It helps you measure your Next.js app's speed, SEO, accessibility, and PWA readiness.
    • Open Chrome, go to your deployed Next.js site, and open DevTools.
    • Go to the Lighthouse tab and run an audit for Mobile or Desktop.
    • It evaluates metrics like First Contentful Paint, Largest Contentful Paint, and Time to Interactive.
    • Use the results to identify bottlenecks like large images, unoptimized JS, or excessive layout shifts.
    • Apply suggestions like using next/image, lazy loading, and reducing third-party scripts.
    Lighthouse is essential for optimizing user experience and improving search engine rankings.
  • implement performance monitoring in production?
    Performance monitoring in a production Next.js app can be achieved using third-party tools that track web vitals, errors, and user behavior in real time.
    • Use tools like Sentry, LogRocket, Datadog, or New Relic to collect metrics and logs.
    • Leverage the reportWebVitals function in Next.js to capture metrics like CLS, FID, and LCP.
    • Send vitals to your monitoring service from pages/_app.js or app/layout.js.
    • Monitor errors, slow API routes, and unhandled promise rejections.
    • Set up alerts or dashboards to proactively detect regressions in performance.
    This helps maintain a healthy user experience and troubleshoot issues after deployment.
  • How does Next.js handle loading UI for streaming pages?
    Next.js handles loading UI for streaming pages in the App Router using the loading.js file, which is automatically shown while Server Components are being streamed.
    • Create a loading.js inside any route folder to display UI during the initial loading or while waiting for nested routes to render.
    • The file is only used with Server Components and React Suspense boundaries.
    • Supports partial rendering — parent layouts can stream first while child pages load in the background.
    • Improves user-perceived performance with visual feedback instead of a blank screen.
    This native support for streaming makes transitions smoother and helps users stay engaged during data fetches or dynamic rendering.
  • deploy Server Components to Vercel?
    Deploying Server Components to Vercel is seamless because Vercel is built to support the App Router and React Server Components out of the box.
    • Ensure your app uses the app/ directory structure with page.js, layout.js, and Server Components.
    • Push your code to GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket and connect your repository to Vercel.
    • Vercel automatically detects Next.js and builds your project using output: "standalone".
    • Server Components are deployed to Vercel’s serverless infrastructure and rendered dynamically.
    This allows for efficient rendering with built-in caching, streaming, and dynamic computation at scale.
  • How does app/ folder work with Vercel’s Edge Network?
    The app/ folder in Next.js leverages Vercel’s Edge Network by enabling Server Components, streaming, and caching at the edge.
    • Each route in the app/ folder can be dynamically rendered and streamed using React Server Components.
    • Vercel caches static and dynamic segments intelligently using headers and revalidation rules.
    • Layouts and loading.js files support edge streaming, reducing time-to-first-byte (TTFB).
    • When used with Edge Functions, parts of your app can run globally with minimal latency.
    This integration helps deliver fast, scalable experiences while maintaining flexibility in rendering and caching.
  • Edge Functions vs API Routes?
    Edge Functions and API Routes are two server-side execution models in Next.js, each optimized for different use cases.
    • API Routes are Node.js serverless functions that run in Vercel’s Lambda environment. They support full Node APIs but have higher latency.
    • Edge Functions run at Vercel's edge locations, closer to the user, with ultra-low latency and faster cold starts. They use the Web Fetch API (no full Node.js support).
    • Use Edge Functions for quick logic like auth, redirects, personalization, and geolocation.
    • Use API Routes for heavy computation, file handling, or Node.js packages like fs or crypto.
    Choosing between them depends on whether you need global speed (Edge) or full backend power (API Route).
  • deploy Next.js on AWS Lambda or Docker?
    You can deploy a Next.js app on AWS Lambda using the output: "standalone" option and tools like Serverless Framework, AWS SAM, or Lambda@Edge. Docker is also a popular option for containerized deployment.
    • AWS Lambda:
      • In next.config.js, set output: "standalone" to generate a minimal Node.js app.
      • Use server.js with aws-serverless-express or adapt your app to API Gateway + Lambda.
      • Deploy using Serverless Framework or Terraform with proper Lambda configuration.
    • Docker:
      • Create a Dockerfile using the standalone build.
      • Use node:alpine or node:slim images for smaller containers.
      • Expose port 3000 and use CMD ["node", "server.js"] to start the app.
    These methods allow you to run dynamic Next.js apps in flexible, scalable server environments.
  • handle cold starts and latency in SSR?
    Cold starts and latency in Server-Side Rendering (SSR) can affect performance, especially in serverless environments like AWS Lambda. To reduce these issues:
    • Use Edge Functions where possible for lower latency and faster start times.
    • Enable Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) to serve cached pages and reduce SSR hits.
    • Keep serverless functions warm with scheduled CloudWatch events or ping tools.
    • Optimize dependencies and reduce server payload to minimize startup time.
    • Cache responses at the CDN level (e.g., using CloudFront or Vercel’s edge network).
    • Use lazy loading and split large logic across components.
    These strategies improve responsiveness and reduce the performance hit caused by cold starts in server-rendered apps.
  • How does Next.js handle routing internally?
    Next.js uses a file-system based routing system where the folder and file structure under pages/ or app/ automatically becomes available as routes.
    • Each file inside pages/ becomes a route (e.g., pages/about.js → /about).
    • Dynamic routes are defined using brackets (e.g., pages/blog/[slug].js).
    • App Router uses layout.js, page.js, and route groups to define complex nested and parallel routing.
    • Under the hood, Next.js maps each request to a corresponding component using route matchers and handlers via its internal router.
    • Pre-fetching and client-side navigation are handled by the next/link and next/navigation modules.
    This abstraction makes routing declarative, predictable, and optimized for both SSR and static pages.
  • internals of static rendering pipeline?
    The static rendering pipeline in Next.js transforms your pages into HTML at build time to be served directly from a CDN.
    • During build, Next.js calls getStaticProps() (Pages Router) or renders Server Components with no dynamic data (App Router).
    • The HTML output is generated using React’s renderToStaticMarkup() or renderToReadableStream().
    • Each page’s static HTML and optional JSON data are written to the .next directory.
    • These assets are then deployed to CDN (e.g., Vercel Edge Network or S3) for instant delivery.
    • Next.js also generates a routing manifest and fallback files for ISR and dynamic routes.
    This pipeline ensures fast loading by pre-rendering HTML while still supporting dynamic updates via revalidation.
  • How does server-side rendering differ from traditional Node.js SSR?
    Server-side rendering (SSR) in Next.js improves on traditional Node.js SSR by automating routing, data fetching, caching, and performance optimizations.
    • Next.js SSR: Uses getServerSideProps() or Server Components to fetch data and render HTML on each request.
    • Includes built-in features like streaming, caching headers, and route-based code splitting.
    • Automatically integrates with React features like Suspense and Server Actions.
    • Traditional Node.js SSR: Requires manual setup with Express, ReactDOMServer, and route-to-component mapping.
