    • Less optimized for performance and lacks built-in support for static generation or edge deployment.
    Next.js abstracts complex SSR setup while enabling fine-grained control and modern rendering strategies.
  • How does ISR work under the hood?
    Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) in Next.js allows static pages to be updated after deployment without rebuilding the entire site.
    • At build time, static pages are generated and stored in the cache or CDN.
    • When a user requests a page, it is served from the static cache instantly.
    • If the page’s revalidation time has expired, Next.js triggers a background regeneration of that page.
    • The updated HTML replaces the previous version in the cache after the regeneration completes.
    • This is controlled using the revalidate option in getStaticProps (Pages Router) or route segment config (App Router).
    ISR combines the performance of static pages with the flexibility of server-rendered content, keeping sites fast and up-to-date.
  • How does Next.js manage concurrent rendering?
    Next.js uses React’s Concurrent Rendering capabilities, especially in the App Router, to optimize UI responsiveness and user experience.
    • Concurrent rendering allows React to interrupt, pause, or resume rendering work as needed.
    • It enables features like Suspense, lazy loading, streaming, and loading.js.
    • Next.js leverages this to stream Server Components, progressively rendering parts of the page.
    • Only Client Components with interactivity are hydrated on the browser side, improving performance.
    • Concurrent rendering avoids blocking the main thread and allows smooth transitions and updates even during complex operations.
    This leads to faster time-to-interactive, better perceived performance, and more fluid user interfaces.
  • implement Content Security Policy (CSP) in Next.js?
    You can implement a Content Security Policy (CSP) in Next.js using the headers() function in next.config.js to set secure HTTP headers for all pages.
    • Define the CSP string with rules for script-src, style-src, img-src, and other directives.
    • Use nonces or hashes to allow inline scripts or styles securely when needed.
    • Apply the CSP using Content-Security-Policy header for all routes.
    • Test your policy with browser dev tools and report-uri to log violations.
    • Use strict CSP rules to prevent unauthorized scripts from executing on your pages.
    CSP helps protect your Next.js application from XSS attacks by restricting the sources of content that can be loaded.
  • prevent XSS in SSR pages?
    Preventing Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in SSR pages involves sanitizing user-generated content and avoiding unsafe rendering methods.
    • Never render unescaped HTML using dangerouslySetInnerHTML unless the content is sanitized.
    • Use libraries like DOMPurify or sanitize-html to clean user input.
    • Escape variables by default in JSX — Next.js handles this automatically for standard rendering.
    • Set strict Content-Security-Policy headers to block inline scripts and third-party injections.
    • Validate and encode any user-generated content sent to the server or stored in the database.
    These steps protect your server-rendered pages from malicious script injection and content manipulation.
  • handle JWT securely in the browser and server?
    Secure handling of JWT (JSON Web Tokens) in Next.js involves proper storage, transmission, and verification.
    • Store JWTs in HttpOnly, Secure cookies to protect them from XSS access.
    • Avoid storing JWTs in localStorage or sessionStorage, which are accessible via JavaScript.
    • Use middleware or getServerSideProps to read and verify tokens server-side.
    • Implement short expiration times and rotate tokens using refresh tokens stored in cookies.
    • Use HTTPS to prevent token interception over the network.
    • Verify JWT signatures on the server using trusted algorithms like HS256 or RS256.
    This approach minimizes security risks while maintaining stateless authentication for your app.
  • some security best practices for public APIs?
    Securing public APIs is crucial to prevent misuse, abuse, and data breaches. Key best practices include:
    • Rate Limiting: Limit the number of API requests per IP or user to prevent abuse and DDoS attacks.
    • Authentication: Require API keys, OAuth tokens, or JWTs to validate the client identity.
    • Authorization: Ensure users can only access resources they are permitted to use.
    • Input Validation: Sanitize and validate all incoming data to prevent injection attacks (XSS, SQLi, etc.).
    • HTTPS Only: Serve your API over HTTPS to protect against man-in-the-middle attacks.
    • CORS Restrictions: Set proper CORS headers to control which domains can access your API.
    • Logging & Monitoring: Track access patterns, failures, and suspicious activity in real time.
    These practices help ensure your API remains stable, protected, and resilient against common threats.
  • secure environment variables and secrets?
    Securing environment variables and secrets ensures sensitive data like API keys, credentials, and tokens are not exposed or misused.
    • Use .env.local: Store secrets in local environment files that are gitignored and never committed.
    • Vercel / AWS Secrets Manager: Use cloud-based secret management services to store and access secrets securely.
    • Never expose secrets to the client: Only prefix public environment variables with NEXT_PUBLIC_. Server-only variables must stay private.
    • Restrict access: Set appropriate IAM or file permissions so only trusted systems can access the secrets.
    • Rotate keys regularly: Invalidate and replace secrets periodically to reduce the impact of potential leaks.
    • Audit usage: Track how and where secrets are accessed and used across your infrastructure.
    These precautions help protect your application from unauthorized access and data exposure.
  • some best practices for organizing a large Next.js project?
    Organizing a large Next.js project requires scalable folder structure, separation of concerns, and clear conventions.
    • Modular Structure: Use feature-based folders inside app/ or components/ (e.g., auth, dashboard, products).
    • Use Aliases: Configure tsconfig.json or jsconfig.json for import path aliases (e.g., @/components).
    • Group Logic: Keep API logic in lib/, hooks in hooks/, services in services/, and reusable components in ui/.
    • Layouts: Use nested layouts in the App Router to manage consistent UI like headers or sidebars.
    • Testing: Organize unit, integration, and e2e tests in __tests__/ folders near related code.
    A consistent, modular structure enhances team productivity and simplifies onboarding and maintenance.
  • structure a monorepo with multiple Next.js apps?
    A monorepo allows you to manage multiple Next.js apps and shared packages within one repository, using tools like TurboRepo or Nx.
    • Use a root directory structure like:
      • apps/web → main app
      • apps/admin → admin panel
      • packages/ui → shared components
      • packages/utils → shared utility functions
    • Define root-level tsconfig.json, eslint, and prettier config for consistency.
    • Use pnpm workspaces, Yarn workspaces, or npm workspaces to manage dependencies.
    • Use TurboRepo or Nx for task caching, dependency graph, and efficient CI builds.
    This setup allows scalable development of multiple apps with shared logic in one unified codebase.
  • integrate shared UI libraries in a monorepo?
    To integrate a shared UI library in a monorepo with multiple Next.js apps:
    • Create a packages/ui folder for your reusable components.
    • Use React, Tailwind CSS, or any design system to build generic UI components (e.g., Button, Card).
    • Export components using index.ts inside the package.
    • Ensure the UI package has its own tsconfig.json and package.json.
    • Import shared components in your apps via path aliases or workspace references (e.g., import { Button } from "ui").
    • Use transpilePackages in next.config.js to make Next.js transpile the UI package if it uses TypeScript or JSX.
    This promotes DRY principles and maintains a consistent design system across all applications.
  • some common design patterns used in Next.js architecture?
    Next.js projects can adopt several proven design patterns to improve scalability, maintainability, and performance:
    • Modular Architecture: Break the project into reusable, domain-specific modules (e.g., auth, dashboard, products).
    • Container-Presenter Pattern: Separate logic (container) from UI (presenter) components for better testability and reusability.
    • Layout Pattern: Use nested layout.js files in the App Router to manage persistent UI like headers or sidebars.
    • Hooks Pattern: Encapsulate logic in custom hooks (e.g., useAuth, useFetch, useCart).
    • Service Layer Pattern: Abstract API calls or business logic into dedicated service files in lib/ or services/.
    • Repository Pattern: Encapsulate data access logic (e.g., DB queries, API clients) for easier testing and future replacement.
    • Facade Pattern: Combine multiple APIs or components into a simpler interface, often used in shared services or SDKs.
    These patterns help organize large codebases and reduce coupling between components, making code more modular and testable.
  • apply SOLID principles in Next.js?
    The SOLID principles can be applied in a Next.js codebase to ensure clean, maintainable, and scalable architecture:
    • S – Single Responsibility: Each component, hook, or service should have one responsibility (e.g., LoginForm only handles login UI).
    • O – Open/Closed: Components and modules should be open to extension but closed to modification. Use props and composition instead of hardcoded logic.
    • L – Liskov Substitution: Ensure custom components and classes can be substituted without breaking functionality (e.g., extend a base button).
    • I – Interface Segregation: Keep components and services focused — avoid forcing unrelated props or APIs into one module.
    • D – Dependency Inversion: Depend on abstractions like services or hooks instead of hardcoded implementations (e.g., inject API clients or auth services).
    Applying these principles results in modular, extensible, and testable Next.js applications.
  • MongoDB data modeling?
    Designing and structuring documents, relationships, indexes, and validation rules based on real access patterns—even though MongoDB doesn't enforce a schema—to improve performance, consistency, and maintainability. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
  • difference between embedded and referenced models?
    Embedded models store related data within a single document (good for one-to-one or few-many relationships, faster reads, atomic updates). Referenced models store relations via IDs in separate collections (ideal for many-to-many, frequently changing data, avoiding document size limits). :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
  • When should you embed vs reference?
    Embed when data is accessed together and small. Reference when data is large, changes often, or used independently. Evaluate based on access patterns, data growth, and update frequency. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
  • model one-to-many or many-to-many relationships?
    For one-to-many: embed small arrays, or reference when large. For many-to-many: use references across collections, sometimes with junction/bridge collections or extended reference patterns. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}
  • common data modeling patterns and anti-patterns?
    Patterns: embedding for related reads, referencing for normalized data, bucket for time-series, polymorphic for varied types, extended references. Anti-patterns: oversized or deeply nested documents, unbounded arrays, excessive indexes, unneeded collections. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
  • Why does MongoDB still need schema design?
    Despite being schema-less, structure ensures consistency, aids validation, optimizes queries, supports ODMs, and controls growth. Tools like JSON Schema validation and modeling utilities enhance data quality. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}
  • visualize and document MongoDB schemas?
    Use ER-like diagrams via tools like Hackolade, Dataedo, DbSchema, or Moon Modeler. These tools infer nested structures and references, and can generate interactive HTML or PDF documentation. :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}
  • practical tips for schema design performance?
    Align schema with query patterns; embed when data co-occurs; index commonly queried fields; avoid huge docs; shard with appropriate keys; consider document growth via bucketing. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

  • Explain the Architecture of NestJS in detail. 
          
NestJS Architecture Overview

NestJS follows a layered and modular architecture inspired by Angular.
It is built on top of Node.js and typically uses Express or Fastify as the HTTP platform.

The architecture is designed to build scalable and maintainable backend applications.

--------------------------------------------------

Main Architectural Components

1. Modules
2. Controllers
3. Providers (Services)
4. Middleware
5. Guards
6. Pipes
7. Interceptors
8. Exception Filters

--------------------------------------------------

1. Modules

Modules are the fundamental building blocks of a NestJS application.
Every application has at least one module called the Root Module.

Modules organize the application into logical units.

Example:

@Module({
  imports: [],
  controllers: [UserController],
  providers: [UserService]
})
export class UserModule {}

Types of Modules:

Root Module
Feature Modules
Shared Modules
Dynamic Modules

Example Root Module:

@Module({
  imports: [UserModule, AuthModule]
})
export class AppModule {}

--------------------------------------------------

2. Controllers

Controllers handle incoming HTTP requests and return responses to the client.

They define API routes and delegate business logic to services.

Example:

@Controller('users')
export class UserController {

  constructor(private userService: UserService) {}

  @Get()
  getUsers() {
    return this.userService.findAll();
  }

  @Post()
  createUser() {
    return this.userService.createUser();
  }
}

--------------------------------------------------

3. Providers (Services)

Providers contain business logic.

They are injectable classes managed by NestJS Dependency Injection system.

Example:

@Injectable()
export class UserService {

  findAll() {
    return ["User1", "User2"];
  }

  createUser() {
    return "User Created";
  }
}

Advantages:

Loose coupling
Easy testing
Reusable logic

--------------------------------------------------

4. Middleware

Middleware functions execute before the request reaches the controller.

Common use cases:

Logging
Authentication
Body parsing
Request modification

Example:

@Injectable()
export class LoggerMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {

  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: Function) {
    console.log("Incoming Request");
    next();
  }
}

--------------------------------------------------

5. Guards

Guards determine whether a request should be handled or rejected.

Used mainly for authentication and authorization.

Example:

@Injectable()
export class AuthGuard implements CanActivate {

  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {

    const request = context.switchToHttp().getRequest();

    return request.headers.authorization === "valid-token";
  }
}

Usage:

@UseGuards(AuthGuard)
@Get()
getUsers() {
  return [];
}

--------------------------------------------------

6. Pipes

Pipes are used for data validation and transformation.

They run before the controller method executes.

Example:

@Get(':id')
getUser(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number) {
  return id;
}

Custom Pipe Example:

@Injectable()
export class ValidationPipe implements PipeTransform {

  transform(value: any) {

    if (!value) {
      throw new BadRequestException("Invalid Input");
    }

    return value;
  }
}

--------------------------------------------------

7. Interceptors

Interceptors allow you to intercept requests and responses.

Common use cases:

Logging
Response transformation
Caching
Performance monitoring

Example:

@Injectable()
export class LoggingInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {

  intercept(context: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler) {

    console.log("Before request");

    return next.handle();
  }
}

--------------------------------------------------

8. Exception Filters

Exception filters handle errors globally or locally.

They allow developers to customize error responses.

Example:

@Catch(HttpException)
export class HttpExceptionFilter implements ExceptionFilter {

  catch(exception: HttpException, host: ArgumentsHost) {

    const ctx = host.switchToHttp();
    const response = ctx.getResponse();

    response.status(500).json({
      message: exception.message
    });
  }
}

--------------------------------------------------

NestJS Request Lifecycle

Client Request
     ↓
Middleware
     ↓
Guards
     ↓
Interceptors (Before)
     ↓
Pipes
     ↓
Controller
     ↓
Service / Provider
     ↓
Database
     ↓
Interceptors (After)
     ↓
Exception Filters
     ↓
Response

--------------------------------------------------

Dependency Injection System

NestJS has a powerful Dependency Injection container.

It automatically creates and manages service instances.

Example:

constructor(private userService: UserService) {}

Benefits:

Loose coupling
Better testing
Clean architecture

--------------------------------------------------

Platform Layer

NestJS can run on multiple platforms:

Express (default)
Fastify (high performance)

Example:

const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, new FastifyAdapter());

--------------------------------------------------

Database Layer

NestJS integrates easily with databases:

TypeORM
Mongoose
Prisma
Sequelize

Example:

MongooseModule.forRoot("mongodb://localhost:27017/mydb")

--------------------------------------------------

Summary

NestJS architecture follows a modular layered design.

Client Request
     ↓
Controller
     ↓
Service
     ↓
Repository / Database

Supporting layers include:

Middleware
Guards
Pipes
Interceptors
Exception Filters

This architecture provides:

Scalability
Maintainability
Testability
Clean code structure

--------------------------------------------------

Interview Short Answer (25 LPA)

NestJS follows a modular architecture consisting of Modules, Controllers,
and Providers. It uses Dependency Injection and separates concerns through
middleware, guards, pipes, interceptors, and exception filters to build
scalable and maintainable backend applications.
  • Explain the architecture of NestJS. 
          
NestJS Architecture is inspired by Angular and follows a modular architecture.

Core Building Blocks:

1. Module
- The root structure of a NestJS application.
- Groups related controllers and providers.

Example:
@Module({
  imports: [],
  controllers: [UserController],
  providers: [UserService],
})
export class UserModule {}

2. Controller
- Handles incoming HTTP requests.
- Returns responses to the client.

Example:
@Controller('users')
export class UserController {
  constructor(private userService: UserService) {}

  @Get()
  getUsers() {
    return this.userService.findAll();
  }
}

3. Provider (Service)
- Contains business logic.
- Injectable via Dependency Injection.

@Injectable()
export class UserService {
  findAll() {
    return [];
  }
}

Architecture Flow:

Client Request
      ↓
Middleware
      ↓
Guards
      ↓
Interceptors (before)
      ↓
Pipes
      ↓
Controller
      ↓
Service / Provider
      ↓
Database
      ↓
Interceptors (after)
      ↓
Response

Benefits:
- Dependency Injection
- Highly scalable
- Modular structure
- Easy testing
  • What are Pipes in NestJS? Explain in detail. 
          
Pipes in NestJS are used to transform or validate incoming data before it reaches
the controller method.

They operate on the arguments being passed to a route handler and run just before
the controller logic is executed.

Main Purposes of Pipes:

1. Data Validation
Check if incoming data is correct.

2. Data Transformation
Convert incoming data into the required format.

Example:
Convert string "10" → number 10

--------------------------------------------------

Where Pipes Run in Request Lifecycle

Client Request
      ↓
Middleware
      ↓
Guards
      ↓
Interceptors (before)
      ↓
Pipes
      ↓
Controller
      ↓
Service
      ↓
Response

--------------------------------------------------

Built-in Pipes in NestJS

NestJS provides several built-in pipes:

ParseIntPipe
ParseBoolPipe
ParseUUIDPipe
ParseArrayPipe
ValidationPipe
DefaultValuePipe

Example:

@Get(':id')
getUser(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number) {
  return id;
}

Explanation:

If id = "10"
ParseIntPipe converts it into number 10.

If id = "abc"
NestJS throws an error automatically.

--------------------------------------------------

Example: ValidationPipe

ValidationPipe is commonly used with class-validator
to validate request body data.

DTO Example:

export class CreateUserDto {
  name: string;
  age: number;
}

Controller Example:

@Post()
createUser(@Body(new ValidationPipe()) body: CreateUserDto) {
  return body;
}

If invalid data is sent, NestJS automatically throws a validation error.

--------------------------------------------------

Creating Custom Pipe

You can create your own pipe by implementing PipeTransform.

Example:

@Injectable()
export class PositiveNumberPipe implements PipeTransform {

  transform(value: number) {

    if (value < 0) {
      throw new BadRequestException("Number must be positive");
    }

    return value;
  }
}

Usage:

@Get(':id')
getUser(@Param('id', PositiveNumberPipe) id: number) {
  return id;
}

--------------------------------------------------

Types of Pipes

Parameter-level Pipe
Applied to a specific parameter.

@Get(':id')
getUser(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number)

Method-level Pipe

@UsePipes(ValidationPipe)
@Post()
createUser()

Controller-level Pipe

@UsePipes(ValidationPipe)
@Controller('users')

Global Pipe

app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe());

--------------------------------------------------

Why Pipes Are Important

Validate input data
Transform request data
Improve security
Prevent invalid data reaching business logic
Keep controllers clean

--------------------------------------------------

Interview Short Answer

Pipes in NestJS are used to validate and transform incoming request data before
it reaches the controller. They help ensure that only valid and properly
formatted data is processed by the application.
  • What is JWT Token? (Short Interview Answer) 
          
JWT (JSON Web Token)

JWT is a compact and secure token used for authentication and authorization
between client and server.

It enables stateless authentication, meaning the server does not store
session data.

JWT Structure:

Header.Payload.Signature

Header
Contains token type and signing algorithm.

Payload
Contains user information (claims).

Signature
Used to verify that the token has not been modified.

Authentication Flow:

1. User logs in.
2. Server generates JWT token.
3. Client stores token.
4. Client sends token in request header.

Example:

Authorization: Bearer token_here

Server verifies token using secret key.

Interview One-Line Answer:

JWT is a stateless authentication token containing Header, Payload,
and Signature, used to securely verify user identity in APIs.
  • What is a JWT Token? Explain in detail. 
          
JWT (JSON Web Token)

JWT stands for JSON Web Token.  
It is a compact, secure way to transmit information between two parties as a JSON object.

JWT is commonly used for authentication and authorization in modern APIs.

Example Use Case:

1. User logs in
2. Server verifies credentials
3. Server generates JWT token
4. Client stores token
5. Client sends token with every request

--------------------------------------------------

JWT Structure

A JWT token has three parts separated by dots:

Header.Payload.Signature

Example:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9
.
eyJ1c2VySWQiOjEwLCJuYW1lIjoiSm9obiJ9
.
SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c

Structure:

HEADER
PAYLOAD
SIGNATURE

--------------------------------------------------

1. Header

The header contains metadata about the token.

Example:

{
  "alg": "HS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}

Explanation:

alg = Algorithm used to sign the token
typ = Token type (JWT)

After encoding (Base64):

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9

--------------------------------------------------

2. Payload

The payload contains the actual data (claims).

Claims are statements about the user.

Example:

{
  "userId": 10,
  "email": "john@email.com",
  "role": "admin"
}

Types of Claims:

Registered Claims
iss (issuer)
exp (expiration)
sub (subject)
aud (audience)

Public Claims
Custom fields defined by developers.

Private Claims
Custom claims used between two systems.

Encoded Payload Example:

eyJ1c2VySWQiOjEwLCJuYW1lIjoiSm9obiJ9

Important:

Payload is NOT encrypted.
It is only Base64 encoded.

--------------------------------------------------

3. Signature

Signature verifies that the token has not been modified.

Signature creation:

HMACSHA256(
  base64UrlEncode(header) + "." +
  base64UrlEncode(payload),
  secret
)

Example:

signature = HMACSHA256(
  header + "." + payload,
  secret_key
)

This prevents token tampering.

--------------------------------------------------

JWT Authentication Flow

Step 1: User Login

POST /login

User sends:

{
  "email": "john@email.com",
  "password": "123456"
}

--------------------------------------------------

Step 2: Server verifies credentials

If valid → server generates JWT token.

Example:

const token = jwt.sign(
  { userId: 10 },
  "secret_key",
  { expiresIn: "1h" }
);

--------------------------------------------------

Step 3: Client stores token

Usually stored in:

LocalStorage
SessionStorage
HTTP-only Cookie

--------------------------------------------------

Step 4: Client sends token

Every API request includes the token.

Example HTTP Header:

Authorization: Bearer token_here

--------------------------------------------------

Step 5: Server verifies token

Example:

const decoded = jwt.verify(token, "secret_key");

If valid → allow request.

--------------------------------------------------

Advantages of JWT

Stateless authentication
No session storage required
Scalable for microservices
Compact and portable
Works well with REST APIs

--------------------------------------------------

Disadvantages

Payload is visible (not encrypted)
Token cannot be revoked easily
Large payload increases token size

--------------------------------------------------

JWT vs Session Authentication

Session Authentication

Server stores session
Client sends session ID
Stateful system

JWT Authentication

Server does not store session
Client sends token each request
Stateless system

--------------------------------------------------

JWT Example in Node.js

Install library:

npm install jsonwebtoken

Generate token:

const jwt = require("jsonwebtoken");

const token = jwt.sign(
  { userId: 1 },
  "secret_key",
  { expiresIn: "1h" }
);

Verify token:

jwt.verify(token, "secret_key", (err, decoded) => {
  if (err) {
    console.log("Invalid token");
  } else {
    console.log(decoded);
  }
});

--------------------------------------------------

Interview Short Answer

JWT is a compact, URL-safe token used for authentication and authorization.
It consists of three parts: Header, Payload, and Signature. The server
generates the token after login and the client sends it with each request
for verification, enabling stateless authentication.
  • What are Pipes in NestJS?

@Injectable()

Apply Guard:

 ↓

 ↓

  • What are Interceptors in NestJS and where are they used? 
          
Interceptors allow you to intercept and modify requests or responses before
they reach the controller or before sending the response to the client.

1. Logging
2. Response transformation
3. Caching
4. Performance monitoring
5. Error handling

Execution Position:

Request Flow:
Middleware
   ↓
Guards
   ↓
Interceptors (before)
   ↓
Pipes
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Interceptors (after)
   ↓
Response

Example:

@Injectable()
export class LoggingInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {

  intercept(context: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler) {

    console.log("Before request");

    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap(() => console.log("After response"))
    );
  }
}

Apply interceptor:

@Get()
getUsers() {
  return [];
}

  • What are Exception Filters in NestJS? 
          
Exception Filters handle errors thrown in the application.

They allow customizing error responses.

Example:

@Catch(HttpException)
export class HttpExceptionFilter implements ExceptionFilter {

  catch(exception: HttpException, host: ArgumentsHost) {

    const ctx = host.switchToHttp();
    const response = ctx.getResponse();

    const status = exception.getStatus();

    response.status(status).json({
      statusCode: status,
      message: exception.message
    });
  }
}

Apply filter:

@UseFilters(HttpExceptionFilter)
@Get()
getUsers() {
  throw new HttpException("Unauthorized", 401);
}

- A new instance is created for every HTTP request.

  • How do you resolve circular dependency in NestJS? 
          
Circular dependency occurs when two services depend on each other.

Example Problem:

UserService → OrderService
OrderService → UserService

NestJS provides forwardRef() to solve this.

Example:

@Injectable()
export class UserService {

  constructor(
    @Inject(forwardRef(() => OrderService))
    private orderService: OrderService
  ) {}
}

@Module({
  providers: [UserService],
  imports: [forwardRef(() => OrderModule)]
})
export class UserModule {}

Explanation:

forwardRef() delays the resolution of dependency
until runtime.

Best Practice:

Avoid circular dependencies when possible by
refactoring business logic into separate services.

  • What is a RESTful API? 
          
RESTful API stands for Representational State Transfer API.

It is an architectural style used to build web services that communicate
over HTTP and follow REST principles.

A RESTful API allows clients (frontend, mobile apps) to interact with
server resources using standard HTTP methods.

Main HTTP Methods:

GET
Used to retrieve data.

POST
Used to create new resources.

PUT
Used to update existing resources.

DELETE
Used to remove resources.

Example API Endpoints:

GET /users
Fetch all users.

GET /users/10
Fetch user with ID 10.

POST /users
Create a new user.

PUT /users/10
Update user with ID 10.

DELETE /users/10
Delete user with ID 10.

REST Principles:

1. Client-Server Architecture
Frontend and backend are independent.

2. Stateless Communication
Each request contains all necessary information.

3. Resource-Based
Everything is treated as a resource (users, products, orders).

4. Uniform Interface
Standard HTTP methods are used.

Example JSON Response:

{
  "id": 10,
  "name": "John",
  "email": "john@email.com"
}

Advantages:

- Scalable
- Easy to understand
- Platform independent
- Widely used in web and mobile applications
  • What is the difference between Stateful API and Stateless API? 
          
Stateful API:

In a stateful API, the server stores information about the client session.
Each request depends on previous requests.

Example:
Traditional web applications with sessions.

Flow:

Client Login
Server stores session
Client sends session ID
Server retrieves session data

Example:

User logs in
Server stores session in memory or Redis
Next request uses session ID

Problems:

- Hard to scale
- Server must remember client state
- Session storage required


Stateless API:

In a stateless API, the server does NOT store any client session data.

Each request must contain all necessary information.

Example:
REST APIs with JWT authentication.

Flow:

Client Login
Server returns JWT token
Client sends token in every request

Example Request Header:

Authorization: Bearer token123

Advantages:

- Highly scalable
- Easy to distribute across servers
- No session storage needed


Comparison:

Stateful API

Server stores session
Requests depend on previous requests
Harder to scale
Example: Traditional session-based apps


Stateless API

Server does not store session
Each request is independent
Highly scalable
Example: RESTful APIs


Interview One-Line Answer:

Stateful API stores client session data on the server,
while Stateless API requires each request to contain
all the information needed to process it.

  • -------------- Kafka Question -----------------------

  • What is Apache Kafka? 
          
Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used to handle real-time data feeds.

It works as a high-throughput message broker between services. Applications can publish
messages to Kafka topics and other applications can consume those messages.

Kafka is widely used in microservices architecture, log aggregation, and real-time
data processing systems.

Key Features:
- High throughput
- Fault tolerant
- Horizontally scalable
- Persistent message storage

Example Use Case:
An e-commerce system where the Order Service publishes an "order-created" event.
Other services like Shipping Service, Notification Service, and Analytics Service
consume the same event from Kafka.
  • What are the main components of Kafka? 
          
Kafka architecture includes several core components:

Producer
Application that sends messages to Kafka.

Broker
Kafka server that stores messages and handles requests.

Topic
A category or feed name where messages are stored.

Partition
Topics are divided into partitions for scalability and parallel processing.

Consumer
Application that reads messages from Kafka topics.

Consumer Group
Multiple consumers that work together to process messages in parallel.
  • Explain Kafka message flow. 
          
Kafka Message Flow:

Producer → Topic → Partition → Broker → Consumer

Step 1:
Producer sends message to a Kafka topic.

Step 2:
Topic stores the message in partitions.

Step 3:
Kafka broker manages the storage and replication.

Step 4:
Consumers read messages from partitions using offsets.

Example:
Order Service → sends event → Topic "orders"
Shipping Service → consumes "orders" topic
  • Kafka producer example in Node.js 
          
const { Kafka } = require("kafkajs");

const kafka = new Kafka({
  clientId: "my-app",
  brokers: ["localhost:9092"]
});

const producer = kafka.producer();

async function sendMessage() {
  await producer.connect();

  await producer.send({
    topic: "orders",
    messages: [{ value: "Order Created" }]
  });

  await producer.disconnect();
}

sendMessage();
  • Kafka consumer example in Node.js 
          
const { Kafka } = require("kafkajs");

const kafka = new Kafka({
  clientId: "my-app",
  brokers: ["localhost:9092"]
});

const consumer = kafka.consumer({ groupId: "order-group" });

async function run() {
  await consumer.connect();
  await consumer.subscribe({ topic: "orders" });

  await consumer.run({
    eachMessage: async ({ message }) => {
      console.log(message.value.toString());
    }
  });
}

run();
  • Node.js vs Kafka – What is the difference? 
          
Node.js and Kafka serve completely different purposes in a system architecture.

Node.js
-------
Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine.
It is used to build backend applications, APIs, servers, and microservices.

Common uses:
- REST APIs
- Web servers
- Real-time applications
- Backend business logic

Example:
Client → Node.js API → Database


Kafka
-----
Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used for handling large volumes
of messages between services.

It acts as a message broker between producers and consumers.

Example:
Service A (Producer) → Kafka Topic → Service B (Consumer)


Key Difference
--------------
Node.js = Application runtime
Kafka = Messaging/Event streaming system


Architecture Example
--------------------
Without Kafka

Service A → REST API → Service B

With Kafka

Service A → Kafka Topic → Service B
Service C → Kafka Topic → Service D
  • Why do we use Kafka? 
          
Kafka is used when systems need to process large volumes of real-time data
reliably and efficiently.

Main Reasons to Use Kafka

1. Decoupling Microservices
Services do not need direct communication.

Example:
Order Service → Kafka → Email Service


2. High Throughput
Kafka can handle millions of messages per second.


3. Fault Tolerance
Kafka replicates data across multiple brokers so data is not lost.


4. Event Streaming
Kafka allows systems to process events in real time.

Example:
User Login → Kafka → Analytics Service


5. Message Retention
Messages are stored for a configurable period even after consumption.


6. Scalability
Kafka can scale horizontally by adding more brokers and partitions.


Real World Example
------------------

E-commerce System

User places order
        ↓
Order Service publishes event
        ↓
Kafka Topic: order-created
        ↓
Multiple consumers process it

Shipping Service
Payment Service
Notification Service
Analytics Service


Conclusion
----------

Use Node.js when building backend applications.

Use Kafka when multiple services need to exchange large volumes of data
asynchronously and reliably.
  • Explain Kafka architecture. 
            
Kafka architecture consists of several core components:

1. Producer
Applications that publish messages to Kafka topics.

2. Broker
Kafka server that stores and manages messages.

3. Topic
Logical category where messages are stored.

4. Partition
Topics are divided into partitions for scalability and parallel processing.

5. Consumer
Applications that read messages from Kafka topics.

6. Consumer Group
Multiple consumers working together to process messages in parallel.

Example Flow:
Producer → Topic → Partition → Broker → Consumer
  • What is an Offset in Kafka? 
            
Offset is a unique identifier assigned to each message within a partition.

It represents the position of a message in the partition log.

Example:

Partition 0

Offset 0 → message1
Offset 1 → message2
Offset 2 → message3

Consumers track offsets to know which messages have already been processed.

Advantages:
- Enables message replay
- Allows consumers to resume from last processed position
  • What is a Kafka Partition and why is it important? 
            
A partition is a subset of a Kafka topic that allows parallel processing.

Each topic can have multiple partitions.

Benefits:
- Scalability
- Parallel processing
- High throughput

Example:

Topic: orders

Partition 0
Partition 1
Partition 2

Each partition can be consumed by a different consumer
within the same consumer group.
  • What is a Consumer Group in Kafka? 
            
A Consumer Group is a set of consumers that work together
to consume messages from a topic.

Rules:
- Each partition is consumed by only one consumer in the group.
- Multiple consumer groups can read the same topic independently.

Example:

Topic: orders
Partitions: 3

Consumer Group A
Consumer1 → Partition 0
Consumer2 → Partition 1
Consumer3 → Partition 2

Consumer Group B can also read the same topic separately.
  • What is Replication in Kafka? 
            
Replication ensures data durability and fault tolerance.

Each partition has a leader and multiple followers.

Leader
Handles all read and write requests.

Followers
Replicate data from the leader.

If the leader fails, one follower becomes the new leader.

Example:

Broker1 → Leader
Broker2 → Follower
Broker3 → Follower

Benefits:
- High availability
- Fault tolerance
- Data safety
  • What is Exactly Once Semantics in Kafka? 
            
Exactly Once Semantics ensures that a message is processed
only once even if retries happen.

Kafka achieves this using:

- Idempotent Producers
- Transactions
- Offset management

Without this feature:
A message could be processed multiple times.

Use Case:
Financial transactions
Payment systems
Order processing
  • What is Kafka Consumer Lag? 
            
Consumer Lag is the difference between the latest offset
in a partition and the offset processed by a consumer.

Example:

Latest Offset = 500
Consumer Offset = 450

Lag = 50

Large lag indicates:
- Slow consumer
- Processing bottleneck
- System overload

Monitoring lag is critical in production systems.
  • What is Kafka Retention Policy? 
            
Kafka retention policy defines how long messages are stored
in a topic.

Messages remain in Kafka even after they are consumed.

Example:

Retention Time: 7 days

Kafka will delete messages older than 7 days.

Types:
1. Time-based retention
2. Size-based retention

Benefits:
- Allows replaying events
- Useful for analytics
  • Kafka vs RabbitMQ 
            
Kafka and RabbitMQ are both messaging systems
but designed for different use cases.

Kafka
- Distributed log system
- Very high throughput
- Event streaming
- Used in big data systems

RabbitMQ
- Traditional message queue
- Good for task queues
- Lower throughput compared to Kafka

Kafka stores messages for a long time,
while RabbitMQ deletes messages after consumption.
  • Real-world use cases of Kafka 
            
Kafka is widely used in large-scale systems.

Common Use Cases:

1. Microservices communication
Services communicate asynchronously.

2. Log aggregation
Collect logs from multiple servers.

3. Real-time analytics
Streaming user activity to analytics systems.

4. Event sourcing
Store events instead of state.

5. Data pipelines
Moving data between systems.

Example Architecture:

User Service → Kafka → Analytics Service
Order Service → Kafka → Notification Service
Payment Service → Kafka → Fraud Detection
  • Why is Kafka preferred in microservices architecture?

Advantages:

1. Loose coupling
Services do not depend directly on each other.

2. Scalability
Consumers can scale independently.

3. Fault tolerance

4. Replay capability
Events can be replayed from stored logs.

Example:

Order Service → Kafka Topic

Consumers:
- Email Service

All services can process the same event independently.
  • Kafka Tutorial – What is Apache Kafka? 
            
Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used to handle
real-time data feeds between systems.

It works as a message broker where producers send messages and consumers
read those messages.

Kafka is designed for:
- High throughput

Example:

  • Kafka Core Components 
            
Kafka architecture includes several important components:

1. Producer
Application that sends messages to Kafka.

Example:
Order service sending "order-created" event.


2. Broker
Kafka server that stores messages.


3. Topic
A category or channel where messages are stored.

Example topics:
- orders
- payments
- user-login


4. Partition
Each topic is divided into partitions for scalability.

Example:
Topic: orders
Partition 0
Partition 1
Partition 2


5. Consumer
Application that reads messages from Kafka.


6. Consumer Group
Group of consumers sharing the work of consuming messages.
  • Kafka Message Flow 
            
Kafka Message Flow:

Producer → Topic → Partition → Broker → Consumer


Step 1
Producer sends message to a topic.


Step 2
Kafka stores the message inside partitions.


Step 3
Broker manages partitions and replication.


Step 4
Consumers read messages using offsets.


Example:

User places order
        ↓
Order Service (Producer)
        ↓
Kafka Topic: orders
        ↓
Consumers:
Shipping Service
Email Service
Analytics Service
  • How to install and run Kafka locally 
            
Step 1: Download Kafka

Download from:
https://kafka.apache.org/downloads


Step 2: Start Zookeeper

bin/zookeeper-server-start.sh config/zookeeper.properties


Step 3: Start Kafka Server

bin/kafka-server-start.sh config/server.properties


Step 4: Create a Topic

bin/kafka-topics.sh --create \
--topic test-topic \
--bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
--partitions 3 \
--replication-factor 1


Step 5: Start Producer

bin/kafka-console-producer.sh \
--topic test-topic \
--bootstrap-server localhost:9092


Step 6: Start Consumer

bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh \
--topic test-topic \
--from-beginning \
--bootstrap-server localhost:9092
  • Kafka Producer Example in Node.js 
            
Install library

npm install kafkajs


Producer Example

const { Kafka } = require("kafkajs");

const kafka = new Kafka({
  clientId: "my-app",
  brokers: ["localhost:9092"]
});

const producer = kafka.producer();

async function sendMessage() {
  await producer.connect();

  await producer.send({
    topic: "orders",
    messages: [
      { value: "Order Created" }
    ]
  });

  await producer.disconnect();
}

sendMessage();
  • Kafka Consumer Example in Node.js 
            
const { Kafka } = require("kafkajs");

const kafka = new Kafka({
  clientId: "my-app",
  brokers: ["localhost:9092"]
});

const consumer = kafka.consumer({ groupId: "order-group" });

async function run() {

  await consumer.connect();

  await consumer.subscribe({
    topic: "orders",
    fromBeginning: true
  });

  await consumer.run({
    eachMessage: async ({ message }) => {

      console.log(
        message.value.toString()
      );

    }
  });

}

run();

  • What is an Idempotent Producer in Kafka? 
            
An Idempotent Producer ensures that messages are written to Kafka exactly once,
even if retries happen due to network failures.

Normally:
Producer retry → duplicate messages can be produced.

With Idempotent Producer:
Kafka ensures no duplicate messages are written.

How it works:
Kafka assigns a Producer ID and sequence number to each message.

Benefit:
Prevents duplicate data in distributed systems.

Use Case:
Financial transactions
Order processing systems
  • What is Consumer Rebalancing in Kafka? 
            
Consumer Rebalancing happens when the number of consumers
in a consumer group changes.

Kafka redistributes partitions among consumers.

When does rebalance occur?

1. A new consumer joins the group
2. A consumer crashes
3. A consumer leaves the group
4. Topic partition count changes

Example:

Topic partitions = 4

Consumers = 2

Consumer1 → Partition 0,1
Consumer2 → Partition 2,3

If Consumer3 joins:
Kafka rebalances partitions among all consumers.

Problem:
During rebalance, consumers temporarily stop processing messages.
  • What are Offset Commit Strategies in Kafka? 
            
Offset commit determines how Kafka tracks message consumption.

Types of offset commits:

1. Auto Commit
Kafka automatically commits offsets at intervals.

Pros:
Simple implementation.

Cons:
Risk of message loss or duplication.


2. Manual Commit
Consumer manually commits offset after processing message.

Pros:
More control
Safer processing

Example flow:

Consume message
Process message
Commit offset

If processing fails, offset is not committed.
  • What is Log Compaction in Kafka? 
            
Log compaction ensures that Kafka retains only the latest value
for each message key.

Example:

Key: user1 → value: active
Key: user1 → value: inactive

After compaction:
Only the latest message remains.

Result:
user1 → inactive

Benefits:
- Saves storage
- Maintains latest state
- Useful for event sourcing

Use Cases:
User profiles
Configuration data
State stores
  • What are Kafka Transactions? 
            
Kafka transactions allow producers to send multiple messages
atomically.

Meaning:
Either all messages succeed or none are written.

Example:

Producer sends:
Order created
Payment completed
Inventory updated

If any step fails:
Transaction is aborted.

Benefits:
Ensures data consistency across services.

Used with:
Exactly Once Semantics.
  • Why is Kafka extremely high throughput? 
            
Kafka achieves high throughput due to several design choices.

1. Sequential disk writes
Messages are written sequentially to disk.

2. Batching
Multiple messages are sent in batches.

3. Zero-copy transfer
Kafka avoids unnecessary memory copies.

4. Partition parallelism
Multiple partitions allow parallel reads/writes.

5. Pull model
Consumers pull data instead of brokers pushing.

These optimizations allow Kafka to process millions of messages per second.
  • How does Kafka scale horizontally? 
            
Kafka scales by adding more brokers and partitions.

Example:

Initial cluster:

Broker1
Broker2

Topic partitions:
Partition0 → Broker1
Partition1 → Broker2

Scaling:

Add Broker3
Create more partitions.

Now consumers can process data in parallel across brokers.

Benefits:
- Increased throughput
- Improved fault tolerance
- Better load distribution
  • Does Kafka guarantee message ordering? 
            
Kafka guarantees ordering only within a partition.

Example:

Partition 0
Message1
Message2
Message3

These messages will be consumed in order.

However, ordering is NOT guaranteed across multiple partitions.

Solution:
Use message keys so related messages go to the same partition.

Example:
Key = userID
All events for that user go to the same partition.
  • How does Kafka handle backpressure? 
            
Backpressure occurs when producers send messages faster
than consumers can process them.

Kafka handles this using:

1. Consumer pull model
Consumers control how fast they read data.

2. Consumer lag monitoring
Detect slow consumers.

3. Batching and buffering
Kafka buffers messages before sending.

4. Scalable consumer groups
Add more consumers to increase processing speed.
  • How is Kafka used in large-scale system design? 
            
Example: Uber-like system

Ride Service → Kafka Topic: ride-request
        ↓
Consumers:

Driver Matching Service
Notification Service
Pricing Service
Analytics Service

Benefits:

1. Services are loosely coupled
2. Each service scales independently
3. Messages can be replayed
4. Real-time processing is possible

Kafka acts as the central event streaming backbone.
  • What is Apache Kafka?

    Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used for building real-time data pipelines and streaming applications. It allows producers to publish messages to topics and consumers to read those messages.

    Key features:

    • High throughput
    • Fault tolerance
    • Horizontal scalability
    • Real-time event streaming
  • What are the core components of Kafka?
    • Producer – sends messages to Kafka topics
    • Consumer – reads messages from topics
    • Broker – Kafka server that stores data
    • Topic – logical channel where messages are stored
    • Partition – splits topic for parallel processing
    • Zookeeper / KRaft – manages cluster metadata
  • What is a Kafka Topic?

    A topic is a logical category where messages are stored. Producers write data to topics and consumers read from topics. 

    Example

Topic: order-events

Messages:
order1
order2
order3
  • What is a Partition in Kafka?

    A partition is a unit of parallelism in Kafka. Each topic is divided into multiple partitions so that messages can be processed concurrently by consumers. 

    Topic: orders

Partition 0
Partition 1
Partition 2

    This allows high scalability and distributed processing.

  • What is a Kafka Consumer Group?

    A consumer group is a group of consumers working together to consume messages from a topic.

    Kafka distributes partitions among consumers in the group so each partition is processed by only one consumer. 

    Topic partitions = 3
Consumers = 3

Consumer1 → Partition0
Consumer2 → Partition1
Consumer3 → Partition2
  • What is Kafka Offset?

    Offset is the unique identifier for each message within a partition. It represents the position of a message in the log. 

    Partition 0

Offset 0 → msg1
Offset 1 → msg2
Offset 2 → msg3

    Consumers track offsets to know which messages are already processed.

  • What is replication in Kafka?

    Replication means copying partitions across multiple brokers to provide fault tolerance. 

    Replication Factor = 3

Broker1 → Leader
Broker2 → Follower
Broker3 → Follower

    If the leader broker fails, a follower automatically becomes the leader.

  • What is the difference between Kafka Producer and Consumer?
    Producer Consumer
    Sends messages to Kafka Reads messages from Kafka
    Writes to topic Subscribes to topic
    Push data Pull data
  • How does Kafka ensure fault tolerance?

    Kafka ensures fault tolerance using:

    • Partition replication
    • Leader and follower brokers
    • Automatic leader election
    • Consumer offset tracking

    Even if a broker fails, data is still available on replica brokers.

  • When should Kafka be used in microservices?

    Kafka is useful when:

    • services need asynchronous communication
    • systems require event-driven architecture
    • large scale real-time data processing is needed
    • decoupling between services is required
    Example Microservice Flow

Order Service → Kafka Topic → Payment Service → Notification Service

  • How do you handle zero downtime deployment in ECS for a Node.js application? 
    
Zero downtime deployments in ECS are handled using rolling updates in ECS Services.

Process:

1. New container tasks are started.
2. Load balancer gradually shifts traffic to new tasks.
3. Old tasks are stopped only after new tasks become healthy.

Best practices:

• Use Application Load Balancer (ALB)
• Configure health checks
• Set minimum healthy percent = 100
• Set maximum percent = 200

This ensures users never experience downtime during deployment.

  • What is Terraform? 
    
Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool developed by HashiCorp.

It allows developers and DevOps engineers to create, manage, and automate
cloud infrastructure using code instead of manual configuration.

Terraform can provision infrastructure on multiple cloud platforms
such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
  • Why is Terraform used? 
    
Without Terraform infrastructure must be created manually.

Example:

1 Login to AWS Console
2 Create EC2 instance
3 Configure security groups
4 Setup load balancer
5 Configure database

With Terraform the same infrastructure can be created using code
and a single command:

terraform apply

Benefits:

• automation
• faster infrastructure setup
• reduced manual errors
  • What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)? 
    
Infrastructure as Code means managing infrastructure using
configuration files instead of manual setup.

Examples of infrastructure created using Terraform:

• EC2 instances
• VPC networks
• Load balancers
• ECS clusters
• Security groups
  • Explain Terraform architecture. 
    
Terraform architecture flow:

Developer
   |
Terraform Code (.tf files)
   |
Terraform CLI
   |
Cloud Provider API
   |
Infrastructure Created

Terraform communicates with cloud providers using providers.
  • What are Terraform providers? 
    
Providers allow Terraform to interact with cloud platforms.

Examples:

• AWS provider
• Azure provider
• Google Cloud provider

Providers expose resources that Terraform can manage.
  • What are Terraform resources? 
    
Resources represent actual infrastructure components.

Examples:

aws_instance
aws_vpc
aws_s3_bucket
aws_ecs_cluster

Each resource defines the infrastructure object to create.
  • What are Terraform variables? 
    
Variables allow reusable configuration.

Example:

variable "instance_type" {
  default = "t2.micro"
}

Variables help reuse the same code for different environments.
  • What is the Terraform state file? 
    
Terraform stores infrastructure information in a state file.

File name:

terraform.tfstate

The state file tracks:

• existing infrastructure
• resource dependencies
• configuration changes
  • Explain Terraform workflow. 
    
Terraform workflow:

terraform init
terraform plan
terraform apply
terraform destroy

terraform init
Initializes Terraform project.

terraform plan
Shows what changes will be applied.

terraform apply
Creates infrastructure.

terraform destroy
Deletes infrastructure.
  • Example: Create AWS EC2 using Terraform. 
    
provider "aws" {
 region = "ap-south-1"
}

resource "aws_instance" "example" {
 ami           = "ami-123456"
 instance_type = "t2.micro"

 tags = {
  Name = "NodeServer"
 }
}

Commands:

terraform init
terraform apply
  • Advantages of Terraform. 
    
Major advantages:

• infrastructure automation
• version control with Git
• reusable configuration
• multi-cloud support
• faster deployments
  • Terraform vs Manual Infrastructure Setup.

------------------------------------------------
Speed              Slow              Fast

Reproducibility    No                Yes
  • Give a simple interview definition of Terraform. 
    
Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code tool that allows developers
to define and provision cloud infrastructure using configuration
files instead of manual setup.
  • What are Terraform Modules? 
    
Terraform modules are reusable containers for multiple resources.

Modules allow developers to organize infrastructure code into reusable
and maintainable components.

Example:

module "vpc" {
 source = "./modules/vpc"
}

Benefits:

• code reuse
• cleaner infrastructure structure
• easier maintenance
  • What is Terraform Remote State? 
    
Terraform state file stores information about infrastructure.

Remote state means storing the state file in a remote location instead
of locally.

Common remote state storage:

• AWS S3
• Terraform Cloud
• Azure Storage

Benefits:

• team collaboration
• state locking
• better security
  • What is Terraform State Locking? 
    
State locking prevents multiple users from modifying infrastructure
at the same time.

Example:

User A runs terraform apply
User B tries to run terraform apply

Terraform will block User B until User A finishes.

State locking is commonly implemented using:

• AWS DynamoDB
• Terraform Cloud
  • What are Terraform Workspaces? 
    
Workspaces allow managing multiple environments using the same
Terraform configuration.

Example environments:

• dev
• staging
• production

Commands:

terraform workspace new dev
terraform workspace select dev

Each workspace maintains a separate state file.
  • What is Terraform Provisioner? 
    
Provisioners are used to execute scripts on resources after they
are created.

Example:

resource "aws_instance" "example" {
 provisioner "local-exec" {
  command = "echo Instance created"
 }
}

Provisioners should be used only when necessary.
  • What are Terraform Data Sources? 
    
Data sources allow Terraform to fetch existing infrastructure data
instead of creating new resources.

Example:

data "aws_ami" "latest" {
 most_recent = true
 owners = ["amazon"]
}

Used when referencing existing resources.
  • What is Terraform Dependency Graph? 
    
Terraform automatically builds a dependency graph of resources.

Example:

VPC → Subnet → EC2 Instance

Terraform ensures resources are created in the correct order.

Command to visualize graph:

terraform graph
  • What is Terraform Drift? 
    
Terraform drift occurs when infrastructure changes outside Terraform.

Example:

A developer manually changes an EC2 instance from the AWS console.

Terraform state and actual infrastructure become different.

Terraform detects drift during:

terraform plan
  • How does Terraform handle infrastructure updates? 
    
Terraform compares:

Current state (terraform.tfstate)
vs
Desired configuration (.tf files)

Steps:

1 terraform plan identifies changes
2 terraform apply updates resources

Terraform only modifies the resources that changed.
  • What is the Terraform Registry? 
    
Terraform Registry is a public repository of reusable Terraform modules
and providers.

Example modules available:

• VPC module
• Kubernetes module
• ECS module

Official registry:

https://registry.terraform.io

Benefits:

• reusable infrastructure
• faster development
  • What are Terraform Backend configurations? 
    
Backend configuration defines where Terraform state is stored.

Example using AWS S3:

terraform {
 backend "s3" {
  bucket = "terraform-state-bucket"
  key    = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
  region = "ap-south-1"
 }
}

Backends support:

• remote state storage
• state locking
• collaboration
  • What are Terraform best practices? 
    
Important best practices:

• use modules for reusable infrastructure
• store state remotely
• use version control (Git)
• separate environments (dev, staging, prod)
• avoid hardcoding values
• use variables and secrets management
  • How does Terraform help in DevOps automation? 
    
Terraform automates infrastructure provisioning in CI/CD pipelines.

Example workflow:

Developer pushes code
 |
CI pipeline runs Terraform
 |
Infrastructure automatically created
 |
Application deployed

Benefits:

• faster deployments
• consistent environments
• infrastructure automation

  • What is Strapi in Node.js? 
    Strapi is an open-source Headless CMS built using Node.js.  
It allows developers to quickly create APIs without writing a large amount of backend code.

Strapi automatically generates REST and GraphQL APIs for your application.

--------------------------------------------------

1. What is a Headless CMS?

A Headless CMS means the backend (content management system) is separated
from the frontend.

Example Architecture:

Frontend (React / Next.js / Angular)
          ↓
      API Request
          ↓
        Strapi
          ↓
      Database

Strapi only provides APIs and admin panel, not the frontend UI.

--------------------------------------------------

2. Why Developers Use Strapi?

Benefits:

• Fast backend development  
• Auto-generated REST APIs  
• GraphQL support  
• Admin dashboard for managing content  
• Authentication and roles  
• File upload support  
• Works with multiple databases  

Supported Databases:

• PostgreSQL  
• MySQL  
• SQLite  
• MongoDB (older versions)

--------------------------------------------------

3. Example Use Case

Suppose you are building a Movie Website.

Without Strapi:

Node.js + Express
Write models
Write controllers
Write routes
Write admin panel
Write authentication

With Strapi:

Install Strapi
Create "Movie" content type
Strapi automatically creates:

GET /movies
POST /movies
PUT /movies/:id
DELETE /movies/:id

Admin panel to manage movies.

--------------------------------------------------

4. Install Strapi

Requirements:
Node.js v18+

Command:

npx create-strapi-app@latest my-project --quickstart

This command will:

• Create a Strapi project
• Install dependencies
• Setup database
• Start admin panel

Admin Panel URL:

http://localhost:1337/admin

--------------------------------------------------

5. Example API Response

GET /api/movies

{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "title": "The Dark Knight",
      "rating": 9.0
    }
  ]
}

--------------------------------------------------

6. When Should You Use Strapi?

Strapi is good for:

• CMS websites
• Blogs
• E-commerce backend
• Mobile app APIs
• Content management systems
• Rapid backend development

--------------------------------------------------

7. When NOT to Use Strapi?

Avoid Strapi when:

• You need highly complex backend logic
• You need ultra-high performance microservices
• You want full control over backend architecture

In those cases use:

Node.js + Express / NestJS

--------------------------------------------------

Conclusion

Strapi is a powerful Node.js headless CMS that helps developers
quickly build APIs and manage content without writing large
amounts of backend code..

  • What is Strapi?
    Strapi is an open-source headless CMS built with Node.js that allows developers to create APIs quickly. It provides a powerful admin panel to manage content and automatically generates REST and GraphQL APIs. Strapi is commonly used as a backend for web, mobile, and frontend frameworks like React or Next.js.
  • What is a Headless CMS?
    A headless CMS is a content management system that separates the backend (content management) from the frontend (presentation layer). It provides APIs to deliver content to different platforms such as websites, mobile apps, and IoT devices.
  • What are the main features of Strapi?
    Main features include: - Auto-generated REST and GraphQL APIs - Customizable content types - Built-in admin dashboard - Authentication and role-based permissions - Plugin system - Media library for file uploads
  • Which databases are supported by Strapi?
    Strapi supports multiple databases such as: - PostgreSQL - MySQL - MariaDB - SQLite - MongoDB (supported in older versions)
  • What is a Content Type in Strapi?
    A Content Type defines the structure of the data stored in Strapi. It includes fields such as text, number, date, media, relation, etc. Content types allow developers to model the data for applications.
  • What are Collection Types and Single Types in Strapi?
    Collection Types store multiple entries like blogs, products, or users. Single Types store a single entry like homepage settings or site configuration.
  • How does authentication work in Strapi?
    Strapi uses JWT-based authentication. Users can register and login through API endpoints, and the server returns a JWT token which is used to access protected APIs.
  • What are Strapi roles and permissions?
    Strapi provides role-based access control (RBAC). Administrators can define which roles can access specific APIs such as create, read, update, or delete content.
  • What is the Strapi plugin system?
    Strapi allows developers to extend functionality using plugins. Plugins can add new features like authentication providers, email services, or custom APIs.
  • How do you create a custom API in Strapi?
    Developers can create custom APIs by generating controllers, services, and routes using the Strapi CLI or manually inside the API folder structure.
  • What is the Strapi admin panel?
    The admin panel is a web interface provided by Strapi that allows users to manage content, users, roles, permissions, and plugins without writing code.
  • Can Strapi be used with GraphQL?
    Yes, Strapi supports GraphQL through a plugin. Once installed, developers can query data using GraphQL instead of REST APIs.
  • How does Strapi handle file uploads?
    Strapi provides a built-in media library. Files can be uploaded and stored locally or on cloud services like AWS S3, Cloudinary, or Azure.
  • How can Strapi be deployed?
    Strapi can be deployed on platforms like Docker containers, AWS, DigitalOcean, Heroku, or Kubernetes clusters.
  • What are the advantages of Strapi?
    Advantages include: - Quick API development - Built-in admin panel - Headless architecture - Customizable backend - Open-source and extensible
  • What is the architecture of Strapi?
    Strapi follows a layered architecture consisting of: 1. Admin Panel (React-based UI for managing content) 2. API Layer (REST / GraphQL endpoints) 3. Controller Layer (handles request and response) 4. Service Layer (business logic) 5. Data Access Layer (ORM using database connectors) 6. Database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite etc.) This architecture helps maintain separation of concerns and improves scalability.
  • What are the main core layers in Strapi architecture?
    The main layers include: - Router Layer (defines API routes) - Controller Layer (handles HTTP requests) - Service Layer (business logic) - Model Layer (data schema) - Database Layer (stores data)
  • How does Strapi generate APIs automatically?
    When a developer creates a content type, Strapi automatically generates: - REST endpoints - Database schema - Controllers - Services This automation reduces development time and allows rapid API creation.
  • What is the role of controllers in Strapi?
    Controllers handle incoming HTTP requests, process the request, call the service layer for business logic, and return responses to clients.
  • What is the role of services in Strapi architecture?
    Services contain the core business logic of the application. Controllers call services to perform operations like fetching data, applying validation, or executing business rules.
  • What ORM does Strapi use?
    Strapi uses a database abstraction layer built on top of an ORM that interacts with SQL databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL. This allows developers to interact with the database using JavaScript.
  • How does Strapi handle scalability?
    Strapi can scale using: - Load balancers - Containerization (Docker) - Horizontal scaling with Kubernetes - External database systems like PostgreSQL - CDN for media delivery
  • What is the plugin architecture in Strapi?
    Strapi has a plugin-based architecture that allows developers to extend functionality by adding new modules such as authentication providers, GraphQL support, email services, or custom APIs.
  • How does Strapi manage content relationships?
    Strapi supports relational data models such as: - One-to-One - One-to-Many - Many-to-Many These relationships help structure complex data models for applications.
  • How can Strapi integrate with frontend applications?
    Strapi provides REST and GraphQL APIs which can be consumed by frontend frameworks like React, Angular, Vue, or mobile applications.
  • What are lifecycle hooks in Strapi?
    Lifecycle hooks allow developers to execute custom logic during database operations such as beforeCreate, afterCreate, beforeUpdate, and afterDelete.
  • How does Strapi handle authentication and authorization?
    Strapi uses JWT authentication and role-based access control (RBAC). Roles define permissions for accessing APIs and managing content.
  • How does Strapi manage file storage?
    Strapi uses a media library that can store files locally or integrate with cloud storage providers like AWS S3 or Cloudinary.
  • How can you customize APIs in Strapi?
    APIs can be customized by modifying: - Controllers - Services - Routes - Middleware This allows developers to implement custom business logic.
  • How does Strapi support microservices architecture?
    Strapi can be used as a content service in a microservices architecture. It exposes APIs that other services or applications can consume.

  • What is setTimeout()? Give example. 
          
setTimeout()

setTimeout() is a JavaScript function used to execute a function
once after a specified delay (in milliseconds).

Syntax

setTimeout(function, delay)

Example

console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Hello after 2 seconds");
}, 2000);

console.log("End");

Output

Start
End
Hello after 2 seconds

Explanation

The setTimeout callback runs after the call stack becomes empty
and the delay time has passed.

--------------------------------------------------

Example 2

function greet() {
  console.log("Welcome!");
}

setTimeout(greet, 3000);

This will execute greet() after 3 seconds.
  • How does the Node.js event loop work internally?
    Node.js uses a single-threaded, non-blocking, event-driven architecture powered by the V8 JavaScript engine and libuv library. The event loop allows Node.js to handle many concurrent operations without creating multiple threads for each request. Event Loop Phases: 1. Timers Phase Executes callbacks scheduled by setTimeout() and setInterval(). 2. Pending Callbacks Executes I/O callbacks deferred to the next loop iteration. 3. Idle / Prepare Internal Node.js operations. 4. Poll Phase Retrieves new I/O events and executes related callbacks. 5. Check Phase Executes setImmediate() callbacks. 6. Close Callbacks Handles socket close events. Example: setTimeout(() => console.log("Timer"), 0); setImmediate(() => console.log("Immediate")); Node.js processes these tasks asynchronously via the event loop while delegating heavy I/O operations to the libuv thread pool. This architecture allows Node.js to efficiently handle thousands of concurrent connections.
  • How do you scale Node.js applications for high traffic systems?
    Node.js applications can be scaled using both vertical and horizontal scaling strategies. 1. Node.js Cluster Module Allows Node.js to spawn multiple worker processes using multiple CPU cores. Example: const cluster = require("cluster"); const os = require("os"); if (cluster.isMaster) { const cpuCount = os.cpus().length; for (let i = 0; i < cpuCount; i++) { cluster.fork(); } } else { require("./server"); } 2. Load Balancing Use Nginx or cloud load balancers to distribute traffic across instances. 3. Container Scaling Deploy multiple containers using Kubernetes or Docker Swarm. 4. Stateless Architecture Store session data in Redis instead of memory. 5. Microservices Break large applications into independent services. 6. Caching Layer Use Redis or CDN to reduce database load. These strategies allow Node.js systems to handle millions of users.
  • Node.js vs Java for microservices architecture?
    Both Node.js and Java are widely used for microservices but have different strengths. Node.js Advantages: - Event-driven architecture - High performance for I/O-heavy applications - Fast API development - JavaScript full stack development Java Advantages: - Strong type safety - Mature ecosystem - Better for CPU-intensive workloads - Enterprise-grade frameworks like Spring Boot Comparison: Node.js - Non-blocking architecture - Lightweight services - Faster startup time Java - Multithreaded architecture - Higher memory usage - Strong enterprise tooling Typical Use Cases: Node.js - Real-time apps - API gateways - Streaming platforms Java - Banking systems - Complex enterprise applications - Heavy data processing services
  • How do you design a high-performance Node.js API?
    Designing a high-performance Node.js API involves several architectural and coding practices. 1. Use Asynchronous Programming Always use async/await instead of blocking operations. Example: const user = await userService.getUser(id); 2. Use Connection Pooling Database connection pooling reduces latency. 3. Use Caching Cache frequently requested data using Redis. 4. API Rate Limiting Prevent abuse using middleware like express-rate-limit. 5. Use Compression Enable gzip compression to reduce response size. 6. Optimize Database Queries Use indexes and avoid N+1 queries. 7. Logging and Monitoring Use tools like Winston, Prometheus, or Grafana. 8. Use CDN Serve static assets via CDN. 9. Use API Gateway Implement centralized authentication and routing. These strategies significantly improve performance and scalability.
  • When should you use message queues like Kafka or RabbitMQ?
    Message queues are used when systems need asynchronous communication between services. Use Cases: 1. Microservices Communication Decouple services so they do not depend on synchronous HTTP calls. 2. Event-Driven Architecture Services publish events and other services consume them. Example: Order Service → Kafka → Payment Service 3. High Throughput Systems Kafka can handle millions of messages per second. 4. Background Processing Offload heavy tasks like sending emails or generating reports. Example: User Registration → Queue → Email Service 5. Fault Tolerance If a service fails, messages remain in the queue. Kafka - Best for event streaming - High throughput systems RabbitMQ - Best for task queues - Reliable message delivery Message queues improve scalability, reliability, and system decoupling.
  • How would you handle millions of concurrent users in Node.js?
    Handling millions of concurrent users requires distributed architecture and optimized infrastructure. 1. Horizontal Scaling Deploy multiple Node.js instances behind a load balancer. 2. Stateless Servers Store session data in Redis instead of server memory. 3. Microservices Architecture Split large applications into independent services. 4. CDN Usage Serve static content using CDN to reduce server load. 5. Database Scaling Use read replicas and sharding. 6. Event Streaming Use Kafka for high-throughput messaging. 7. Caching Layer Cache API responses using Redis. 8. Auto Scaling Use cloud auto-scaling groups in AWS, GCP, or Azure. 9. API Gateway Centralize authentication, routing, and rate limiting. Example Architecture: Client → CDN → Load Balancer → Node.js Cluster → Redis Cache → Database Cluster This distributed architecture can support millions of concurrent users with low latency.
  • What is API Gateway architecture and how is it implemented in a Node.js microservices system? 
    API Gateway is a central entry point that manages requests from clients 
and routes them to appropriate backend microservices.

Instead of clients calling many services directly, they interact with 
a single gateway.

Responsibilities of API Gateway
--------------------------------
1. Request routing
2. Authentication and authorization
3. Rate limiting
4. Caching
5. Load balancing
6. API composition
7. Logging and monitoring

Architecture Example
--------------------

Client
  |
  v
API Gateway (Node.js / Nginx)
  |
  |---- User Service
  |---- Order Service
  |---- Payment Service
  |---- Notification Service


Advantages
-----------
• Simplifies client communication
• Centralized security
• Prevents direct exposure of microservices
• Enables throttling and request filtering

Node.js Implementation Example
------------------------------

const express = require("express");
const httpProxy = require("http-proxy-middleware");

const app = express();

app.use("/users",
httpProxy.createProxyMiddleware({
    target: "http://user-service:3001",
    changeOrigin: true
}));

app.use("/orders",
httpProxy.createProxyMiddleware({
    target: "http://order-service:3002",
    changeOrigin: true
}));

app.listen(3000, () => {
    console.log("API Gateway running on port 3000");
});

Popular API Gateway Tools
-------------------------
• Kong
• AWS API Gateway
• NGINX
• Express Gateway

Architect Perspective
---------------------
API Gateways help manage microservices complexity and improve security, 
observability, and scalability in distributed systems.
  • How do you debug and detect memory leaks in Node.js applications? 
    Memory leaks occur when objects remain in memory even after they 
are no longer needed.

Over time this causes increased RAM usage and application crashes.

Common Causes
-------------
1. Global variables
2. Unclosed database connections
3. Event listeners not removed
4. Large caches
5. Closures retaining references

Example Memory Leak
-------------------

let cache = [];

app.get("/data", (req, res) => {
    cache.push(new Array(1000000));
    res.send("Stored");
});

The array continuously grows and memory usage increases.

Tools for Debugging
-------------------

1. Chrome DevTools Heap Snapshot
2. Node.js --inspect flag
3. Clinic.js
4. heapdump
5. PM2 monitoring

Heap Analysis Example
---------------------

node --inspect server.js

Open Chrome:
