  • difference between ~ and ^ in package.json dependencies?
    • ^1.2.3 allows updates to any minor or patch version, e.g., 1.x.x but not 2.0.0.
    • ~1.2.3 allows updates only to patch versions, e.g., 1.2.x but not 1.3.0.
    • In short, ^ is more permissive (minor + patch), ~ is more restrictive (patch only).
  • Worker threads?
    Worker threads enable running JavaScript in parallel threads. Unlike the main thread, they can handle CPU-intensive tasks without blocking the event loop, improving performance. 
    Worker threads enable parallel execution in Node.js for heavy tasks, keeping the main thread non-blocking.
Worker threads are a way to run JavaScript code in parallel on multiple threads in Node.js. 

While Node.js is single-threaded by default (using an event loop), 
Worker Threads enable CPU-intensive tasks to be executed without blocking the main event loop, improving performance for compute-heavy operations.

Introduced in Node.js v10.5.0 (stable since v12), the worker_threads module allows you to create and manage threads that run scripts independently. 
Each worker has its own event loop, memory, and execution context, enabling true parallelism.

Use cases include heavy computations, data processing, or any synchronous tasks that would otherwise block the main thread and degrade app responsiveness.

Communication between the main thread and worker threads happens via messaging using postMessage() and listening to message events. 
Workers can share memory efficiently using SharedArrayBuffer.


Example usage:

  const { Worker }  = require('worker_threads');
  const worker      = new Worker('./workerScript.js');
  worker.on('message', msg => console.log('From worker:', msg));
  worker.postMessage('start');
  
    
  const { Worker }  = require('worker_threads');
  const path        = require('path');
  const worker      = new Worker(path.resolve(__dirname, './workerScript.js'));

  worker.on('message',  (msg)   => {  console.log('From worker:', msg);     });
  worker.on('error',    (err)   => {  console.error('Worker error:', err);  });
  worker.on('exit',     (code)  => {  console.log(`Worker exited with code ${code}`); });
  
  // Simulate sending a large JSON string for processing
  const largeJson   = JSON.stringify({  users: Array.from({ length: 100000 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i, name: `User${i}` }))  });
  worker.postMessage(largeJson);
  
    
  const { parentPort } = require('worker_threads');
  parentPort.on('message', (jsonString) => {
    try {
      const data = JSON.parse(jsonString);

      // Do some CPU-heavy processing
      const transformed = data.users.map(user => ({
        id: user.id,
        name: user.name.toUpperCase(), // Example transformation
      }));

      // Send back just a summary
      parentPort.postMessage({
        status: 'success',
        count: transformed.length,
        sample: transformed.slice(0, 5) // send first 5 records
      });
    } catch (error) {
      parentPort.postMessage({ status: 'error', message: error.message });
    }
  });
  • Package-lock.json?
    package-lock.json is automatically generated by npm when installing dependencies. It locks the exact versions of installed packages and their sub-dependencies to ensure consistency across different environments. While package.json defines dependency ranges (e.g., ^1.2.3), package-lock.json stores the exact versions (e.g., 1.2.3) used during installation.

    This ensures that every developer or deployment environment installs the same dependency tree, avoiding bugs caused by version differences. It also improves performance by caching dependency metadata. This file should be committed to version control in most projects.

  • 🎯 Abstraction in Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)

    Abstraction?

    Abstraction is the concept of hiding complex implementation details and showing only the essential features of an object.

    It helps reduce complexity by exposing only what is necessary.

    Real-World Example

    When you drive a car, you interact with the steering wheel, pedals, and gear. You don’t need to know how the engine works internally — that's abstraction.

    How It Works in OOP

    • Achieved using abstract classes and interfaces.
    • Only relevant operations are exposed through public methods.
    • Internal logic is hidden from the user of the object.

    Example in Java

    abstract class Animal {
  abstract void makeSound();
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  void makeSound() {
    System.out.println("Bark");
  }
}

public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Animal a = new Dog();
    a.makeSound();  // Output: Bark
  }
}

    Here, the user of the Animal class knows it has a makeSound() method, but not how it is implemented.

    Benefits of Abstraction

    • Improves code readability and maintainability
    • Hides unnecessary details from the user
    • Supports loose coupling and high cohesion
    • Makes the application more secure by exposing only relevant parts

    🔍 Abstraction vs Interface in OOP

    Definition

    Abstraction is the concept of hiding implementation details and exposing only essential features. It can be implemented using abstract classes or interfaces.

    Interface is a contract that specifies what methods a class should implement, without defining how they are implemented.

    Comparison Table

    Feature Abstract Class Interface
    Purpose Used for partial abstraction and shared code. Used to define a full contract for implementing classes.
    Method Implementation Can have both abstract and concrete methods. Cannot have implementation (except default/static in modern languages).
    Multiple Inheritance Not supported in many languages (e.g., Java). Can implement multiple interfaces.
    Constructors Can have constructors. Cannot have constructors.
    Access Modifiers Can use public, protected, private, etc. Methods are public by default.
    Use Case When classes share common behavior with differences. When you want to enforce a common API without shared code.

    Example in Java

    Abstract Class

    abstract class Animal {
  abstract void sound();

  void breathe() {
    System.out.println("Breathing...");
  }
}

    Interface

    interface Flyable {
  void fly();
}

class Bird implements Flyable {
  public void fly() {
    System.out.println("Flying...");
  }
}

    Quick Summary

    • Abstraction is a broader concept; an abstract class is one way to implement it.
    • Interface is a pure abstraction tool used for enforcing contracts between classes.
  • 🔐 OAuth 2.0 Overview

    OAuth 2.0?

    OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that allows third-party applications to obtain limited access to a user's resources without exposing their credentials.

    Roles in OAuth 2.0

    • Resource Owner: The user who owns the data.
    • Client: The application requesting access to the resource.
    • Authorization Server: Issues access tokens after authenticating the user.
    • Resource Server: Hosts the protected resources and validates the token.

    OAuth 2.0 Grant Types

    • Authorization Code: Used for server-side applications. Secure and most commonly used.
    • Implicit: Used for public clients like single-page apps. Less secure (now discouraged).
    • Resource Owner Password Credentials: User provides credentials directly. Used in trusted apps.
    • Client Credentials: Used for machine-to-machine communication.

    OAuth 2.0 Flow: Authorization Code Grant

    1. User is redirected to Authorization Server to log in.
    2. User grants permission to the app.
    3. Authorization Server redirects back with an authorization code.
    4. App exchanges the code for an access token.
    5. App uses the token to access protected resources.

    Access & Refresh Tokens

    • Access Token: Used to access protected resources. Short-lived.
    • Refresh Token: Used to obtain a new access token when it expires. Long-lived.

    Security Tips

    • Use HTTPS for all communication.
    • Never expose client secrets in frontend apps.
    • Use PKCE with public clients (e.g., mobile apps, SPAs).
    • Use short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens securely.
  • Middleware? Types of middleware
    Middleware in Express.js is a function that processes requests and responses during the request-response cycle.
    It has access to the req and res objects and the next middleware function in the stack via the next() callback.

    Middleware functions can perform tasks like:
    1. Executing code
    2. Modifying req and res objects
    3. Ending the request-response cycle
    4. Calling the next middleware

    Types of middleware :
    1. Application-level: Bound to an Express app using app.use() or route methods.
    2. Router-level: Bound to an instance of express.Router().
    3. Error-handling: Special middleware with four arguments (err, req, res, next) to catch errors.
    4. Built-in: Provided by Express, e.g., express.json(), express.static().
    5. Third-party: Such as cors, helmet, morgan.
    Example: 
    app.use((req, res, next) => {
console.log('Request URL:', req.url);
next(); // Pass control to next middleware
});
    Middleware enables modular, reusable, and organized handling of HTTP requests, essential for building scalable Express.js applications.

  • Cluster vs Worker*** cluster.fork()
    In Node.js, both Cluster and Worker Threads are used for parallel processing, but they serve different purposes and have distinct architectures.
    Read More

    1. The cluster module allows you to create child processes (workers) that share the same server port.
      It's used to take advantage of multi-core systems to handle concurrent requests efficiently.
      It is used to utilize multiple CPU cores, improving performance for concurrent requests.
      const cluster = require('cluster');

    2. The worker_threads module allows JavaScript code to run in parallel on multiple threads.
      Useful for CPU-intensive tasks (like hashing, image processing) without blocking the main event loop.
      A **worker** is an individual child process created by the cluster.
      Each worker runs its own Node.js instance and handles a portion of the server load.
      They can communicate with the master process via IPC (inter-process communication).
      A **worker** is an individual child process created by the cluster.
      Each worker runs its own Node.js instance and handles a portion of the server load.
      They can communicate with the master process via IPC (inter-process communication).
      const { Worker, isMainThread, parentPort, workerData } = require('worker_threads');

    Node.js is single-threaded by default. Using the cluster module allows your app to : Handle more requests concurrently.
    1. Avoid a single point of failure (if one worker crashes, others keep running).
    2. Use all CPU cores on a server.
    3. All workers share the same server port.
    4. Each worker is a separate Node.js process (not thread).
    5. Workers don’t share memory – use IPC or external stores (like Redis) for shared state.


    🔄 Cluster vs Worker Comparison
    Aspect Cluster Worker
    Definition Main controller module to spawn child processes Individual child process spawned by the cluster
    Role Manages multiple workers Handles incoming requests or tasks
    Code Location Master process Worker process
    Use Case Load balancing and CPU core utilization Actual request processing
    Communication Interacts with workers via IPC Communicates with master via IPC

    🔍 Comparison: Manual cluster vs PM2

    Feature Manual cluster PM2
    Setup Manual coding required Easy CLI-based
    Load balancing Handled via cluster Built-in
    Process Monitoring Not built-in Dashboard + CLI
    Crash Recovery Manual restart Automatic restart
    Logging Requires setup Built-in logging
    Production Readiness Not ideal alone ✅ Highly recommended
  • Clustering? & cluster vs worker*** cluster.fork()
    Clustering enables using multiple CPU cores by spawning worker processes that share the same server port, improving performance and load handling.
    Clustering in Node.js is a technique to create multiple child processes (workers) that share the same server port, allowing you to take advantage of multi-core CPU systems. Since Node.js runs on a single thread by default, clustering helps improve performance and reliability by distributing incoming requests across several worker processes. The core module cluster enables spawning of worker processes. Each worker runs its own event loop and instance of the Node.js runtime, enabling parallel processing of requests.
    Key benefits:
    • Improved Performance: Utilizes multiple CPU cores to handle more concurrent connections.
    • Fault Tolerance: If one worker crashes, the master process can spawn a new worker, improving app resilience.
    • Load Balancing: The master process balances incoming requests between workers.
    Basic usage example: 
    const cluster = require('cluster');
const http = require('http');
const numCPUs = require('os').cpus().length;

if (cluster.isMaster) {
  for (let i = 0; i < numCPUs; i++) {
    cluster.fork();
  }
  cluster.on('exit', (worker) => {
    console.log(`Worker ${worker.process.pid} died, spawning a new one.`);
    cluster.fork();
  });
} 
else {
  http.createServer((req, res) => {
    res.end('Hello from worker ' + process.pid);
  }).listen(8000);
}
    Clustering boosts Node.js scalability but requires careful management of shared resources and state.
  • Performance?
    Use clustering, caching (Redis), async operations, database indexing, code profiling, monitoring (e.g., New Relic), and limit synchronous code. Minimize memory leaks and optimize queries.
    Optimizing performance in large-scale Node.js applications involves multiple strategies:
    1. Use Asynchronous Code: Always prefer non-blocking async operations to avoid blocking the event loop.
    2. Load Balancing & Clustering: Use the cluster module or external load balancers to utilize multiple CPU cores.
    3. Caching: Cache frequent data using in-memory stores like Redis or Memcached to reduce database load.
    4. Database Optimization: Use indexing, connection pooling, and optimized queries to improve database interaction.
    5. Avoid Memory Leaks: Monitor heap usage, manage object lifecycles carefully, and use profiling tools like Chrome DevTools or Clinic.js.
    6. Use Streams: Process large data efficiently with streams to minimize memory footprint.
    7. Efficient Logging: Use asynchronous logging libraries and avoid excessive logging in production.
    8. Minimize Dependencies: Avoid bloated or unused npm packages to reduce startup time.
    9. Profiling & Monitoring: Continuously profile your app using tools like New Relic, Datadog, or built-in profilers.
    10. Use CDN & Compression: Serve static assets via CDN and compress responses with gzip or brotli.
    Regular code reviews, performance testing, and keeping dependencies up-to-date help maintain high performance.
  • Difference between process.nextTick() and setImmediate()?
    process.nextTick() schedules a callback to execute immediately after the current operation completes, before the event loop continues. It has higher priority and runs before any I/O events or timers.
    setImmediate() schedules a callback to run on the next iteration (tick) of the event loop, after I/O events callbacks.

    In short, process.nextTick() : runs before any I/O tasks, can starve I/O, blocking the event loop. setImmediate() : runs after I/O events in the event loop.
  • secure a Node.js application?
    Securing a Node.js application involves multiple layers of protection:
    1. HTTP Headers: Use helmet middleware to set secure HTTP headers and prevent common attacks like XSS, clickjacking, and MIME-sniffing.
    2. Rate Limiting: Implement request throttling using express-rate-limit to protect against brute-force and DDoS attacks.
    3. Input Validation & Sanitization: Use libraries like express-validator or Zod to validate and sanitize incoming data to avoid injection attacks.
    4. Authentication & Authorization: Use secure token-based auth like JWT. Never store sensitive info in plain text—always hash passwords with bcrypt.
    5. Use HTTPS: Encrypt communication using SSL certificates to secure data in transit.
    6. Avoid Eval & Unsafe Code: Never use eval() or Function() with untrusted data. These can lead to RCE (Remote Code Execution).
    7. Dependency Management: Use npm audit and tools like snyk to identify and fix vulnerable packages.
    8. Secure Cookies: Use HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite flags on cookies.
    9. Environment Variables: Keep secrets and configs in .env files. Never hard-code credentials.
    10. Logging & Monitoring: Monitor with tools like Winston, Morgan, or services like Datadog or New Relic. Regularly update Node.js and dependencies to stay protected.

  • What are Conditional Types in TypeScript? How do they work?

    Conditional Types allow types to be chosen based on a condition.

    Syntax:

    
T extends U ? X : Y

    If type T extends U, the result type is X, otherwise Y.

    
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

type A = IsString<string>;   // true
type B = IsString<number>;   // false

    Conditional types are heavily used in advanced utility types and generic libraries.

}

  • GraphQL ? ****
    GraphQL offers several advantages over traditional REST APIs:
    • Flexible Queries: Clients can request exactly the data they need, reducing over-fetching and under-fetching.
    • Single Endpoint: All data queries and mutations happen through one endpoint, simplifying API management.
    • Strongly Typed Schema: The schema defines the types and relationships, enabling better validation and tooling.
    • Efficient Data Loading: Supports batching and caching to minimize redundant data fetching.
    • Improved Developer Experience: Introspection and auto-generated documentation make development faster and easier.
    • Real-time Data: Supports subscriptions for live updates.
    These features make GraphQL ideal for complex, evolving APIs and frontend-driven development. 
      const { graphqlHTTP } = require('express-graphql');
  
  app.use(
    '/graphql',
    graphqlHTTP({
      schema,
      graphiql: true,
    })
  );

  const {
    GraphQLObjectType,
    GraphQLString,
    GraphQLID,
    GraphQLList,
    GraphQLSchema
  } = require('graphql');
  
  // Sample in-memory data
  const managers = [
    { id: '1', name: 'CEO', email: 'ceo@company.com', subManagerIds: ['2', '3'] },
    { id: '2', name: 'VP Eng', email: 'vpengg@company.com', subManagerIds: ['4'] },
    { id: '3', name: 'VP Marketing', email: 'vpmarketing@company.com', subManagerIds: ['7'] },
    { id: '4', name: 'Dummy Zero Manager', email: 'em@company.com', subManagerIds: ['5'] },
    { id: '5', name: 'Dummy One Manager', email: 'em@company.com', subManagerIds: ['6'] },
    { id: '6', name: 'Dummy Two Manager', email: 'em@company.com', subManagerIds: [] },
    { id: '7', name: 'Dummy Three Manager', email: 'em@company.com', subManagerIds: [] },
  ];
  
  // Manager Type with Recursive subManagers
  const ManagerType = new GraphQLObjectType({
    name: 'Manager',
    fields: () => ({
      id: { type: GraphQLID },
      name: { type: GraphQLString },
      email: { type: GraphQLString },
      subManagers: {
        type: new GraphQLList(ManagerType),
        resolve(parent) {
          return managers.filter(m => parent.subManagerIds.includes(m.id));
        }
      }
    }),
  });
  
  // Root Query
  const RootQuery = new GraphQLObjectType({
    name: 'RootQueryType',
    fields: {
      manager: {
        type: ManagerType,
        args: { id: { type: GraphQLID } },
        resolve(_, args) {
          return managers.find(m => m.id === args.id);
        }
      },
      allManagers: {
        type: new GraphQLList(ManagerType),
        resolve() {
          return managers;
        }
      }
    }
  });
  
  const Mutation = new GraphQLObjectType({
    name: 'Mutation',
    fields: {
      addManager: {
        type: ManagerType,
        args: {
          name: { type: GraphQLString },
          email: { type: GraphQLString },
          parentId: { type: GraphQLID }, // optional parent manager
        },
        resolve(_, args) {
          const newManager = {
            id: String(managers.length + 1),
            name: args.name,
            email: args.email,
            subManagerIds: [],
          };
  
          managers.push(newManager);
  
          // If parentId is provided, attach as sub-manager
          if (args.parentId) {
            const parent = managers.find((m) => m.id === args.parentId);
            if (parent) {
              parent.subManagerIds.push(newManager.id);
            }
          }
  
          return newManager;
        }
      }
    }
  });
  
  
  
  // Export Schema
  module.exports = new GraphQLSchema({
    query: RootQuery,
    mutation: Mutation,
  });

const {
  GraphQLObjectType,
  GraphQLSchema,
  GraphQLString,
  GraphQLList,
  GraphQLID,
  GraphQLNonNull
} = require('graphql');
const Manager = require('./manager.model');

const ManagerType = new GraphQLObjectType({
  name: 'Manager',
  fields: () => ({
    id:     { type: GraphQLID },
    name:   { type: GraphQLString },
    email:  { type: GraphQLString },
    images: { type: new GraphQLList(GraphQLString) }
  })
});

const RootQuery = new GraphQLObjectType({
  name: 'Query',
  fields: () => ({
    managers: {
      type: new GraphQLList(ManagerType),
      resolve: async () => Manager.find()
    },
    manager: {
      type: ManagerType,
      args: { id: { type: GraphQLID } },
      resolve: async (_, { id }) => Manager.findById(id)
    }
  })
});

const Mutation = new GraphQLObjectType({
  name: 'Mutation',
  fields: () => ({
    addManager: {
      type: ManagerType,
      args: {
        name:  { type: new GraphQLNonNull(GraphQLString) },
        email: { type: new GraphQLNonNull(GraphQLString) }
      },
      resolve: async (_, args) => {
        const manager = new Manager(args);
        return await manager.save();
      }
    }
  })
});

module.exports = new GraphQLSchema({
  query: RootQuery,
  mutation: Mutation
});
  • design patterns in Node.js?
    Design patterns are reusable solutions to common software design problems. In Node.js, popular patterns include:
    1. Singleton: Ensures a class has only one instance (e.g., database connection).
    2. Factory: Creates objects without exposing the instantiation logic.
    3. Observer: Implements pub-sub mechanisms (e.g., EventEmitter).
    4. Middleware: Common in Express apps for request handling.
    5. Module Pattern: Uses closures to encapsulate logic. Using design patterns improves code organization, reusability, and maintainability in scalable Node.js applications.
  • Explain Singleton, Factory, Observer, Middleware, and Module patterns in Node.js
    Singleton: Restricts a class to one instance. Useful for shared resources like DB connections. Ensures consistent state across the app.

    Factory: Creates objects without specifying exact classes. It abstracts object creation, allowing flexible and interchangeable products.

    Observer: Implements event-driven communication where objects subscribe to events and get notified on changes. Node’s EventEmitter is a classic example.

    Middleware: Functions that intercept requests in a chain to process or modify them. Common in Express.js for logging, authentication, or error handling.

    Module Pattern: Uses closures to encapsulate private variables and expose a public API. Helps in organizing code into reusable, maintainable parts.

    These patterns help write modular, scalable, and maintainable Node.js applications.
  • SOLID in software development?
    SOLID is a set of five design principles aimed at making software designs more understandable, flexible, and maintainable:

    S - Single Responsibility Principle: A class should have only one reason to change.
    O - Open/Closed Principle: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.
    L - Liskov Substitution Principle: Subclasses should be replaceable by their base classes without affecting correctness.
    I - Interface Segregation Principle: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don’t use.
    D - Dependency Inversion Principle: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules but on abstractions.

    Applying SOLID improves code quality and eases maintenance.
  • Data types in JavaScript?
    JavaScript has two main types of data types:

    1. Primitive Types:
    - String: e.g., "hello"
    - Number: e.g., 123, 3.14
    - Boolean: true or false
    - Undefined: a variable declared but not assigned
    - Null: intentional absence of any value
    - Symbol: unique and immutable value
    - BigInt: for large integers beyond Number limits

    2. Non-Primitive (Reference) Types:
    - Object: includes arrays, functions, dates, etc.

    Primitive types are compared by value, while objects are compared by reference.
  • difference between var, let, and const in JavaScript?
    These three keywords are used to declare variables in JavaScript but differ in scope, hoisting, and mutability.

    1. var

    • Scope: Function-scoped
    • Hoisting: Hoisted and initialized with undefined
    • Re-declaration: Allowed
    • Use: Considered outdated; avoid in modern code
    
  function test() {
    var x = 1;
    if (true) {
      var x = 2;
      console.log(x); // 2
    }
    console.log(x); // 2
  }

    2. let

    • Scope: Block-scoped
    • Hoisting: Hoisted but not initialized (temporal dead zone)
    • Re-declaration: Not allowed in same scope
    • Use: For variables that will change
    
  let x = 1;
  x = 2; // Allowed

    3. const

    • Scope: Block-scoped
    • Hoisting: Hoisted but not initialized
    • Re-assignment: Not allowed
    • Use: For variables that shouldn't change (e.g., constants)
    
  const y = 10;
  y = 20; // ❌ Error
  const obj = { a: 1 };
  obj.a = 2; // ✅ Allowed (reference not reassigned)

    Summary Table:

    Keyword Scope Hoisted Re-declarable Re-assignable
    var Function Yes (undefined) Yes Yes
    let Block Yes (but TDZ) No Yes
    const Block Yes (but TDZ) No No (but object props mutable)
  • Currying?
    Currying is a functional programming technique where a function is transformed into a sequence of functions, each taking a single argument. Instead of taking all arguments at once, a curried function takes them one by one. It improves code reusability and function composition. Example: 
    
// Normal function
function add(a, b) {
return a + b;
}

// Curried version
function curriedAdd(a) {
return function(b) {
return a + b;
};
}

console.log(curriedAdd(2)(3)); // 5
    Currying is useful for creating customizable and reusable function pipelines.
  • OAuth 2.0?
    OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that enables third-party applications to obtain limited access to user resources on a server without exposing user credentials. It works by issuing access tokens after user consent, which the application uses to access protected resources.
    Key roles:
    - Resource Owner: User granting access
    - Client: Application requesting access
    - Authorization Server: Issues tokens
    - Resource Server: Hosts protected resources
    Common grant types:
    - Authorization Code
    - Implicit
    - Resource Owner Password Credentials
    - Client Credentials
    OAuth 2.0 improves security by decoupling authentication and authorization, widely used in APIs and social logins.
  • the difference between Token and Session?
    Session:
    - Server stores user state and session ID.
    - Client holds session ID in cookies.
    - Requires server-side memory or storage.
    - Easier to invalidate on logout.
    Token (e.g., JWT):
    - Self-contained, stateless authentication.
    - Token holds user info, signed by server.
    - Stored client-side (localStorage/cookies).
    - Scales better, no server memory needed.
    Summary:
    Sessions are server-managed; tokens are client-managed. Tokens are popular for APIs and stateless apps; sessions suit traditional web apps.
  • AWS API Gateway?
    AWS API Gateway is a fully managed service that enables developers to create, publish, maintain, monitor, and secure APIs at any scale. It acts as a front door for applications to access backend services like AWS Lambda, EC2, or external endpoints. Key features:
    - Supports RESTful and WebSocket APIs.
    - Handles request routing, throttling, authorization, and monitoring.
    - Integrates with AWS services for security (Cognito, IAM).
    - Enables caching to improve performance.
    API Gateway simplifies building scalable, secure, and reliable APIs with minimal infrastructure management.
  • cloud computation?
    Cloud computation (or cloud computing) refers to the on-demand delivery of computing services—such as servers, storage, databases, networking, software, and analytics—over the internet ("the cloud") instead of on local servers or personal devices. Key Characteristics:
    • On-Demand: Resources are available when needed, without manual intervention.
    • Scalability: Easily scale resources up or down based on demand.
    • Pay-as-you-go: Users pay only for the resources they consume.
    • Accessibility: Services can be accessed from anywhere via the internet.
    Main Cloud Service Models:
    • IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): Offers virtualized computing resources (e.g., AWS EC2, Google Compute Engine).
    • PaaS (Platform as a Service): Provides a platform for developers to build applications (e.g., Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk).
    • SaaS (Software as a Service): Delivers software applications over the internet (e.g., Google Workspace, Salesforce).
    Common Use Cases:
    • Hosting websites and web apps
    • Data backup and disaster recovery
    • Big data analytics and machine learning
    • Streaming services and content delivery

  });

    import { z } from "zod";

    1. String

stringSchema.parse("hello");          // ✅ valid
// stringSchema.parse(123);           // ❌ throws error

const limitedString = z.string().min(5).max(10);
limitedString.parse("abcdef");       // ✅ valid

    2. Number

    const numberSchema = z.number();

numberSchema.parse(123);              // ✅ valid
// numberSchema.parse("123");         // ❌ throws error

// Number with min/max
const rangedNumber = z.number().min(10).max(100);
rangedNumber.parse(50);               // ✅ valid
// rangedNumber.parse(5);             // ❌ too small

    3. Integer

    const intSchema = z.number().int();

intSchema.parse(10);                  // ✅ valid
// intSchema.parse(10.5);             // ❌ not an integer

    4. Boolean

    const boolSchema = z.boolean();

boolSchema.parse(true);               // ✅ valid
// boolSchema.parse("true");          // ❌ throws error

    5. Date

    const dateSchema = z.date();

dateSchema.parse(new Date());         // ✅ valid
// dateSchema.parse("2021-01-01");    // ❌ throws error, use z.string() with .refine for date strings

    6. Array

    const arraySchema = z.array(z.string());

arraySchema.parse(["a", "b", "c"]);   // ✅ valid
// arraySchema.parse(["a", 1]);       // ❌ mixed types

    7. Tuple

    const tupleSchema = z.tuple([z.string(), z.number()]);

tupleSchema.parse(["abc", 123]);      // ✅ valid
// tupleSchema.parse([123, "abc"]);   // ❌ wrong order/types

    8. Object

    const objSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string(),
  age: z.number().int().positive(),
});

objSchema.parse({ name: "John", age: 30 }); // ✅ valid
// objSchema.parse({ name: "John" });       // ❌ missing age

    9. Enum

    const colorEnum = z.enum(["Red", "Green", "Blue"]);

colorEnum.parse("Red");                // ✅ valid
// colorEnum.parse("Yellow");          // ❌ invalid enum value

    10. Literal

    const literalSchema = z.literal("specificValue");

literalSchema.parse("specificValue"); // ✅ valid
// literalSchema.parse("other");       // ❌ not matching literal

    11. Union

    const unionSchema = z.union([z.string(), z.number()]);

unionSchema.parse("hello");            // ✅ valid
unionSchema.parse(123);                // ✅ valid
// unionSchema.parse(true);            // ❌ invalid type

    12. Intersection

    const base = z.object({ id: z.string() });
const extension = z.object({ age: z.number() });

const intersectionSchema = base.and(extension);

intersectionSchema.parse({ id: "abc", age: 25 }); // ✅ valid
// intersectionSchema.parse({ id: "abc" });       // ❌ missing age

    13. Optional and Nullable

    const optionalSchema = z.string().optional();
optionalSchema.parse(undefined);      // ✅ valid
optionalSchema.parse("hello");         // ✅ valid

const nullableSchema = z.string().nullable();
nullableSchema.parse(null);            // ✅ valid
nullableSchema.parse("world");         // ✅ valid

    14. Default

    const defaultSchema = z.string().default("defaultValue");

defaultSchema.parse(undefined);       // "defaultValue"
defaultSchema.parse("input");          // "input"

    15. Record

    // Object with string keys and number values
const recordSchema = z.record(z.number());

recordSchema.parse({ a: 1, b: 2 });   // ✅ valid
// recordSchema.parse({ a: "one" });   // ❌ invalid value type

    16. Custom Validation

});

customSchema.parse("Apple");           // ✅ valid
// customSchema.parse("dummy");       // ❌ validation error

        import { z } from "zod";
    
    function runValidationExamples() {
      try {
        // 1. String
        const stringSchema = z.string();
        console.log("String:", stringSchema.parse("hello"));
    
        // String with min/max length
        const limitedString = z.string().min(5).max(10);
        console.log("Limited String:", limitedString.parse("abcdef"));
    
        // 2. Number
        const numberSchema = z.number();
        console.log("Number:", numberSchema.parse(123));
    
        // Number with min/max
        const rangedNumber = z.number().min(10).max(100);
        console.log("Ranged Number:", rangedNumber.parse(50));
    
        // 3. Integer
        const intSchema = z.number().int();
        console.log("Integer:", intSchema.parse(10));
    
        // 4. Boolean
        const boolSchema = z.boolean();
        console.log("Boolean:", boolSchema.parse(true));
    
        // 5. Date
        const dateSchema = z.date();
        console.log("Date:", dateSchema.parse(new Date()));
    
        // 6. Array
        const arraySchema = z.array(z.string());
        console.log("Array:", arraySchema.parse(["a", "b", "c"]));
    
        // 7. Tuple
        const tupleSchema = z.tuple([z.string(), z.number()]);
        console.log("Tuple:", tupleSchema.parse(["abc", 123]));
    
        // 8. Object
        const objSchema = z.object({
          name: z.string(),
          age: z.number().int().positive(),
        });
        console.log("Object:", objSchema.parse({ name: "John", age: 30 }));
    
        // 9. Enum
        const colorEnum = z.enum(["Red", "Green", "Blue"]);
        console.log("Enum:", colorEnum.parse("Red"));
    
        // 10. Literal
        const literalSchema = z.literal("specificValue");
        console.log("Literal:", literalSchema.parse("specificValue"));
    
        // 11. Union
        const unionSchema = z.union([z.string(), z.number()]);
        console.log("Union (string):", unionSchema.parse("hello"));
        console.log("Union (number):", unionSchema.parse(123));
    
        // 12. Intersection
        const base = z.object({ id: z.string() });
        const extension = z.object({ age: z.number() });
        const intersectionSchema = base.and(extension);
        console.log(
          "Intersection:",
          intersectionSchema.parse({ id: "abc", age: 25 })
        );
    
        // 13. Optional and Nullable
        const optionalSchema = z.string().optional();
        console.log("Optional (undefined):", optionalSchema.parse(undefined));
        console.log("Optional (string):", optionalSchema.parse("hello"));
    
        const nullableSchema = z.string().nullable();
        console.log("Nullable (null):", nullableSchema.parse(null));
        console.log("Nullable (string):", nullableSchema.parse("world"));
    
        // 14. Default
        const defaultSchema = z.string().default("defaultValue");
        console.log("Default (undefined):", defaultSchema.parse(undefined));
        console.log("Default (input):", defaultSchema.parse("input"));
    
        // 15. Record
        const recordSchema = z.record(z.number());
        console.log("Record:", recordSchema.parse({ a: 1, b: 2 }));
    
        // 16. Custom validation
        const customSchema = z.string().refine((val) => val.startsWith("A"), {
          message: "Must start with 'A'",
        });
        console.log("Custom validation:", customSchema.parse("Apple"));
      } catch (e) {
        if (e instanceof z.ZodError) {
          console.error("Validation error:", e.errors);
        } else {
          console.error(e);
        }
      }
    }
    
    runValidationExamples();
  • Input Validation

    Input validation is the process of verifying user input to ensure it meets the expected format, type, or value constraints before further processing.

    2. Zod Validation Example

    Install: npm install zod

    import { z } from "zod";
      
      const userSchema = z.object({
        username: z.string().min(3),
        age: z.number().int().positive(),
      });
      
      const result = userSchema.safeParse({
        username: "JohnDoe",
        age: 25,
      });
      
      if (!result.success) {
        console.log(result.error.format());
      } else {
        console.log("Valid:", result.data);
      }

    ✅ Pros of Zod:

    • Functional and immutable
    • Type-safe with TypeScript
    • No decorators needed

    🚫 Cons of Zod:

    • Not decorator-based (if you prefer that style)

    3. Class Validator Example

    Install: npm install class-validator class-transformer

    import { IsString, IsInt, MinLength, IsPositive } from "class-validator";
      import { plainToInstance } from "class-transformer";
      
      class CreateUserDto {
        @IsString()
        @MinLength(3)
        username: string;
      
        @IsInt()
        @IsPositive()
        age: number;
      }
      
      const input = { username: "JohnDoe", age: 25 };
      const user = plainToInstance(CreateUserDto, input);
      
      import { validate } from "class-validator";
      
      validate(user).then(errors => {
        if (errors.length > 0) {
          console.log("Validation failed:", errors);
        } else {
          console.log("Valid:", user);
        }
      });

    ✅ Pros of Class Validator:

    • Decorator-based (OOP-friendly)
    • Widely used in NestJS
    • Supports class-transformer for parsing/transforming inputs

    🚫 Cons of Class Validator:

    • More verbose setup
    • Requires decorators and class-based code

    4. When to Use Which?

    • Zod: Best for functional programming, schema-first validation, and fast prototyping.
    • Class Validator: Ideal for OOP-style architecture and NestJS applications.

    5. Summary Table

    Feature Zod Class Validator
    Style Functional OOP / Decorator-based
    TypeScript Support Excellent (type inference) Good (requires class definitions)
    Integration Framework-agnostic Popular in NestJS
    Dependencies Lightweight Requires decorators & class-transformer

  • Example : 01 : Koa 
    
  //npm install koa koa-router koa-bodyparser mongoose

  const Koa = require('koa');
  const Router = require('koa-router');
  const bodyParser = require('koa-bodyparser');
  const mongoose = require('mongoose');
  
  const app = new Koa();
  const router = new Router();
  
  // Connect to MongoDB
  mongoose.connect('mongodb://localhost:27017/studentdb', {
    useNewUrlParser: true,
    useUnifiedTopology: true,
  });
  
  // Student Schema
  const StudentSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
    name: String,
    age: Number,
    department: String,
    email: String,
  });
  
  const Student = mongoose.model('Student', StudentSchema);
  
  // Middleware
  app.use(bodyParser());
  
  // Create student
  router.post('/students', async (ctx) => {
    const newStudent = new Student(ctx.request.body);
    const saved = await newStudent.save();
    ctx.body = saved;
  });
  
  // Get all students
  router.get('/students', async (ctx) => {
    const students = await Student.find();
    ctx.body = students;
  });
  
  // Get one student by ID
  router.get('/students/:id', async (ctx) => {
    const student = await Student.findById(ctx.params.id);
    if (!student) {
      ctx.status = 404;
      ctx.body = { error: 'Student not found' };
    } else {
      ctx.body = student;
    }
  });
  
  // Update student
  router.put('/students/:id', async (ctx) => {
    const updated = await Student.findByIdAndUpdate(ctx.params.id, ctx.request.body, {
      new: true,
    });
    if (!updated) {
      ctx.status = 404;
      ctx.body = { error: 'Student not found' };
    } else {
      ctx.body = updated;
    }
  });
  
  // Delete student
  router.delete('/students/:id', async (ctx) => {
    const deleted = await Student.findByIdAndDelete(ctx.params.id);
    if (!deleted) {
      ctx.status = 404;
      ctx.body = { error: 'Student not found' };
    } else {
      ctx.body = { message: 'Student deleted successfully' };
    }
  });
  
  // Apply routes
  app.use(router.routes()).use(router.allowedMethods());
  
  // Start server
  app.listen(3000, () => {
    console.log('Koa server running on http://localhost:3000');
  });

  • Express.js 🆚 LoopBack?
    • Feature Comparison
      Feature Express.js LoopBack
      Type Web framework API framework built on top of Express
      Level Minimal, unopinionated Full-featured, opinionated
      Use Case General-purpose web apps and APIs Rapid API creation, especially REST and OpenAPI
      Ease of Use Lightweight and flexible, but more manual Easier for building complex APIs out of the box
      Boilerplate Minimal, you write routes, logic, etc. manually Provides scaffolding, CLI tools, and auto-generated APIs
      ORM Support Needs third-party libraries like Sequelize, TypeORM Built-in powerful ORM (supports SQL, MongoDB, etc.)
      Data Sources No built-in support Rich support: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, REST, SOAP, etc.
      Auto REST APIs No, routes must be manually written Yes, auto-generated from models
      Swagger / OpenAPI Requires third-party tools Built-in OpenAPI spec generation
      GraphQL Support Needs separate setup Available with extensions/plugins
      Learning Curve Easy to start, grows with complexity Steeper learning curve due to built-in features
      Community & Ecosystem Massive, widely used Smaller but focused on enterprise APIs
      Maintained By Open source (Node.js community) Initially IBM, now maintained by StrongLoop and the community
      Version Active (v4+) Active (LoopBack 4 is latest major version)
    • When to Use Express.js
      • You want full control over app structure.
      • Building custom web apps or microservices.
      • Prefer simplicity and modular architecture.
      • Integrating backend with React, Angular, etc.
    • When to Use LoopBack
      • Building enterprise-grade REST APIs.
      • Need fast API development from data models.
      • Require Swagger/OpenAPI UI support.
      • Support for multiple data sources and connectors.
      • Want auto-generated model-based APIs.
    • Summary

      Express.js is great for flexibility and custom workflows. LoopBack is ideal for API-first, enterprise-level backend development.

      Pro Tip: Use Express for custom logic or small services. Choose LoopBack for large-scale API platforms with database and third-party integrations.

  • LoopBack
    • OpenAPI?

      OpenAPI is a standard specification for describing RESTful APIs. It offers a language-agnostic way to define, document, and consume APIs. Tools like Swagger UI are commonly used with it.

    • Official Definition
      The OpenAPI Specification (OAS) defines a standard, programming language-agnostic interface description for REST APIs. It allows humans and computers to understand the service without accessing the source code.
    • Key Features
      Feature Description
      API Documentation Automatically generates docs for API endpoints
      Language-Agnostic Works with any language (Node.js, Java, etc.)
      Tool Support Swagger UI, Postman, Redoc, Codegen
      Schema Definition Define models and request/response schemas
      Interactive Docs Try APIs live from a browser
      Contract-First Dev Design APIs before writing code
      Code Generation Generate SDKs and servers in many languages
    • Example (OpenAPI 3.0 YAML) 
      
  openapi: 3.0.0
  info:
    title: Book Store API
    version: 1.0.0
  paths:
    /books:
      get:
        summary: List all books
        responses:
          '200':
            description: A JSON array of books
            content:
              application/json:
                schema:
                  type: array
                  items:
                    $ref: '#/components/schemas/Book'
  components:
    schemas:
      Book:
        type: object
        properties:
          id:
            type: integer
          title:
            type: string
          author:
            type: string
    • Benefits
      • Developer-friendly interactive documentation
      • Promotes standardization and consistency
      • Supports mock servers, testing, validation
      • Works well with Postman, CI/CD pipelines
    • Popular Tools that Use OpenAPI
      Tool Purpose
      Swagger UI Interactive API documentation
      Swagger Editor Design and preview OpenAPI specs
      OpenAPI Generator Generate SDKs and server stubs
      Postman Import OpenAPI specs to test APIs
      Redoc Generate clean, modern API docs
    • Use Cases
      • API-first development
      • Automated API documentation
      • Generating client SDKs
      • Mocking and testing APIs
      • API governance and validation
    • Need Code Example?

      Let me know if you want a working OpenAPI integration example in Express, NestJS, or LoopBack.

  • Fastify vs LoopBack
    Feature Fastify LoopBack
    Type Web framework focused on speed API framework built on top of Express
    Performance Extremely fast, optimized for low overhead Good performance but more abstraction
    Flexibility Minimal and unopinionated Highly opinionated and structured
    Use Case Microservices, performance-critical apps Enterprise-grade REST API development
    Built-in Features Lightweight plugins, needs manual setup Auto REST APIs, OpenAPI, validations, models
    Schema Validation Built-in with JSON Schema Built-in with decorators and types
    ORM/DB Support Needs manual integration (e.g. Prisma, TypeORM) Built-in repository pattern and datasource connectors
    Swagger / OpenAPI Available via plugins Built-in OpenAPI support
    Learning Curve Easy to learn, less magic Steeper due to structure and features
    Community & Ecosystem Growing rapidly, plugin-based Stable, used in enterprise API platforms
    Maintenance Actively maintained by community Maintained by community and OpenJS Foundation

    When to use Fastify:

    • You need high-performance HTTP APIs
    • You want full control over plugins and architecture
    • You are building lightweight microservices

    When to use LoopBack:

    • You need a structured enterprise-grade API solution
    • You want auto-generated REST endpoints
    • You are dealing with multiple datasources and business models

    Conclusion: Fastify is great for minimal, fast, and custom services. LoopBack shines in full-featured, model-driven API platforms for enterprise-grade applications.

  • LoopBack vs NestJS
    Feature LoopBack NestJS
    Framework Type Full-featured API framework built on Express Modular, progressive Node.js framework inspired by Angular
    Architecture Model-driven, declarative Modular, layered (controllers, services, providers)
    Learning Curve Steeper due to auto-generated components and decorators Moderate, easier for Angular/TypeScript developers
    Use Case Enterprise APIs, especially data-heavy REST services General-purpose backend development (REST, GraphQL, WebSockets)
    ORM Support Built-in repository and connector system Supports TypeORM, Sequelize, Prisma, MikroORM, Mongoose, etc.
    Database Support Strong integration with SQL and NoSQL via connectors Flexible, depends on chosen ORM
    OpenAPI/Swagger Built-in OpenAPI support Built-in Swagger via decorators
    Microservices Limited, but can be extended First-class microservice support with transport layers (Redis, NATS, Kafka)
    GraphQL Partial support via community plugins First-class support with @nestjs/graphql
    Testing Supported with Mocha, Chai Excellent support with Jest and built-in test utilities
    Community & Ecosystem Smaller, mostly focused on enterprises Very active and growing rapidly
    CLI Support Yes, LoopBack CLI with generators Yes, Nest CLI for scaffolding and generation

    When to Use LoopBack:

    • You need rapid REST API creation from models
    • You work with multiple databases or legacy SOAP/REST services
    • You need built-in OpenAPI and model validation

    When to Use NestJS:

    • You prefer modern TypeScript development
    • You are building scalable microservices or GraphQL APIs
    • You want full control over architecture and testing

    Conclusion: LoopBack is ideal for model-driven enterprise APIs with auto-generated endpoints. NestJS is better suited for modular, testable, and scalable applications with diverse use cases (REST, GraphQL, microservices).

  • Fastify vs NestJS
    Feature Fastify NestJS
    Framework Type Minimal and high-performance web framework Modular and scalable Node.js framework built with TypeScript
    Performance Very fast and optimized for speed Good performance, uses Fastify or Express as HTTP adapter
    Architecture Unopinionated, plugin-based Opinionated, inspired by Angular (controllers, services, modules)
    Use Case Microservices, serverless functions, fast APIs Enterprise apps, REST APIs, GraphQL, WebSockets
    TypeScript Support Good, but not enforced First-class TypeScript support by default
    Built-in Features Minimal, most features require plugins Includes DI, testing, pipes, interceptors, filters
    Swagger/OpenAPI Via fastify-swagger plugin Built-in decorators and Swagger module
    Microservices Custom setup needed First-class microservice support with transports like Redis, NATS, Kafka
    GraphQL Support Manual integration needed Integrated via @nestjs/graphql module
    Learning Curve Low, simple and direct Moderate, especially if new to Angular-style architecture
    Testing Manual setup with tools like tap or jest Built-in support with Jest and testing utilities
    Community & Ecosystem Smaller but growing Large, active, and rapidly growing

    When to Use Fastify:

    • You need high-speed APIs with low overhead
    • You prefer flexibility and a plugin-driven architecture
    • You are building microservices or serverless endpoints

    When to Use NestJS:

    • You want a full-fledged framework with structure and features
    • You are building large-scale enterprise apps
    • You need built-in support for REST, GraphQL, and microservices

    Conclusion: Fastify is ideal for lightweight, blazing-fast applications with custom setups. NestJS is better for structured, feature-rich, and scalable applications with enterprise-level needs.

  • implement custom authentication in LoopBack 4?
    You use LoopBack's authentication component, create a custom strategy, and bind it using @authenticate decorator.
  • interceptors used for in LoopBack?
    Interceptors are used to add logic before or after method invocations, for tasks like logging, validation, or error handling.
  • define a many-to-many relationship?
    Use @hasMany through with an intermediate model that has two belongsTo relations pointing to the main entities.
  • purpose of the inclusion resolver?
    It enables you to fetch related models in a single query using the filter include syntax.
  • override a repository method?
    Extend the base method in your repository class and implement custom logic as needed.
  • use of a service proxy?
    Service proxies allow LoopBack to consume external REST or SOAP APIs as if they were local services.
  • validate input data in a controller method?
    Use @requestBody with a schema definition, or define validation rules in the model using jsonSchema.
  • mixins in LoopBack 4?
    Mixins are reusable classes that can add behavior to models, repositories, or controllers through inheritance.
  • difference between repository pattern and service pattern?
    Repository is for data access logic, while service pattern is used for business logic, possibly across multiple models.
  • write unit tests for a controller?
    Use the @loopback/testlab package to create a test client and send requests to controller methods.
  • use environment variables in LoopBack 4?
    Use dotenv to load .env files and access variables using process.env inside config files or datasources.
  • How to handle lifecycle events in LoopBack 4?
    Use observers that implement the LifeCycleObserver interface and register them in application.ts.
  • apply global middleware?
    Register a middleware function using app.middleware and pass a binding key or handler function.
  • secure specific endpoints?
    Use the @authenticate decorator on controller methods to restrict access based on user roles or strategies.
  • How to log all incoming HTTP requests?
    Create a custom logging middleware and bind it to run before the request reaches the controller.
  • components in LoopBack?
    Components are extension packages that can register models, repositories, controllers, bindings, and lifecycle observers.
  • inject a repository into another repository?
    Use @repository.getter to lazily inject a dependent repository to avoid circular dependencies.
  • handle transactions in LoopBack with MongoDB?
    MongoDB transaction support requires using sessions manually and is supported when using replica sets.
  • define dynamic endpoints?
    Use path parameters like /items/{id} and define them with @param.path.string or @param.path.number.
  • expose a GraphQL endpoint in LoopBack?
    LoopBack does not support GraphQL out of the box, but you can integrate it manually using Apollo Server with Express.
  • extend the OpenAPI specification of an endpoint?
    Use the @operation decorator or add custom metadata in @get, @post, etc., to add tags, descriptions, or responses.
  • customize the default error response?
    Override the Sequence handler and catch exceptions to format custom error messages.
  • a binding in LoopBack?
    A binding is a way to register values or providers into the IoC container so they can be injected elsewhere.
  • bind a custom configuration value?
    Use app.bind('config.key').to(value) and inject it where needed using @inject('config.key').
  • access the current authenticated user?
    Inject the securityBindings.USER key using @inject and access the user's profile object.
  • add custom headers to a response?
    Inject the Response object using @inject(RestBindings.Http.RESPONSE) and modify headers directly.
  • use of @lifeCycleObserver?
    It marks a class to be run at application start or stop, useful for resources like connections or cron jobs.
  • write integration tests for APIs?
    Use supertest and the app instance from your application to perform requests and assert responses.
  • pass query parameters to a controller method?
    Use @param.query.string or @param.query.number decorators for optional filter parameters.
  • return custom response formats?
    Use the controller method to structure the JSON response manually before returning it.
  • LoopBack?
    LoopBack is a Node.js framework for building APIs and connecting them with backend data sources.
  • latest version of LoopBack?
    The latest version is LoopBack 4, a complete rewrite with TypeScript and modular architecture.
  • create a new LoopBack application?
    You use the command lb4 app to scaffold a new LoopBack 4 application.
  • a model in LoopBack?
    A model represents the shape of application data, usually mapping to a database table or collection.
  • a repository in LoopBack?
    A repository handles the logic of data access and persistence using models and datasources.
  • a controller in LoopBack?
    A controller handles incoming HTTP requests and maps them to business logic or repository calls.
  • connect LoopBack to MongoDB?
    Use lb4 datasource and select the MongoDB connector, then provide the connection URL.
  • a datasource in LoopBack?
    A datasource configures how LoopBack connects to external systems like databases or APIs.
  • @model decorator used for?
    It defines a class as a LoopBack model with metadata for validation and schema generation.
  • purpose of the @property decorator?
    It defines a property of a model and its metadata like type, required status, and id generation.
  • What command is used to create a model?
    Use lb4 model to create a new model and define its properties.
  • What command creates a repository?
    Use lb4 repository and select the model and datasource.
  • dependency injection in LoopBack?
    Dependency injection is used to inject services or repositories into classes using decorators like @inject.
  • generate a controller in LoopBack?
    Use lb4 controller and choose REST Controller with CRUD operations.
  • define a one-to-many relation?
    Use @hasMany in the source model and @belongsTo in the target model.
  • @hasMany decorator?
    It defines a one-to-many relationship between two models.
  • @belongsTo decorator?
    It defines a reverse relationship where one model belongs to another.
  • test LoopBack APIs?
    You can use tools like Postman or built-in Swagger UI at /explorer endpoint.
  • /explorer route used for?
    It serves the Swagger UI where you can test and explore your LoopBack API endpoints.
  • LoopBack CLI used for?
    The CLI helps scaffold models, datasources, repositories, controllers, and more.
  • Can you customize REST endpoints in LoopBack?
    Yes, you can define custom routes and logic inside controller methods.
  • How to define validation rules on model properties?
    Use the @property decorator with options like required: true, jsonSchema, or enum.
  • difference between Entity and Model base classes?
    Entity includes an id property and is used for persisted models; Model is for non-persisted data structures.
  • an inclusion resolver?
    It allows including related models in query results using the include filter.
  • enable relations in controller endpoints?
    Use repository factory methods like createHasManyRepositoryFor and registerInclusionResolver.
  • an observer in LoopBack?
    An observer is a class that listens to application lifecycle events like start and stop.
  • How to define environment-specific configurations?
    Use .env files and process.env in your configuration or datasource files.
  • Can LoopBack expose GraphQL APIs?
    Not out of the box, but community extensions and custom implementation can expose GraphQL endpoints.
  • interceptors in LoopBack?
    Interceptors are functions that run before or after method invocations for cross-cutting concerns like logging.
  • How to run a LoopBack project?
    Run npm start or node . to start the LoopBack REST server.
  • implement multi-tenancy in LoopBack 4?
    Multi-tenancy can be implemented by customizing repositories to scope data by tenant ID and using interceptors or custom providers to inject tenant context.
  • extend the default REST sequence in LoopBack 4?
    You create a custom sequence class by implementing SequenceHandler and bind it in the application using app.sequence.
  • use of BindingScopes in LoopBack?
    BindingScopes define how often a binding is resolved: singleton for app-wide, transient for new instances every time, and context for per-request instantiation.
  • How to write a custom authentication strategy?
    Create a class implementing AuthenticationStrategy, define a name, and implement the authenticate method to validate tokens or credentials.
  • use context bindings to inject dynamic values?
    Use context.bind to register values dynamically and context.get or @inject to retrieve them in classes or methods.
  • implement CQRS in LoopBack?
    CQRS can be implemented by separating read and write operations into different repositories or services, and using events or messaging for synchronization.
  • implement event-driven architecture in LoopBack?
    Use observers or service bindings that publish events using libraries like EventEmitter, RabbitMQ, or Kafka, and consume them in listeners.
  • life cycle observers used for in LoopBack 4?
    Lifecycle observers are used to run initialization or cleanup logic during application start and stop events.
  • register dynamic routes at runtime?
    You can use app.route or app.handler to programmatically register routes with custom handlers during boot.
  • define polymorphic relations in LoopBack 4?
    Polymorphic relations are not natively supported but can be modeled using custom logic with discriminator fields and multiple repository lookups.
  • How to override default CRUD endpoints in a controller?
    Skip lb4 controller CRUD generation and manually implement the endpoints using custom logic and decorated methods like @get, @post.
  • configure logging and monitoring?
    Integrate logging libraries like Winston or Pino using middleware or interceptors, and forward logs to monitoring services like ELK or CloudWatch.
  • structure a monorepo with multiple LoopBack services?
    Use Nx or Lerna to manage multiple LoopBack apps and libraries within a shared monorepo workspace for microservices or modular architecture.
  • implement complex filters like OR, AND with relations?
    Use the filter syntax with where conditions and logical operators, and include nested filters in scope of relations using include.
  • How to enforce schema validation for nested JSON objects?
    Use @model and @property with type object and define jsonSchema with required fields and constraints.
  • use LoopBack 4 with GraphQL?
    You can use third-party packages like apollo-server-express and manually bind models and resolvers to create GraphQL endpoints.
  • a context view in LoopBack 4?
    A ContextView is a dynamic binding observer that tracks multiple bindings in the application context for features like watching for service changes.
  • How to handle database migrations programmatically?
    Use schemaMigration with auto-migrate or auto-update in application.ts or booters to sync models to DB at runtime.
  • restrict access by role or permission?
    Implement an authorization component with custom voter functions and use @authorize decorators in controller methods.
  • How to implement soft deletes in LoopBack 4?
    Add an isDeleted field and override the delete methods in the repository to update the flag instead of removing the record.
  • add API versioning in LoopBack?
    Prefix controllers with versioned routes like /v1/users and separate logic or models per version if needed.
  • How to manage multiple datasources in a single app?
    Create separate datasource files and bind them using different names. Assign each model its own datasource via repository.
  • How to write a custom parameter decorator?
    Create a function using createParamDecorator and access the request or context to resolve the value.
  • perform file uploads in LoopBack 4?
    Use the formidable package or multer middleware in a custom controller method, and parse the multipart request manually.
  • How to apply global rate limiting in LoopBack?
    Use middleware like express-rate-limit and register it with app.middleware in the application configuration.
  • How to secure REST APIs with OAuth2 in LoopBack?
    Integrate Passport strategies for OAuth2 and use @authenticate with a custom strategy that handles token validation.
  • How to stream large files through a LoopBack endpoint?
    Use the response object and Node.js streams to pipe large files in a controller without loading them entirely into memory.
  • How to override OpenAPI metadata globally?
    Customize the spec enhancement in application.ts by modifying app.api or providing a custom OpenApiSpecEnhancer.
  • build a multi-module plugin-based system?
    Use custom components to modularize features and register them dynamically in the application during boot.
  • How to expose health check or metrics endpoints?
    Implement a custom controller for /health and integrate with Prometheus by exposing a /metrics route using prom-client.

    DB Connection 

    import {juggler} from '@loopback/repository';
    import {inject, lifeCycleObserver, LifeCycleObserver} from '@loopback/core';

    @lifeCycleObserver('datasource')
    export class MongodbDataSource extends juggler.DataSource
    implements LifeCycleObserver {
        static dataSourceName = 'MongoDB';

        constructor(
            @inject('datasources.config.MongoDB', {optional: true})
            dsConfig: object = {
            name: 'MongoDB',
            connector: 'mongodb',
            url: 'mongodb://localhost:27017/testdb',
            },
        ) {
            super(dsConfig);
        }
    }
    
    
    Models

    import {Entity, model, property, hasMany} from '@loopback/repository';
    import {State} from './state.model';
    
    @model()
    export class Country extends Entity {
      @property({type: 'string', id: true, generated: true})
      id?: string;
    
      @property({type: 'string', required: true})
      name: string;
    
      @hasMany(() => State)
      states: State[];
    }
    
    
    
    import {Entity, model, property, belongsTo} from '@loopback/repository';
    import {Country} from './country.model';
    
    @model()
    export class State extends Entity {
      @property({type: 'string', id: true, generated: true})
      id?: string;
    
      @property({type: 'string', required: true})
      name: string;
    
      @belongsTo(() => Country)
      countryId: string;
    }
    
    
    Repository

    import {DefaultCrudRepository, HasManyRepositoryFactory, repository} from '@loopback/repository';
    import {Country, State} from '../models';
    import {MongodbDataSource} from '../datasources';
    import {inject, Getter} from '@loopback/core';
    import {StateRepository} from './state.repository';
    
    export class CountryRepository extends DefaultCrudRepository<
      Country,
      typeof Country.prototype.id
    > {
      public readonly states: HasManyRepositoryFactory;
    
      constructor(
        @inject('datasources.MongoDB') dataSource: MongodbDataSource,
        @repository.getter('StateRepository')
        protected stateRepositoryGetter: Getter,
      ) {
        super(Country, dataSource);
        this.states = this.createHasManyRepositoryFactoryFor(
          'states',
          stateRepositoryGetter,
        );
        this.registerInclusionResolver('states', this.states.inclusionResolver);
      }

    Unit Testing    

    import {Client, expect} from '@loopback/testlab';
    import {CountryStateApiApplication} from '../../application';
    import {setupApplication} from './test-helper';

    let app: CountryStateApiApplication;
    let client: Client;

    describe('Country-State API', () => {
        before('setupApplication', async () => {
            ({app, client} = await setupApplication());
        });

        after(async () => {
            await app.stop();
        });

        it('creates a country', async () => {
            const country = {name: 'India'};
            const res = await client.post('/countries').send(country).expect(200);
            expect(res.body).to.containDeep(country);
            expect(res.body).to.have.property('id');
        });

        it('creates a state and links to country', async () => {
            const countryRes = await client.post('/countries').send({name: 'USA'});
            const countryId = countryRes.body.id;

            const state = {name: 'California', countryId};
            const stateRes = await client.post('/states').send(state).expect(200);

            expect(stateRes.body).to.containDeep(state);
        });

        it('lists countries with related states', async () => {
            const india = await client.post('/countries').send({name: 'India'});
            const countryId = india.body.id;
            await client.post('/states').send({name: 'West Bengal', countryId});
            await client.post('/states').send({name: 'Gujarat', countryId});

            const res = await client.get('/countries?filter[include][]=states');
            const foundCountry = res.body.find((c: any) => c.id === countryId);
            expect(foundCountry.states).to.be.an.Array();
            expect(foundCountry.states).length(2);
        });

        it('lists states with related country', async () => {
            const res = await client.get('/states?filter[include][]=country');
            for (const state of res.body) {
            expect(state.country).to.be.an.Object();
            expect(state.country.name).to.be.String();
            }
        });
    });

  import {Country} from '../models';
  import {CountryRepository} from '../repositories';
  
  export class CountryController {
    constructor(
      @repository(CountryRepository)
      public countryRepository : CountryRepository,
    ) {}
  
    @post('/countries')
    @response(200, {
      description: 'Country model instance',
      content: {'application/json': {schema: getModelSchemaRef(Country)}},
    })
    async create(
      @requestBody({
        content: {
          'application/json': {
            schema: getModelSchemaRef(Country, {
              title: 'NewCountry',
              exclude: ['id'],
            }),
          },
        },
      })
      country: Omit,
    ): Promise {
      return this.countryRepository.create(country);
    }
  
    @get('/countries/count')
    @response(200, {
      description: 'Country model count',
      content: {'application/json': {schema: CountSchema}},
    })
    async count(
      @param.where(Country) where?: Where,
    ): Promise {
      return this.countryRepository.count(where);
    }
  
    @get('/countries')
    @response(200, {
      description: 'Array of Country model instances',
      content: {
        'application/json': {
          schema: {
            type: 'array',
            items: getModelSchemaRef(Country, {includeRelations: true}),
          },
        },
      },
    })
    async find(
      @param.filter(Country) filter?: Filter,
    ): Promise {
      return this.countryRepository.find(filter);
    }
  
    @patch('/countries')
    @response(200, {
      description: 'Country PATCH success count',
      content: {'application/json': {schema: CountSchema}},
    })
    async updateAll(
      @requestBody({
        content: {
          'application/json': {
            schema: getModelSchemaRef(Country, {partial: true}),
          },
        },
      })
      country: Country,
      @param.where(Country) where?: Where,
    ): Promise {
      return this.countryRepository.updateAll(country, where);
    }
  
    @get('/countries/{id}')
    @response(200, {
      description: 'Country model instance',
      content: {
        'application/json': {
          schema: getModelSchemaRef(Country, {includeRelations: true}),
        },
      },
    })
    async findById(
      @param.path.string('id') id: string,
      @param.filter(Country, {exclude: 'where'}) filter?: FilterExcludingWhere
    ): Promise {
      return this.countryRepository.findById(id, filter);
    }
  
    @patch('/countries/{id}')
    @response(204, {
      description: 'Country PATCH success',
    })
    async updateById(
      @param.path.string('id') id: string,
      @requestBody({

          'application/json': {
            schema: getModelSchemaRef(Country, {partial: true}),
          },

  const fastify = require('fastify')({ logger: true });
  const mongoose = require('mongoose');
  
  // Connect to MongoDB
  mongoose.connect('mongodb://localhost:27017/hoteldb', {
    useNewUrlParser: true,
    useUnifiedTopology: true,
  });
  
  // Define Hotel Schema
  const HotelSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
    name: String,
    city: String,
    address: String,
    price: Number,
  });
  const Hotel = mongoose.model('Hotel', HotelSchema);
  
  // Create Hotel
  fastify.post('/hotels', async (request, reply) => {
    try {
      const hotel = new Hotel(request.body);
      const saved = await hotel.save();
      reply.code(201).send(saved);
    } catch (err) {
      reply.code(500).send({ error: err.message });
    }
  });
  
  // Get All Hotels
  fastify.get('/hotels', async (request, reply) => {
    const hotels = await Hotel.find();
    reply.send(hotels);
  });
  
  // Get Hotel by ID
  fastify.get('/hotels/:id', async (request, reply) => {
    try {
      const hotel = await Hotel.findById(request.params.id);
      if (!hotel) {
        return reply.code(404).send({ error: 'Hotel not found' });
      }
      reply.send(hotel);
    } catch (err) {
      reply.code(500).send({ error: err.message });
    }
  });
  
  // Update Hotel
  fastify.put('/hotels/:id', async (request, reply) => {
    try {
      const updated = await Hotel.findByIdAndUpdate(request.params.id, request.body, {
        new: true,
      });
      if (!updated) {
        return reply.code(404).send({ error: 'Hotel not found' });
      }
      reply.send(updated);
    } catch (err) {
      reply.code(500).send({ error: err.message });
    }
  });
  
  // Delete Hotel
  fastify.delete('/hotels/:id', async (request, reply) => {
    try {
      const deleted = await Hotel.findByIdAndDelete(request.params.id);
      if (!deleted) {
        return reply.code(404).send({ error: 'Hotel not found' });
      }
      reply.send({ message: 'Hotel deleted successfully' });
    } catch (err) {
      reply.code(500).send({ error: err.message });
    }
  });
  
  // Start Server
  const start = async () => {
    try {
      await fastify.listen({ port: 3000 });
      console.log('Server running at http://localhost:3000');
    } catch (err) {
      fastify.log.error(err);
      process.exit(1);
    }
  };
  
  start();

      // server.js
  const fastify = require('fastify')({ logger: true })
  
  // Register a basic route with validation
  fastify.route({
    method: 'POST',
    url: '/user',
    schema: {
      body: {
        type: 'object',
        required: ['name', 'email'],
        properties: {
          name: { type: 'string' },
          email: { type: 'string', format: 'email' },
        }
      },
      response: {
        200: {
          type: 'object',
          properties: {
            id: { type: 'number' },
            name: { type: 'string' },
            email: { type: 'string' }
          }
        }
      }
    },
    handler: async (request, reply) => {
      const { name, email } = request.body
      return { id: 1, name, email }
    }
  })
  
  // Global error handler
  fastify.setErrorHandler(function (error, request, reply) {
    fastify.log.error(error)
    reply.status(500).send({ error: 'Something went wrong' })
  })
  
  // Start server
  const start = async () => {
    try {
      await fastify.listen({ port: 3000 })
      fastify.log.info(`Server running at http://localhost:3000`)
    } catch (err) {
      fastify.log.error(err)
      process.exit(1)
    }
  }
  
  start()
