  • AWS Lambda and how does it work?

    AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs your code in response to events and automatically manages the underlying compute resources.

    • You write code (functions).
    • Upload it to Lambda.
    • Set a trigger (e.g., API Gateway, S3, DynamoDB).
    • Lambda scales automatically and runs only when triggered.
    • You pay only for the time your code runs (billed per millisecond).
  • Lambda Triggers and Examples?

    A trigger is an AWS service/event that invokes a Lambda function. Examples include:

    Trigger Source Example Use Case
    API Gateway RESTful APIs
    S3 Process image upload
    DynamoDB Streams Audit logs on table change
    CloudWatch Events Scheduled tasks (cron jobs)
    SNS/SQS Event-driven messaging
  • Cold Starts in AWS Lambda?

    A cold start occurs when a Lambda function is invoked after a period of inactivity or when AWS scales up new instances.

    • Causes delay due to bootstrapping environment
    • More noticeable in VPC-connected or large-sized functions
    • Can be mitigated using:
      • Provisioned Concurrency
      • Keeping functions warm via CloudWatch or scheduled triggers
  • Limits of AWS Lambda?
    Feature Default Limit (as of 2024)
    Timeout Up to 15 minutes (900 seconds)
    Memory 128 MB to 10,240 MB (10 GB)
    Package Size 50 MB (direct upload) / 250 MB (S3)
    Environment Variables 4 KB
    Concurrency 1,000 per account (soft limit)
    Ephemeral Storage 512 MB default (up to 10 GB optional)
  • How does Lambda handle state and scalability?
    • State: Lambda is stateless. Each invocation is isolated. Use external systems like DynamoDB, S3, or Redis to manage state.
    • Scalability: Lambda automatically scales out by running multiple copies in response to incoming events.
    • No need to manage servers or instances.
    • Can scale from zero to thousands of parallel executions.
  • Lambda?
    AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that lets you run code without provisioning or managing servers.
    Lambda handles the rest—scaling, monitoring, patching, and running your application in response to events.

    Key features of AWS Lambda include:
    • No server management
    • Automatic scaling
    • Sub-second metering (pay only for usage)
    • Event-driven invocation (triggers from over 200 AWS services)
    • Built-in fault tolerance
    • Supports environment variables, versioning, and aliases
    • Integration with VPC, Layers, and Container Images
    AWS Lambda provides a powerful and flexible serverless compute platform. Its key features include:
    • Event-Driven Execution: Automatically triggered by AWS services (e.g., S3, API Gateway, DynamoDB) or external events.
    • No Server Management: No need to provision or manage infrastructure. AWS handles everything.
    • Automatic Scaling: Lambda scales automatically with the number of incoming events.
    • Pay-per-Use Pricing: Billed per millisecond based on the number of requests and compute time used.
    • Supports Multiple Languages: Includes Node.js, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, and custom runtimes.
    • Short-Lived Functions: Functions run up to 15 minutes and then terminate automatically.
    • Built-in Monitoring: Integrated with CloudWatch for logs and metrics.
    • Environment Variables: Store configuration and secrets per environment (e.g., dev, prod).
    • Versioning & Aliases: Create immutable versions of code and route traffic with named aliases.
    • VPC Support: Access private resources in a VPC securely.
    • Provisioned Concurrency: Pre-warm instances to avoid cold starts for latency-sensitive workloads.
    • Lambda Layers: Package and share libraries or dependencies across multiple functions.
  • Lambda: Keeping functions warm using scheduled CloudWatch Events

    In AWS Lambda, cold starts happen when your function is invoked after being idle, causing latency due to container initialization. One common technique to keep Lambda functions warm is using Amazon CloudWatch Events (EventBridge) to invoke the function on a regular schedule.

    ✅ Steps to Keep Lambda Warm with CloudWatch Scheduled Events

    1. Create a CloudWatch Event Rule

    This will run every 5 minutes (or less) to trigger the Lambda and keep it warm.

    Example: rate expression:
    rate(5 minutes)

    Example: cron expression:
    cron(0/5 * * * ? *)

    2. Attach Lambda as the Target

    Use the AWS Management Console or CLI to set the Lambda function as the target of the scheduled rule.

    3. Lambda Code (Optional: Check source to filter warm-up calls)
    exports.handler = async (event) => {
if (event.source === 'aws.events') {
  console.log("Warm-up ping received");
  return "Lambda is warm";
}

// Normal Lambda logic here
console.log("Normal execution");
return "Processed request";
};

    🛠️ AWS CLI Example

    aws events put-rule \
    --name keep-lambda-warm \
    --schedule-expression "rate(5 minutes)"
  
  aws lambda add-permission \
    --function-name myLambdaFunction \
    --statement-id allow-scheduled-invoke \
    --action 'lambda:InvokeFunction' \
    --principal events.amazonaws.com \
    --source-arn arn:aws:events:<region>:<account-id>:rule/keep-lambda-warm
  
  aws events put-targets \
    --rule keep-lambda-warm \
    --targets "Id"="1","Arn"="arn:aws:lambda:<region>:<account-id>:function:myLambdaFunction"

    🔥 Best Practices

    • Use a lightweight payload to reduce cost.
    • For multiple Lambdas, consolidate into a single “warming” function that calls others asynchronously.
    • Use Provisioned Concurrency for critical APIs (more reliable but has cost).
  • Step-by-Step: Create a CloudWatch Event Rule to keep an API warm

    This guide shows how to use Amazon EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) to ping an API endpoint like:

    https://pc0wd3fim2.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/

    ✅ Goal

    Invoke a Lambda function or API Gateway endpoint every 5 minutes to keep it warm and avoid cold starts.

    🧩 Step-by-Step: Using AWS Console to Call an API URL

    🟢 1. Go to EventBridge
    • Sign in to the AWS Console
    • Open Amazon EventBridge from the "Management & Governance" section
    🟢 2. Create Rule
    • Click “Rules” > “Create rule”
    • Rule name: keep-api-warm
    • Description: Keep API Gateway warm
    • Event Source: “EventBridge (default bus)”
    • Rule type: “Schedule”
    🟢 3. Set Schedule
    • Select: rate expression
    • Input: rate(5 minutes)
    🟢 4. Add Target (API Gateway or Custom URL)

    Since you are calling an external API endpoint:

    • Choose Target type: API destination
    • Click Create a new API destination
    🔧 Set up API Destination
    • Name: KeepWarmDestination
    • Method: GET or POST (depending on your endpoint)
    • Endpoint URL: https://pc0wd3fim2.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/
    • Create a Connection (e.g., AnonymousConnection) if no auth is needed
    • Choose No authentication or API Key as required

    Then click Next, review, and Create rule.

    ✅ Result

    EventBridge will call your API endpoint every 5 minutes to prevent cold starts.

    ⚠️ Notes

    • Ensure the API doesn’t require a specific payload (default is empty).
    • Monitor usage via CloudWatch Logs.
    • You can also create a “warm-up Lambda” that pings the endpoint if more flexibility is needed.
  • How does AWS Lambda pricing work?
    AWS Lambda charges are based on:
    • Number of requests: First 1 million requests/month are free. After that, it's $0.20 per million requests.
    • Duration: Billed per millisecond from the time your code begins executing until it returns or otherwise terminates. Depends on the memory allocated.
    Example: If your function runs for 200ms and uses 128MB memory, you only pay for that exact duration and size.
  • What triggers can invoke a Lambda function?
    Lambda can be triggered by various AWS services, including:
    • API Gateway (HTTP requests)
    • S3 (file uploads, deletions)
    • DynamoDB Streams
    • SNS (notifications)
    • SQS (queues)
    • CloudWatch Events & Logs
    • Cognito, Alexa Skills, EventBridge, etc.
    Lambda can also be triggered manually using the AWS SDK or CLI.
  • supported languages in AWS Lambda?
    AWS Lambda natively supports:
    • Node.js
    • Python
    • Java
    • Go
    • C# (.NET Core)
    • Ruby
    It also supports custom runtimes and container images, allowing you to use any language.
  • maximum execution time of a Lambda function?
    The maximum timeout for a Lambda function is 15 minutes (900 seconds) per invocation. You can configure the timeout in the Lambda function settings depending on your use case.
  • monitor a Lambda function?
    Lambda integrates with AWS CloudWatch to provide monitoring:
    • CloudWatch Logs: Automatically captures console output and errors.
    • CloudWatch Metrics: Tracks invocation count, duration, error count, throttles, and more.
    • CloudWatch Alarms: Trigger notifications based on metric thresholds.
    • X-Ray: For distributed tracing and performance analysis.
  • a cold start in AWS Lambda?
    A cold start occurs when AWS needs to create a new container to run your Lambda function—for example, when there's no existing warm instance available. It includes the time taken to:
    • Provision the runtime container
    • Download your function code
    • Initialize dependencies
    Cold starts introduce extra latency (usually 100ms–1s). They are more noticeable with VPC-configured or infrequently used functions.
  • reduce cold start time?
    You can reduce cold start time in AWS Lambda by:
    • Using lighter runtimes like Node.js or Go (faster startup)
    • Minimizing initialization code and package size
    • Keeping functions warm using scheduled CloudWatch Events
    • Avoiding VPC connections unless required (or optimizing them)
    • Using Provisioned Concurrency (pre-warms containers to eliminate cold starts)
  • difference between synchronous and asynchronous invocation?
    Synchronous Invocation: Caller waits for the function to process and return a result. Example: API Gateway.
    Asynchronous Invocation: Caller sends the request and continues without waiting for a response. Example: S3 or SNS.
    Differences:
    • Synchronous = real-time; Asynchronous = event-based
    • Synchronous errors are returned immediately; asynchronous are logged
  • How does concurrency work in Lambda?
    Concurrency is the number of instances that can run in parallel:
    • Unreserved concurrency: Default limit shared across functions (e.g. 1000)
    • Reserved concurrency: Guarantees a specific number of concurrent executions for a function
    • Provisioned concurrency: Keeps containers initialized and ready to respond instantly
    If concurrency limit is hit, excess requests are throttled.
  • default memory limit and how can it be changed?
    Default Memory: 128 MB
    Range: 128 MB to 10,240 MB (10 GB), in 1 MB increments.
    You can change it from:
    • AWS Console → Lambda → Configuration → Memory
    • Or via CLI: aws lambda update-function-configuration
  • handle errors in AWS Lambda?
    You can handle errors in Lambda using:
    • Try-catch blocks: Handle exceptions in your code
    • Return meaningful error responses (for synchronous calls)
    • Dead Letter Queues (DLQs): Capture failed async invocations
    • CloudWatch Logs: View stack traces and error details
    • Retries: Lambda automatically retries failed async events (2 times by default)
  • Can a Lambda function call another Lambda function?
    Yes, a Lambda function can invoke another Lambda using the AWS SDK or AWS CLI. This is useful for microservice architectures or function chaining.
    Example in Node.js: 
    const AWS = require('aws-sdk');
const lambda = new AWS.Lambda();
lambda.invoke({
FunctionName: 'anotherLambdaFunction',
Payload: JSON.stringify({ key: 'value' })
}, (err, data) => { ... });
    Make sure the calling Lambda has the IAM permission lambda:InvokeFunction.
  • version and alias a Lambda function?
    Versioning: Every time you publish a function version, AWS creates an immutable snapshot of the code and configuration.
    Alias: Acts as a pointer to a specific version. Useful for traffic shifting (e.g., prod, beta aliases).
    Example:
    • $LATEST → Draft code
    • 1, 2, etc. → Published versions
    • alias: prod → version: 5
  • Lambda@Edge?
    Lambda@Edge is an extension of AWS Lambda that lets you run functions at AWS edge locations. It's integrated with Amazon CloudFront and is used for:
    • Customizing CDN content before it's delivered
    • Implementing security/auth at the edge
    • Personalizing content based on headers, cookies, etc.
    • Modifying requests/responses without origin call
    It improves performance and reduces latency by moving compute closer to the user.
  • difference between Lambda and EC2?
    AWS Lambda: Serverless, event-driven compute service. No server management; pay-per-invocation.
    EC2: Virtual server in the cloud. You manage OS, scaling, patching.

    Key Differences:
    • Lambda is event-based; EC2 is instance-based
    • Lambda scales automatically; EC2 needs manual or auto-scaling setup
    • Lambda is billed per millisecond; EC2 is billed per second or hour
    • Lambda can't be used for long-running tasks (max 15 minutes); EC2 can run indefinitely
  • deploy a Lambda function?
    You can deploy a Lambda function using:
    • AWS Console: Upload .zip or use inline editor
    • AWS CLI: Use aws lambda create-function or update-function-code
    • Infrastructure as Code: Tools like AWS SAM, Serverless Framework, Terraform, or CloudFormation
    • CI/CD Pipelines: Using CodePipeline, GitHub Actions, or Jenkins
  • How can environment variables be used in Lambda?
    Lambda supports environment variables to:
    • Store config values (DB URLs, API keys, etc.)
    • Separate environment-specific settings (dev, test, prod)
    Access: Use process.env.VARIABLE_NAME in your function code.
    Security: You can encrypt them using KMS and manage access with IAM policies.
  • How does IAM relate to Lambda function permissions?
    AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls who can:
    • Create, modify, delete Lambda functions
    • Assign permissions to Lambda functions
    • Invoke functions or access resources Lambda interacts with
    Lambda uses execution roles (IAM roles) to interact with other AWS services securely.
  • Lambda execution role?
    The execution role is an IAM role assumed by the Lambda function at runtime. It defines:
    • Which AWS services the function can access (e.g., S3, DynamoDB)
    • Permission to write logs to CloudWatch
    Policy Example: 
    {
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "logs:CreateLogStream"],
    "Resource": "*"
  }
  • connect Lambda to VPC?
    Lambda can access private VPC resources (e.g., RDS, EC2) by assigning:
    • VPC ID
    • Subnets with NAT Gateway (for internet access)
    • Security groups (to control access)
    This allows your Lambda to operate securely within your VPC.
  • integrate AWS Lambda with API Gateway?
    You can expose your Lambda function via REST or HTTP APIs using API Gateway:
    • Create a REST API in API Gateway
    • Define resources and methods (e.g., GET /users)
    • Set integration type as Lambda function
    • Deploy the API to a stage (e.g., /prod)
    This setup allows clients to invoke Lambda functions over HTTPS.
  • use of the Lambda Layers feature?
    Lambda Layers are a way to package and reuse shared code or dependencies across multiple functions. Use cases:
    • Third-party libraries (e.g., bcrypt, pandas)
    • Custom utility modules
    • Large binaries or compiled packages
    Benefits: Reduces deployment size and duplication across functions.
  • difference between Lambda and Step Functions?
    AWS Lambda: Executes single tasks triggered by events.
    AWS Step Functions: Orchestrates multiple AWS services/functions in workflows with logic.
    Comparison:
    • Lambda = compute unit; Step Functions = workflow engine
    • Step Functions handle retries, timeouts, branching, error catching
    • Useful for building complex apps like ETL pipelines, order processing, etc.
  • AWS Step Functions in context of AWS Lambda?

    AWS Step Functions is a visual workflow service that lets you coordinate multiple AWS services — especially Lambda functions — into serverless workflows using state machines.

    🔄 Use Case

    You use Step Functions when you need to:

    • Orchestrate multiple Lambda functions in sequence or parallel
    • Handle retries, timeouts, and error-catching logic easily
    • Implement workflows like:
      • Order processing
      • Approval flows
      • ETL pipelines
      • ML model training

    🔧 Example: Step Functions + AWS Lambda

    🎯 Workflow:

    User triggers workflow →
Step 1: Validate Order (Lambda)
Step 2: Check Inventory (Lambda)
Step 3: Charge Payment (Lambda)
Step 4: Send Notification (Lambda)

    🧾 State Machine Definition (Amazon States Language - JSON)

    {
"Comment": "Order Processing Workflow",
"StartAt": "ValidateOrder",
"States": {
  "ValidateOrder": {
    "Type": "Task",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:function:ValidateOrder",
    "Next": "CheckInventory"
  },
  "CheckInventory": {
    "Type": "Task",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:function:CheckInventory",
    "Next": "ChargePayment"
  },
  "ChargePayment": {
    "Type": "Task",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:function:ChargePayment",
    "Next": "SendNotification"
  },
  "SendNotification": {
    "Type": "Task",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:function:SendNotification",
    "End": true
  }
}
}

    ✅ Benefits

    Feature Benefit
    Visual Workflows Easy to debug, visualize, and trace steps
    Error Handling Built-in retry, catch, and fallback states
    Sequential + Parallel Define series and branching flows
    Audit + Logging Integrated with CloudWatch Logs
    Pay-per-state Charged per state transition, cost-effective

    🔐 IAM Permissions

    Each Lambda used in Step Functions must:

    • Allow execution from Step Functions
    • Be invoked with appropriate IAM roles

    🧪 Bonus: Step Functions + Express Workflows

    If you need faster execution and lower costs for short-duration tasks, use:

    • Express Workflows for high-volume, event-driven workloads
    • Standard Workflows for long-running workflows (up to 1 year)
  • AWS SES?
    AWS SES (Simple Email Service) is a cloud-based email sending service designed to help digital marketers and application developers send marketing, notification, and transactional emails securely and cost-effectively.
  • common use cases of AWS SES?
    • Sending transactional emails (e.g., OTPs, order confirmations)
    • Marketing and promotional campaigns
    • System alerts and notifications
    • Bulk email distribution
  • verify a domain or email in SES?
    You verify a domain/email by adding a DNS TXT record provided by SES or clicking a verification link sent to the specified email address. Domain verification is required for bulk or production email sending.
  • SES sending limits and how do you increase them?
    SES limits depend on the region and whether your account is in the sandbox or production. You can increase limits by requesting a production access upgrade via AWS Support.
  • difference between sandbox and production mode in SES?
    • Sandbox: Used for testing; you can only send emails to verified addresses.
    • Production: After approval, you can send to unverified addresses and higher volume.
  • send email using AWS SES in Node.js?
    Use the @aws-sdk/client-ses package. You configure the SES client and call SendEmailCommand or SendRawEmailCommand depending on the use case (e.g., attachments).
  • monitor SES email deliveries?
    SES integrates with Amazon CloudWatch, SNS, and event destinations to monitor bounces, complaints, deliveries, and rejections. You can set alarms based on metrics.
  • bounces and complaints in SES?
    • Bounce: When an email is rejected by the recipient's mail server.
    • Complaint: When a recipient marks the email as spam.
    Both affect your sender reputation and should be handled via SNS notifications or CloudWatch alerts.
  • send email with attachments using SES?
    You must use SendRawEmailCommand and build the MIME message manually, including attachments in base64-encoded format with correct content-type headers.
  • authenticate your domain for better deliverability?
    Set up DNS records:
    • SPF: To authorize AWS SES as a sender
    • DKIM: To sign emails cryptographically
    • DMARC: To specify how to handle failed SPF/DKIM checks
  • AWS SSM (Systems Manager)?
    AWS SSM (AWS Systems Manager) is a service that lets you view and control your cloud and on-premises infrastructure.
    It helps manage EC2 instances, patch updates, automate tasks, run scripts, and store configuration secrets.
  • key components of AWS SSM?
    • SSM Agent: Installed on instances to allow communication with SSM
    • Run Command: Execute shell scripts/commands remotely
    • Parameter Store: Secure storage for configuration values and secrets
    • Automation: Reusable workflows for tasks like patching or provisioning
    • Session Manager: Secure shell access to EC2 without SSH or bastion
    • Patch Manager: Automate OS patching
  • use SSM Parameter Store?
    You can store configuration values and secrets using SSM Parameter Store. Parameters can be plaintext or encrypted using KMS. They are accessed programmatically via AWS SDK, CLI, or environment variables.
  • difference between standard and advanced parameters in Parameter Store?
    • Standard: Free up to 10,000 parameters, no expiration, basic features
    • Advanced: Support for higher limits, parameter policies (like expiration), and parameter versions history
  • How does Session Manager improve security?
    Session Manager enables shell access to EC2 instances without SSH keys or open ports. It logs session activity, integrates with CloudTrail, and supports encryption for secure auditing.
  • What IAM permissions are required for SSM to work with EC2?
    The EC2 instance must have an attached IAM role with policies like AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. Additional permissions are needed for accessing Parameter Store, logging, etc.
  • execute remote commands using AWS SSM?
    Use SSM Run Command via AWS Console, CLI, or SDK. It allows execution of commands on target EC2 instances (with SSM agent) without needing SSH or opening inbound ports.
  • Automation Documents (SSM Documents)?
    Automation Documents (SSM Docs) are JSON/YAML templates defining actions for Systems Manager. You can use AWS-provided or custom documents to automate patching, backups, deployments, etc.
  • role of AWS SSM in CI/CD pipelines?
    AWS SSM can be integrated in CI/CD pipelines to:
    • Deploy code or run scripts after a build
    • Update configuration values via Parameter Store
    • Use Run Command to restart services or run health checks
  • best practices when using AWS SSM?
    • Use IAM roles with least privilege
    • Enable logging and auditing via CloudWatch and CloudTrail
    • Rotate and encrypt secrets using Parameter Store + KMS
    • Use Session Manager instead of SSH for instance access
    • Tag and organize SSM documents and parameters
  • AWS Kinesis?
    AWS Kinesis is a platform for real-time data streaming at scale. It enables processing of large streams of data records in real time for analytics, monitoring, and response.
  • components of AWS Kinesis?
    • Kinesis Data Streams (KDS): Collect and process real-time streaming data
    • Kinesis Data Firehose: Load streaming data to S3, Redshift, Elasticsearch, etc.
    • Kinesis Data Analytics: Real-time SQL queries on streaming data
    • Kinesis Video Streams: Stream and store video from devices
  • How does Kinesis Data Stream work?
    Data producers push data records into Kinesis streams. Each stream consists of shards. Consumers (like Lambda, EC2) read and process data from these shards.
  • a shard in Kinesis?
    A shard is the base throughput unit of a Kinesis stream. Each shard supports 1MB/s input and 2MB/s output. You can increase throughput by adding more shards.
  • difference between Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose?
    • Data Streams: Real-time processing; you manage consumers and scaling
    • Firehose: Fully managed; automatically loads to destinations (e.g., S3)
  • retention period for Kinesis Data Streams?
    By default, data is retained for 24 hours. You can extend retention up to 365 days.
  • consume data from a Kinesis stream?
    You can use:
    • AWS Lambda
    • Kinesis Client Library (KCL)
    • Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics
  • common use cases for AWS Kinesis?
    • Log and event data streaming
    • Real-time analytics and dashboards
    • IoT telemetry processing
    • Video stream analysis
  • AWS CloudFormation?
    CloudFormation is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) service that lets you define AWS infrastructure using JSON or YAML templates and deploy it automatically.
  • components of a CloudFormation template?
    • Parameters – Accept input values
    • Resources – Define AWS services to provision
    • Outputs – Export values
    • Mappings – Define conditional values
    • Conditions – Create conditional resources
    • Metadata – Add extra data (e.g., configs)
  • a CloudFormation Stack?
    A stack is a collection of AWS resources created, updated, or deleted together as a unit using a CloudFormation template.
  • use of Change Sets in CloudFormation?
    Change Sets let you preview changes that CloudFormation will make before applying them. This helps prevent unintended resource updates or deletions.
  • How does CloudFormation handle updates to existing stacks?
    CloudFormation compares the new template with the current stack and makes necessary changes. Resources are added/updated/deleted to match the updated template.
  • a nested stack?
    A nested stack is a CloudFormation stack created within another stack. It helps modularize templates and reuse common configurations.
  • manage secrets in CloudFormation templates?
    You can reference secrets stored in AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store using dynamic references (e.g., {{resolve:ssm-secure:parameter-name}}).
  • Can CloudFormation rollback changes on failure?
    Yes. If a stack creation or update fails, CloudFormation automatically rolls back to the previous stable state (unless rollback is explicitly disabled).
  • What tools can you use with CloudFormation for CI/CD?
    You can integrate CloudFormation with CodePipeline, CodeBuild, GitHub Actions, Jenkins, or Terraform (to generate templates).
  • best practices for writing CloudFormation templates?
    • Use YAML over JSON for readability
    • Break large templates into nested stacks
    • Parameterize environment-specific values
    • Use DependsOn for explicit dependencies
    • Enable stack protection and rollback alarms
  • AWS EC2?
    AWS EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) provides scalable virtual servers in the cloud. You can launch instances of different types to host applications, run workloads, or serve web services.
  • EC2 instance types?
    EC2 instance types are categories of virtual machines optimized for different use cases:
    • General Purpose: t3, t4g, m5
    • Compute Optimized: c5, c6g
    • Memory Optimized: r5, x1
    • Storage Optimized: i3, d2
    • Accelerated Computing: p3, inf1
  • an AMI (Amazon Machine Image)?
    An AMI is a pre-configured template that contains the OS, software, and settings needed to launch an EC2 instance. You can use AWS-provided, marketplace, or custom AMIs.
  • difference between EBS and instance store?
    • EBS (Elastic Block Store): Persistent block storage that survives instance termination.
    • Instance Store: Temporary storage that is lost when the instance is stopped or terminated.
  • How do security groups work in EC2?
    Security groups act as virtual firewalls. They control inbound and outbound traffic to instances using rules based on protocols, ports, and IPs. Rules are stateful.
  • difference between key pairs and IAM roles in EC2?
    • Key Pairs: Used for SSH access to EC2 instances.
    • IAM Roles: Assign permissions to EC2 instances to access AWS services (e.g., S3, DynamoDB).
  • make an EC2 instance highly available?
    • Use multiple Availability Zones
    • Launch EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group
    • Use Elastic Load Balancer (ELB)
    • Deploy AMIs for quick recovery
  • spot, on-demand, and reserved instances?
    • On-Demand: Pay-per-use with no commitment.
    • Reserved: Commit to usage over 1 or 3 years for lower cost.
    • Spot: Bid for unused capacity at the lowest price—can be terminated anytime by AWS.
  • automate EC2 instance deployment?
    You can use tools like AWS CloudFormation, Terraform, AWS CDK, or EC2 Launch Templates combined with Auto Scaling Groups for automated and repeatable instance deployment.
  • common EC2 troubleshooting steps?
    • Check system logs using EC2 console
    • Use EC2 Instance Connect if SSH fails
    • Review security group and NACL rules
    • Check instance status checks
    • Verify disk space and memory usage

  • DynamoDB Query 
      1. putItem or put method in AWS SDK.
  docClient.put({ 
      TableName: "Users", 
      Item: { name: "Prasenjit", age: 30 } 
    })


  2. batchWrite to insert multiple items
  docClient.batchWrite({ 
              RequestItems: { 
                "Users": [
                    { PutRequest: { Item: { name: "A", age: 25 } } }, 
                    { PutRequest: { Item: { name: "B", age: 28 } } } 
                ]}})


  3. scan method to get all items
  docClient.scan({ TableName: "Users" })
  
  
  4. Limit parameter with scan or query
  docClient.scan({ TableName: "Users", Limit: 10 })


  5. FilterExpression in scan
  docClient.scan({ TableName: "Users", FilterExpression: "age > :val", ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":val": 25 } })


  6. ProjectionExpression
  docClient.scan({ TableName: "Users", ProjectionExpression: "name, age" })


  7. get with the primary key : How to find a user by ID?
  docClient.get({ TableName: "Users", Key: { id: "user_id_value" } })



  How to sort users by age descending?
  DynamoDB does not support sorting unless age is the sort key. Use query with 
  ScanIndexForward: false if using a GSI/LSI with age as the sort key.
  
  Use ExclusiveStartKey along with Limit to skip items. 
    
  To skip 10, start from the last evaluated key of the 10th item.
  • Example : 01 : DynamoDB 
      // handler.js
  const express     = require('express');
  const serverless  = require('serverless-http');
  
  const app = express();
  app.use(express.json());
  
  const prodcrud = require('./routes/productcrud');
  app.use('/products', prodcrud);
  
  
  module.exports.handler = async (event, context) => {
    return serverless(app)(event, context);
  };
  
    

  const express         = require('express');
  const AWS             = require('aws-sdk');
  const { v4: uuidv4 }  = require('uuid');

  const router          = express.Router();
  const dynamodb        = new AWS.DynamoDB.DocumentClient({ region: 'us-east-1' });
  const TABLE_NAME      = 'Products';

  // List all products
  router.get('/list', async (req, res) => {
    try {
      const data = await dynamodb.scan({ TableName: TABLE_NAME }).promise();
      res.json(data.Items);
    } catch (err) {
      console.log('Err : ',err);
      res.status(500).json({ err, error: 'Failed to fetch products' });
    }
  });

  // Create new product
  router.get('/add', async (req, res) => {
    //const { name, price, description } = req.body;
    const { name, price, description } = {name:"Test 003", price:885544, description:"dummy 007752"};
    const newProduct = {
      id: uuidv4(),
      name,
      price,
      description
    };

    try {
      await dynamodb.put({
        TableName: TABLE_NAME,
        Item: newProduct
      }).promise();

      res.status(201).json(newProduct);
    } catch (err) {
      res.status(201).json({err:"error"});
      res.status(500).json({ error: 'Failed to create product' });
    }
  });

  // Get product by ID
  router.get('/:id', async (req, res) => {
    try {
      const data = await dynamodb.get({
        TableName: TABLE_NAME,
        Key: { id: req.params.id }
      }).promise();

      if (!data.Item) {
        return res.status(404).json({ error: 'Product not found' });
      }

      res.json(data.Item);
    } catch (err) {
      res.status(500).json({ error: 'Failed to fetch product' });
    }
  });

  // Update product by ID
  router.put('/:id', async (req, res) => {
    const { name, price, description } = req.body;

    const params = {
      TableName: TABLE_NAME,
      Key: { id: req.params.id },
      UpdateExpression: 'set #name = :n, price = :p, description = :d',
      ExpressionAttributeNames: {
        '#name': 'name'
      },
      ExpressionAttributeValues: {
        ':n': name,
        ':p': price,
        ':d': description
      },
      ReturnValues: 'ALL_NEW'
    };

    try {
      const data = await dynamodb.update(params).promise();
      res.json(data.Attributes);
    } catch (err) {
      res.status(500).json({ error: 'Failed to update product' });
    }
  });

  // Delete product by ID
  router.delete('/:id', async (req, res) => {
    try {
      await dynamodb.delete({
        TableName: TABLE_NAME,
        Key: { id: req.params.id }
      }).promise();

      res.json({ deleted: true });
    } catch (err) {
      res.status(500).json({ error: 'Failed to delete product' });
    }
  });

  module.exports = router;
  • a Partition Key in DynamoDB?
    The Partition Key in DynamoDB is a required attribute that uniquely identifies each item in a table. It is used to determine the partition (physical storage location) in which the data is stored.

    Every item in the table must have a unique value for the partition key. If you use only a partition key without a sort key, DynamoDB allows only one item per partition key value.

    In the context of a Products table:
    • The partition key could be id, representing the unique identifier for each product.
    Example:
    • id: "p001"
    • name: "Laptop"
    • price: 75000

    DynamoDB uses the value of the partition key to distribute data across partitions and ensure scalability and performance.
  • AWS Service List
    1. AWS Lambda
      Serverless compute allowing you to run code without managing servers—ideal for event-driven functions, APIs, or microservices. Pay only for execution time :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}.
    2. Amazon EC2
      Virtual machines with scalable compute capacity for running custom servers or workloads. Useful when you need full OS control :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}.
    3. Amazon S3
      Highly durable object storage for files, static assets, backups, or data lakes. Great for hosting static websites or storing media :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}.
    4. Amazon RDS
      Managed relational database service supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, etc. Handles backups, scaling, and patching :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}.
    5. Amazon DynamoDB
      Fully managed NoSQL database offering low latency and automatic scaling—ideal for key-value workloads :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}.
    6. Amazon API Gateway
      Creates, secures, and manages APIs at scale—works seamlessly with Lambda or other backends :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}.
    7. AWS CloudFormation
      Infrastructure as Code (IaC) service to declaratively define and manage AWS resources via YAML/JSON templates :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}.
    8. AWS CloudWatch
      Monitoring, logging, and alerting for AWS resources and applications—essential for observability :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}.
    9. Amazon CloudFront
      Global CDN to distribute content with low latency and high transfer speeds, with integrated SSL/DDoS protection :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}.

      CI/CD toolchain for source control, building, testing, and deploying applications within AWS :contentReference[oaicite:11]{index=11}.

      Browser-based IDE and CLI environment for coding and prototyping directly within AWS :contentReference[oaicite:12]{index=12}.
    13. AWS App Runner
      Fully managed container deployment service with automatic scaling—ideal for containerized web apps :contentReference[oaicite:13]{index=13}.

const express = require('express');

let codeVerifier;

(async () => {

  client = new issuer.Client({

    redirect_uris: ['http://localhost:3000/callback'],
    response_types: ['code']
  });
})();

});

  codeVerifier = generators.codeVerifier();

    code_challenge_method: 'S256'
  });

  res.redirect(authUrl);
});

    });

    console.log(tokenSet.claims());

    res.redirect('/dashboard');

        const {
      CognitoUserPool,
      CognitoUserAttribute
    } = require('amazon-cognito-identity-js');
    
    const poolData = {
      UserPoolId: process.env.USER_POOL_ID,
      ClientId: process.env.USER_POOL_CLIENT_ID
    };
    
    const userPool = new CognitoUserPool(poolData);
    
    function registerUser(email, password) {
      return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
        const attributeList = [
          new CognitoUserAttribute({ Name: 'email', Value: email })
        ];
        userPool.signUp(email, password, attributeList, null, (err, data) => {
          err ? reject(err) : resolve(data);
        });
      });
    }
    
    module.exports = { registerUser };

    🔹 src/auth/login.js

        const {
      AuthenticationDetails,
      CognitoUser
    } = require('amazon-cognito-identity-js');
    
    const { CognitoUserPool } = require('amazon-cognito-identity-js');
    
    const poolData = {
      UserPoolId: process.env.USER_POOL_ID,
      ClientId: process.env.USER_POOL_CLIENT_ID
    };
    
    const userPool = new CognitoUserPool(poolData);
    
    function loginUser(email, password) {
      const authDetails = new AuthenticationDetails({ Username: email, Password: password });
      const userData = { Username: email, Pool: userPool };
      const cognitoUser = new CognitoUser(userData);
    
      return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
        cognitoUser.authenticateUser(authDetails, {
          onSuccess: result => resolve({
            idToken: result.getIdToken().getJwtToken(),
            accessToken: result.getAccessToken().getJwtToken(),
            refreshToken: result.getRefreshToken().getToken()
          }),
          onFailure: err => reject(err)
        });
      });
    }
    
    module.exports = { loginUser };

    🔹 src/email/sendVerification.js

        const AWS = require('aws-sdk');
    const ses = new AWS.SES({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION });
    
    async function sendVerificationEmail(email, code) {
      const params = {
        Destination: { ToAddresses: [email] },
        Message: {
          Body: {
            Text: {
              Data: `Your verification code is: ${code}`,
              Charset: 'UTF-8'
            }
          },
          Subject: {
            Data: 'Verify your email',
            Charset: 'UTF-8'
          }
        },
        Source: process.env.SES_EMAIL_SOURCE
      };
      return ses.sendEmail(params).promise();
    }
    
    module.exports = { sendVerificationEmail };

        const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');
    
    exports.handler = async event => {
      const authHeader = event.headers.Authorization || '';
      const token = authHeader.replace('Bearer ', '');
    
      try {
        const decoded = jwt.decode(token);
        return {
          statusCode: 200,
          body: JSON.stringify({ message: 'Authorized', user: decoded })
        };
      } catch (err) {
        return {
          statusCode: 401,
          body: JSON.stringify({ message: 'Unauthorized' })
        };
      }
    };

  • AWS Cognito?
    AWS Cognito is a service provided by Amazon Web Services that enables secure authentication, authorization, and user management for web and mobile applications. It helps developers easily add user sign-up, sign-in, and access control features, and also supports social identity providers like Google, Facebook, and Apple, as well as SAML-based enterprise identity providers.
  • two main components of Cognito?
    The two main components of AWS Cognito are:
    • User Pools: Used for user directory management and user authentication.
    • Identity Pools: Used for granting temporary AWS credentials to access AWS services.
    User Pools manage user sign-up and sign-in workflows, while Identity Pools allow authenticated users to access other AWS services securely.
  • a User Pool in Cognito?
    A User Pool in AWS Cognito is a user directory that provides sign-up and sign-in options for app users. It handles authentication, account recovery, email/phone verification, and multi-factor authentication (MFA). Developers can configure attributes, password policies, and integrate triggers using AWS Lambda for custom workflows. User Pools issue JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for secure access to applications.
  • an Identity Pool?
    An Identity Pool in AWS Cognito is used to provide users with temporary AWS credentials to access other AWS services. It supports both authenticated users (from User Pools or external providers) and unauthenticated (guest) users. Identity Pools integrate with AWS IAM to grant fine-grained access to AWS resources like S3, DynamoDB, and Lambda.
  • difference between User Pool and Identity Pool?
    The main difference is in their purpose and functionality:
    • User Pool: Manages user authentication, registration, sign-in, and user profiles. It issues JWT tokens (ID, access, and refresh tokens).
    • Identity Pool: Provides AWS credentials to access AWS services. It can be linked to a User Pool or federated identity providers to authorize access to AWS resources.
    In short, User Pools handle authentication, and Identity Pools handle authorization to AWS services.
  • What authentication methods does Cognito support?
    AWS Cognito supports multiple authentication methods including:
    • Email and password-based login
    • Phone number with OTP (SMS) login
    • Social identity providers like Google, Facebook, Apple, Amazon
    • SAML 2.0-based enterprise identity providers (e.g., Active Directory)
    • OpenID Connect (OIDC) providers
    It also supports Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) and custom authentication flows via Lambda triggers.
  • Can Cognito be used for both mobile and web apps?
    Yes, AWS Cognito can be used for both mobile and web applications. It offers SDKs for Android, iOS, and JavaScript, making integration easy across platforms. Cognito supports secure authentication, user management, and AWS resource access in a cross-platform environment, making it suitable for full-stack applications.
  • How does Node.js work with AWS Cognito and Lambda?
    Node.js can be used to build backend services that interact with AWS Cognito for user authentication and with AWS Lambda for executing serverless functions. Here's how they work together:
    • User Authentication: Use AWS Cognito in Node.js to handle user sign-up, sign-in, token generation, and verification.
    • Token Validation: Backend Node.js APIs can validate JWT tokens from Cognito to ensure requests are authenticated.
    • Lambda Integration: Lambda functions written in Node.js can be triggered by Cognito events (such as sign-up, pre-token generation, or post-confirmation).
    • Custom Authentication: You can write custom authentication logic in Node.js and use it as a Lambda trigger in your Cognito User Pool.
    • Serverless API: Node.js APIs deployed as Lambda functions can be secured using Cognito-authorized API Gateway endpoints.
    This combination enables a fully serverless authentication and backend environment where Cognito manages users and Node.js Lambda functions manage business logic.
  • AWS Cognito
    1. 1. Create AWS Cognito User Pool
      • Go to AWS Console → Cognito → Create User Pool.
      • Select "Users can sign in with email" and enable email verification.
      • Configure password policy and multi-factor authentication (MFA) if needed.
      • Create a new App Client (without generating a client secret).
      • Save the User Pool ID and App Client ID.
    2. 2. Create AWS Lambda Function (Node.js)
      • Go to AWS Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch.
      • Choose Node.js as the runtime (e.g., Node.js 18).
      • Give it a name, and create or assign a role with permissions for Cognito if needed.
      • Use the inline editor or deploy code from a ZIP or S3.
    3. 3. Setup Project Locally
      • Initialize a Node.js project:
      • npm init -y
      • Install required packages:
      • npm install amazon-cognito-identity-js aws-sdk
      • Create a file structure like:
        • src/auth/register.js
        • src/auth/login.js
        • src/lambda/handler.js
        • test/auth.test.js
    4. 4. Implement User Sign-Up with Cognito
      • Use amazon-cognito-identity-js to register users.
      • Pass email, password, and user attributes to Cognito.
      • Handle user confirmation with a code (if enabled).
    5. 5. Implement Sign-In and Token Retrieval
      • Use the same SDK to authenticate users with email and password.
      • Get the ID token, access token, and refresh token.
      • Use these tokens for secure calls to protected endpoints.
    6. 6. Protect Lambda Function with Token
      • Use API Gateway to expose the Lambda function via HTTP.
      • Set up an Authorizer using the Cognito User Pool.
      • Only valid JWT tokens can invoke the function.
    7. 7. Write Lambda Handler Code
      • Create a handler in src/lambda/handler.js.
      • This function will receive authenticated requests from API Gateway.
      • You can access user claims from event.requestContext.authorizer.claims.
    8. 8. Setup Unit Testing with Jest
      • Install Jest: npm install --save-dev jest
      • Update package.json: set "test": "jest" in scripts.
      • Write tests in test/auth.test.js and test/lambda.test.js.
      • Mock AWS SDK and Cognito SDK using jest.mock().
    9. 9. Example Test Cases
      • Test user registration: should return success message.
      • Test login: should return JWT token.
      • Test Lambda: should return response when token is valid.
    10. 10. Run and Validate
      • Run your Node.js app locally using node.
      • Deploy Lambda via AWS Console or using CLI/Serverless Framework.
      • Run tests: npm test
      • Use Postman or frontend app to sign up, log in, and call Lambda function.
  • Why do we use Storybook in ReactJS?
    Storybook is used in ReactJS to build, test, and showcase UI components in isolation. It provides a focused development environment where individual components can be developed and visually tested without being connected to the entire application. Key reasons to use Storybook include:
    • Component Isolation: Develop components independently from the app's logic and backend.
    • Visual Testing: Preview components in all possible states to catch UI bugs early.
    • Documentation: Automatically generates interactive documentation for each component and its props.
    • Design Collaboration: Helps designers and developers align on UI with live previews.
    • Reusable Components: Encourages the creation of reusable and consistent design systems.
    • Add-ons Support: Enhance functionality with tools for accessibility, responsiveness, and performance checks.
    Using Storybook improves UI development speed, promotes code quality, and enhances team collaboration.
  • How do I upload a 1 GB CSV to a database using Node.js?

    Step-by-Step Guide to Upload 1 GB CSV to DB Using Node.js

    1. Install required packages: You’ll need fast-csv or csv-parser and a DB client like pg (PostgreSQL), mysql2, or mongoose for MongoDB.
    2. Use streaming to handle large files: Use fs.createReadStream() to avoid loading the entire CSV into memory.
    3. Use batch insert or DB transaction: Insert rows in batches (e.g., 1000 rows at a time) to reduce DB write overhead.

    📁 File Structure

    • /upload.html
    • /server.js
    • /uploads/ (CSV files stored here)

    📄 server.js (Node.js)

      const fs = require('fs');
  const path = require('path');
  const csv = require('fast-csv');
  const { Pool } = require('pg'); // Use mysql2 or mongoose if needed
  
  const pool = new Pool({
    user: 'your_user',
    host: 'localhost',
    database: 'your_db',
    password: 'your_password',
    port: 5432,
  });
  
  async function uploadCSV(filePath) {
    const stream = fs.createReadStream(filePath);
    const csvStream = csv.parse({ headers: true });
    const batch = [];
    const batchSize = 1000;
  
    csvStream.on('data', async (row) => {
      batch.push(row);
      if (batch.length === batchSize) {
        csvStream.pause();
        await insertBatch(batch);
        batch.length = 0;
        csvStream.resume();
      }
    });
  
    csvStream.on('end', async () => {
      if (batch.length > 0) {
        await insertBatch(batch);
      }
      console.log('CSV upload complete');
    });
  
    stream.pipe(csvStream);
  }
  
  async function insertBatch(rows) {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    try {
      await client.query('BEGIN');
      for (const row of rows) {
        await client.query('INSERT INTO your_table(col1, col2) VALUES($1, $2)', [row.col1, row.col2]);
      }
      await client.query('COMMIT');
    } catch (err) {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      console.error('Batch insert error:', err);
    } finally {
      client.release();
    }
  }
  
  // Example call
  uploadCSV(path.join(__dirname, 'uploads', 'bigfile.csv'));

    • Handle backpressure with pause() and resume().
    • Use tools like PM2 for long-running processes.

      // https://cloud.elastic.co/
  const express   = require('express');
  const router    = express.Router();
  const { Client }= require('@elastic/elasticsearch');
  
  const client = new Client({
                          node: 'https://my-elasticsearch-project-e8744c.es.us-east-1.aws.elastic.cloud:443',
                          auth: {apiKey: 'OWluZ2taY0JHUXFGSFN2MjdZTkM6ZzNHSU9uLTdXN01ScVR0Q1RtMVpKQQ=='},
                          serverless: true
                      });
  
  const INDEX = 'students';
  router.get('/add', async (req, res) => {
      try {
          const data  = {title:"Rani = 01A ", details:"Loren ipsum dummy data. Loren ipsum dummy data."};
          const result= await client.index({index: INDEX, document: data});
          res.json({ message: 'Student created', id: result._id });
      }
      catch (err) {
          res.status(500).json({ error: err.message });
      }
  });
  
  // Get all students
  router.get('/', async (req, res) => {
      try {
          await client.indices.create({ index: 'students' }, { ignore: [400] });
          const result    = await client.search({index: INDEX, query: { match_all: {} }});
          const students  = result.hits.hits.map(hit => ({
                                                          id: hit._id,
                                                          ...hit._source
                                                      }));
          res.json(students);
      } 
      catch (err) {
          res.status(500).json({ error: err.message });
      }
  });
  
  // Get student by ID
  router.get('/:id', async (req, res) => {
    try {
      const result = await client.get({
        index: INDEX,
        id: req.params.id
      });
      res.json(result._source);
    } catch (err) {
      res.status(404).json({ error: 'Student not found' });
    }
  });
  
  // Update student by ID
  router.put('/:id', async (req, res) => {
    try {
      const result = await client.update({
        index: INDEX,
        id: req.params.id,
        doc: req.body
      });
      res.json({ message: 'Student updated', result });
    } catch (err) {
      res.status(500).json({ error: err.message });
    }
  });
  
  // Delete student by ID
  router.delete('/:id', async (req, res) => {
    try {
      await client.delete({
        index: INDEX,
        id: req.params.id
      });
      res.json({ message: 'Student deleted' });
    } catch (err) {
      res.status(404).json({ error: 'Student not found' });
    }
  });
  
  module.exports = router;
  • Elasticsearch 🆚 MongoDB?
    Feature Elasticsearch MongoDB
    Type Search and analytics engine Document-oriented NoSQL database
    Use Case Full-text search, log analytics, real-time search General-purpose document storage and querying
    Data Format JSON documents (Lucene-based) BSON documents (Binary JSON)
    Query Language Query DSL (JSON-based) MongoDB Query Language (MQL)
    Search Capabilities Highly optimized for full-text, fuzzy, and relevance scoring Basic full-text search via text indexes
    Indexing Automatic and custom analyzers for tokenization Indexes fields with support for compound indexes
    Aggregation Powerful pipeline with metrics, filters, and buckets Aggregation framework for summaries and stats
    Joins No joins (can use nested documents) Supports basic joins using $lookup in aggregation
    Transactions Limited transaction support Supports multi-document ACID transactions
    Consistency Eventual consistency Strong consistency (by default)
    Scalability Highly scalable with built-in sharding Supports sharding for horizontal scaling
    Best For Search-heavy applications (e.g., e-commerce search, log monitoring) General CRUD apps (e.g., user data, orders, CMS)
    Visualization Tools Kibana MongoDB Charts, Compass
    Official Cloud Platform Elastic Cloud MongoDB Atlas
  • an Elasticsearch cluster, node, shard, and replica?
    A cluster is a set of nodes (instances). Each index is divided into shards (primary partitions), with replicas for fault tolerance :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}.
  • indexing and how does it work?
    Indexing stores JSON documents in an index, applying analyzers/tokenizers. It’s near‑real‑time: newest data becomes searchable in about a second :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}.
  • analyzers, tokenizers, and filters?
    Analyzers process text during indexing/search: split into tokens (tokenizers) and modify them (filters). Types include standard, simple, whitespace, stop, keyword, pattern, language-based, custom :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}.
  • Explain basic vs term-based queries.
    Full-text (e.g., match, match_phrase, multi_match) analyze text. Term-based (e.g., term, wildcard, range, fuzzy) search exact terms without analysis :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}.
  • aggregations?
    Aggregations provide metrics and data bucketing (e.g., stats, histograms), enabling analytics and summary queries :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}.
  • How to perform bulk operations?
    Use the bulk API to index/update/delete multiple documents in one request for efficiency :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}.
  • ELK (Elastic) Stack?
    The stack includes Elasticsearch (search backend), Logstash (log ingestion), and Kibana (visualization). Beats and others extend functionality :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}.
  • How does Elasticsearch scale?
    It scales horizontally by adding nodes; shards and replicas distribute data and queries across the cluster :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}.
  • delete an index or document?
    Deleting an index uses the DELETE index API; documents via DELETE index/_doc/id. Bulk operations can also remove many at once :contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}.
  • NRT (Near‑Real‑Time) search?
    NRT means a very short delay (~1 s) between indexing data and its availability in search results :contentReference[oaicite:11]{index=11}.
  • cat API?
    The cat API provides human-readable cluster/index stats via endpoints like _cat/indices, shards, health, nodes, etc. :contentReference[oaicite:12]{index=12}.
  • a custom analyzer and when use it?
    Custom analyzers combine tokenizers and filters tailored for specific languages or use‑cases (e.g., stemming, synonyms) :contentReference[oaicite:13]{index=13}.
  • Explain shards vs replicas.
    Shards split data for distribution; replicas are copies for failover/high availability. Defaults are 5 primary shards and 1 replica :contentReference[oaicite:14]{index=14}.
  • How is Elasticsearch different from a relational database?
    Unlike relational DBs, it is schema-free, optimized for full-text search, uses distributed JSON document model, and lacks ACID transactions :contentReference[oaicite:15]{index=15}.
  • API-first architecture?
    API-first architecture is a software development approach where APIs are designed, documented, and agreed upon before any code is written for the application logic or user interfaces. It treats APIs as first-class citizens, ensuring that they are consistent, reusable, and well-documented from the beginning.

    This strategy enables better collaboration between teams, improves system scalability, supports parallel development, and ensures that front-end and back-end teams can work independently without delays.

    Key Characteristics:
    • APIs are the central point of the design process
    • Contracts (schemas) are defined using tools like OpenAPI or Swagger
    • Development can proceed in parallel across teams
    • Improves reusability and consistency across services

    Benefits:
    • Faster development with fewer integration issues
    • Better developer experience with clear API docs
    • Improves testability and automation
    • Scales well with microservices and front-end/backend separation

    Common Tools:
    • OpenAPI (Swagger)
    • Postman
    • Stoplight
    • API Gateway

  • What is Spring Boot?
    Spring Boot is a framework built on top of Spring that simplifies the development of stand-alone, production-ready Spring-based applications with minimal configuration.
  • What are the main features of Spring Boot?
    Auto-configuration, starter dependencies, embedded servers, production-ready metrics, and minimal XML configuration.
  • What is the difference between Spring and Spring Boot?
    Spring provides a comprehensive framework for Java development, while Spring Boot simplifies the setup and development process with auto-configuration and embedded servers.
  • What is a Spring Boot Starter?
    Starters are a set of convenient dependency descriptors you can include in your application to get common functionality, like spring-boot-starter-web for web apps.
  • How does Spring Boot reduce boilerplate code?
    Through auto-configuration, embedded servers, and opinionated defaults for project structure and dependencies.
  • What is @SpringBootApplication?
    A convenience annotation that combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan.
  • How do you create a Spring Boot project?
    Use Spring Initializr (https://start.spring.io) or IDEs like IntelliJ or Eclipse with Spring support.
  • What is auto-configuration in Spring Boot?
    Spring Boot automatically configures your application based on the dependencies present in the classpath.
  • What is the purpose of application.properties?
    It is used to define configuration values such as server port, datasource URL, and logging level.
  • What is an embedded server?
    Spring Boot includes servers like Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow within the application, so you don’t need to deploy a WAR file externally.
  • What is dependency injection?
    A design pattern where dependencies are provided to a class by the framework instead of being created manually.
  • What is @RestController?
    A combination of @Controller and @ResponseBody, used to build RESTful web services in Spring Boot.
  • What is the difference between @Component, @Service, and @Repository?
    All are specializations of @Component used for different layers: general bean, business logic, and data access respectively.
  • How do you handle exceptions in Spring Boot?
    Use @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods to define global exception handling logic.
  • What is Spring Boot DevTools?
    A module that provides automatic restarts, live reload, and configurations for faster development.
  • What is @Autowired?
    It tells Spring to automatically inject the required bean into a component.
  • How can you change the default port in Spring Boot?
    Add server.port=8081 in application.properties or application.yml.
  • What is Spring Boot Actuator?
    A tool that provides production-ready features like monitoring, health checks, metrics, and environment info.
  • How do you connect to a database in Spring Boot?
    Add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and database driver dependencies, and configure the datasource in application.properties.
  • What is JPA in Spring Boot?
    Java Persistence API (JPA) is used for ORM-based database operations, often with Hibernate as the implementation.
  • What is @Entity?
    Marks a class as a JPA entity that maps to a table in the database.
  • What is a repository in Spring Boot?
    An interface extending JpaRepository or CrudRepository that provides CRUD operations without writing SQL.
  • What is H2 Database?
    An in-memory database useful for development and testing in Spring Boot projects.
  • What is the purpose of @RequestMapping?
    It maps HTTP requests to handler methods in controllers. You can also use shortcuts like @GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc.
  • What is a DTO?
    Data Transfer Object is used to carry data between layers, typically between controller and service.
  • What is @PathVariable?
    Used to extract values from the URI in controller methods.
  • What is @RequestParam?
    Used to extract query parameters from the URL in controller methods.
  • How do you secure a Spring Boot app?
    Use Spring Security with configurations for authentication, authorization, and password encoding.
  • How can you schedule tasks in Spring Boot?
    Use @EnableScheduling and annotate methods with @Scheduled for cron jobs or fixed intervals.
  • What are common Spring Boot dependencies?
    spring-boot-starter-web, spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, spring-boot-starter-security, spring-boot-devtools, spring-boot-starter-actuator.

    package com.example.employee.model;

    import jakarta.persistence.*;
    
    @Entity
    public class Employee {
    
        @Id
        @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
        private Long id;
    
        private String name;
        private String role;
        private String email;
    
        // Getters and setters
        public Long getId() { return id; }
        public void setId(Long id) { this.id = id; }
    
        public String getName() { return name; }
        public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }
    
        public String getRole() { return role; }
        public void setRole(String role) { this.role = role; }
    
        public String getEmail() { return email; }
        public void setEmail(String email) { this.email = email; }
    }
    

    
    package com.example.employee.repository;

    import com.example.employee.model.Employee;
    import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
    
    public interface EmployeeRepository extends JpaRepository {}
    

    

    package com.example.employee.service;

    import com.example.employee.model.Employee;
    import com.example.employee.repository.EmployeeRepository;
    import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
    import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
    
    import java.util.List;
    
    @Service
    public class EmployeeService {
    
        @Autowired
        private EmployeeRepository employeeRepository;
    
        public List getAllEmployees() {
            return employeeRepository.findAll();
        }
    
        public Employee getEmployeeById(Long id) {
            return employeeRepository.findById(id).orElse(null);
        }
    
        public Employee createEmployee(Employee employee) {
            return employeeRepository.save(employee);
        }
    
        public Employee updateEmployee(Long id, Employee employeeData) {
            Employee employee = employeeRepository.findById(id).orElse(null);
            if (employee != null) {
                employee.setName(employeeData.getName());
                employee.setRole(employeeData.getRole());
                employee.setEmail(employeeData.getEmail());
                return employeeRepository.save(employee);
            }
            return null;
        }
    
        public void deleteEmployee(Long id) {
            employeeRepository.deleteById(id);
        }
    }
    

    
    package com.example.employee.controller;

    import com.example.employee.model.Employee;
    import com.example.employee.service.EmployeeService;
    import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
    import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
    
    import java.util.List;
    
    @RestController
    @RequestMapping("/api/employees")
    public class EmployeeController {
    
        @Autowired
        private EmployeeService employeeService;
    
        @GetMapping
        public List getAllEmployees() {
            return employeeService.getAllEmployees();
        }
    
        @GetMapping("/{id}")
        public Employee getEmployeeById(@PathVariable Long id) {
            return employeeService.getEmployeeById(id);
        }
    
        @PostMapping
        public Employee createEmployee(@RequestBody Employee employee) {
            return employeeService.createEmployee(employee);
        }
    
        @PutMapping("/{id}")
        public Employee updateEmployee(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Employee employeeData) {
            return employeeService.updateEmployee(id, employeeData);
        }
    
        @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
        public void deleteEmployee(@PathVariable Long id) {
            employeeService.deleteEmployee(id);
        }
    }

  • What is Git and GitHub? What is the difference? 
          
Git

Git is a distributed version control system used to track changes
in source code during software development.

It allows multiple developers to work on the same project without
overwriting each other's work.

GitHub

GitHub is a cloud-based platform that hosts Git repositories and
provides collaboration tools such as pull requests, issues,
code reviews, and CI/CD integrations.

Difference

Git
- Version control system
- Works locally
- Tracks file changes

GitHub
- Hosting platform for Git repositories
- Enables collaboration
- Provides UI, pull requests, and issue tracking

Interview Short Answer

Git is a version control system, while GitHub is a platform that
hosts Git repositories and enables team collaboration.
  • What is branching in Git and why is it important? 
          
Branching allows developers to work on new features or bug fixes
without affecting the main codebase.

The main branch is usually called:

main or master

Example:

Create a new branch

git checkout -b feature-login

Workflow

main branch
     |
     |--- feature-login
     |--- feature-payment

After development is completed, the branch is merged back into main.

Benefits

- Parallel development
- Safe experimentation
- Better code management
  • What is the difference between Git Merge and Git Rebase? 
          
Git Merge

Merge combines two branches and preserves the commit history.

Example:

git checkout main
git merge feature-login

Result

Creates a merge commit.

History

A --- B --- C
       \     /
        D ---E

Git Rebase

Rebase moves the feature branch commits on top of another branch.

Example

git checkout feature-login
git rebase main

Result

Cleaner linear history.

History

A --- B --- C --- D --- E

Difference

Merge
- Keeps history intact
- Creates merge commit

Rebase
- Rewrites commit history
- Creates cleaner timeline

Interview Tip

Use merge for shared branches and rebase for local branches.
  • What is a Pull Request in GitHub? 
          
Pull Request (PR) is a mechanism used to merge code changes from
one branch into another branch.

It allows developers to review code before merging.

Workflow

1. Create feature branch
2. Push branch to GitHub
3. Create Pull Request
4. Team reviews code
5. Approve and merge

Benefits

- Code review
- Collaboration
- Maintain code quality

Example

feature-login → main
  • What is a merge conflict and how do you resolve it? 
          
Merge conflict occurs when two branches modify the same file
or same line of code.

Example conflict markers:

<<<<<<< HEAD
console.log("version A");
=======
console.log("version B");
>>>>>>> feature-branch

Steps to resolve conflict

1. Open conflicting file
2. Choose correct code
3. Remove conflict markers
4. Stage file

git add filename

5. Commit merge

git commit

Best Practices

- Pull latest changes frequently
- Keep branches small
- Communicate with team

  • What is CI/CD? 
          
CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (or Delivery).

It is a modern DevOps practice used to automate the process of building,
testing, and deploying software.

CI/CD helps developers deliver code changes faster and more reliably.

CI (Continuous Integration)

Developers frequently push code changes to a shared repository.
Each change automatically triggers a build and test process.

Goal:
Detect bugs early and maintain code quality.

CD (Continuous Delivery / Continuous Deployment)

After successful build and tests, the application is automatically
prepared for deployment or deployed directly to production.

--------------------------------------------------

CI/CD Pipeline Flow

Developer writes code
        ↓
Push code to Git repository
        ↓
CI server triggers build
        ↓
Run automated tests
        ↓
Build artifact created
        ↓
Deploy to staging / production
  • What is Continuous Integration?

Each integration triggers:

1. Automated build

Benefits

- Improved code quality
- Team collaboration

Flow

      ↓

      ↓
Automatic deployment to production

  • Explain CI/CD in detail (25 LPA Interview Level). 
          
CI/CD (Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery / Deployment)

CI/CD is a DevOps practice that automates the software development lifecycle
including building, testing, and deploying applications.

The goal is to deliver high-quality software faster and more reliably.

--------------------------------------------------

CI/CD Full Pipeline Architecture

Developer writes code
        ↓
Push to Git Repository (GitHub / GitLab)
        ↓
CI Pipeline Triggered
        ↓
Install Dependencies
        ↓
Build Application
        ↓
Run Automated Tests
        ↓
Static Code Analysis
        ↓
Build Artifact (Docker image / package)
        ↓
Deploy to Staging Environment
        ↓
Run Integration Tests
        ↓
Deploy to Production

--------------------------------------------------

1. Continuous Integration (CI)

Continuous Integration means developers frequently merge code
changes into a shared repository.

Every commit triggers an automated pipeline.

CI Pipeline Steps:

1. Code Checkout
CI server pulls latest code from repository.

2. Dependency Installation

Example:

npm install

3. Build Application

Example:

npm run build

4. Run Automated Tests

Example:

npm test

5. Static Code Analysis

Example tools:

ESLint
SonarQube

Goal:
Detect errors early and ensure code quality.

--------------------------------------------------

2. Continuous Delivery (CD)

Continuous Delivery means the application is always ready
for deployment.

After passing all tests, the application is deployed to
staging environments automatically.

Deployment requires manual approval for production.

Example Flow:

Code Commit
      ↓
Build
      ↓
Automated Testing
      ↓
Deploy to Staging
      ↓
Manual Approval
      ↓
Deploy to Production

--------------------------------------------------

3. Continuous Deployment

Continuous Deployment is an advanced version of Continuous Delivery.

Here deployment to production is fully automated
after successful tests.

Flow:

Commit
   ↓
Build
   ↓
Test
   ↓
Deploy to Production automatically

No manual approval required.

--------------------------------------------------

Difference

Continuous Delivery

Deployment requires manual approval.

Continuous Deployment

Deployment is fully automated.

--------------------------------------------------

CI/CD Pipeline Components

Source Control

GitHub
GitLab
Bitbucket

Build Tools

Maven
Gradle
npm

Testing Tools

Jest
Mocha
JUnit
Selenium

CI/CD Tools

Jenkins
GitHub Actions
GitLab CI
CircleCI
Azure DevOps

Containerization

Docker

Orchestration

Kubernetes

--------------------------------------------------

Example GitHub Actions Pipeline

.github/workflows/node.yml

name: Node CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:

  build:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm install

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build project
      run: npm run build

--------------------------------------------------

CI/CD Best Practices

1. Commit code frequently
2. Keep pipeline fast
3. Use automated testing
4. Use containerized environments
5. Monitor production deployments
6. Implement rollback strategy

--------------------------------------------------

Advanced CI/CD Concepts

Blue-Green Deployment

Two identical environments exist.

Blue = current production
Green = new version

Traffic switches after successful deployment.

Canary Deployment

New version released to a small percentage of users
before full rollout.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC)

Infrastructure defined using code.

Example tools:

Terraform
AWS CloudFormation

--------------------------------------------------

Benefits of CI/CD

Faster development cycles
Reduced manual errors
Higher code quality
Automated testing
Rapid feature delivery
Improved team collaboration

--------------------------------------------------

Interview Short Answer (25 LPA)

CI/CD is a DevOps practice that automates the process of integrating,
testing, building, and deploying applications. Continuous Integration
ensures code changes are automatically built and tested, while Continuous
Delivery and Deployment automate the release process, enabling faster
and more reliable software delivery.
  • Explain CI/CD Step-by-Step using GitHub Actions. 
          
CI/CD Pipeline with GitHub Actions (Step-by-Step)

Step 1: Developer Writes Code
Developer creates a new feature or bug fix in a separate branch.

Example:
feature-login

--------------------------------------------------

Step 2: Push Code to GitHub

git add .
git commit -m "login feature added"
git push origin feature-login

--------------------------------------------------

Step 3: Create Pull Request

Developer creates a Pull Request (PR):

feature-login → main

Team reviews the code before merging.

--------------------------------------------------

Step 4: CI Pipeline Triggered

GitHub Actions automatically triggers the pipeline
when code is pushed or PR is created.

Trigger Example:

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

--------------------------------------------------

Step 5: Checkout Code

CI server downloads the code from repository.

- name: Checkout Code
  uses: actions/checkout@v3

--------------------------------------------------

Step 6: Install Dependencies

Example for Node.js:

- name: Install Dependencies
  run: npm install

--------------------------------------------------

Step 7: Run Code Quality Checks

Example:

- name: Run Lint
  run: npm run lint

--------------------------------------------------

Step 8: Run Automated Tests

- name: Run Tests
  run: npm test

--------------------------------------------------

Step 9: Build Application

- name: Build Project
  run: npm run build

--------------------------------------------------

Step 10: Build Docker Image (Optional)

docker build -t myapp .

--------------------------------------------------

Step 11: Deploy Application

Deploy to staging or production server.

Example:

- name: Deploy
  run: ssh user@server "docker pull myapp"

--------------------------------------------------

Full GitHub Actions Example

name: Node CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: npm install

      - name: Run Tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build
