  • What is SonarQube and how is it used in CI/CD? 
          
SonarQube is a code quality and security analysis tool.

It automatically scans code to detect:

Bugs
Code smells
Security vulnerabilities
Duplicate code

SonarQube Metrics

1. Code Coverage
2. Code Complexity
3. Maintainability
4. Security Issues

--------------------------------------------------

Example CI Pipeline with SonarQube

Step 1: Install Sonar Scanner

npm install sonar-scanner

--------------------------------------------------

Step 2: Configure sonar-project.properties

sonar.projectKey=myproject
sonar.sources=src
sonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000
sonar.login=TOKEN

--------------------------------------------------

Step 3: Run Sonar Scan

sonar-scanner

--------------------------------------------------

Example GitHub Actions Integration

- name: SonarQube Scan
  run: sonar-scanner

--------------------------------------------------

Quality Gate

SonarQube blocks deployment if code quality fails.

Example Rules

Code coverage must be > 80%
No critical vulnerabilities
No duplicated code

--------------------------------------------------

Benefits

Improve code quality
Detect security issues
Maintain coding standards
Prevent technical debt
  • What is a Progressive Web Application (PWA)?

    A Progressive Web Application (PWA) is a web application that uses modern web technologies to provide an experience similar to a native mobile application. PWAs run in a browser but can be installed on a device, work offline, and send push notifications.

    Key Idea:

    • Works like a website
    • Feels like a mobile app
    • Fast, reliable, and installable
    Example:
Twitter Lite
Pinterest PWA
Starbucks PWA
  • What are the main features of Progressive Web Applications?
    • Responsive – Works on desktop, tablet, and mobile.
    • Offline Support – Uses Service Workers to work without internet.
    • Installable – Users can install the app on their device.
    • Fast Loading – Uses caching to load quickly.
    • Push Notifications – Can send notifications to users.
    • Secure – Must run over HTTPS.
  • What are the core components of PWA architecture?

    Progressive Web Applications mainly consist of three core components:

    1. Web App Manifest
    2. Service Worker
    3. HTTPS
    PWA Architecture

User
  |
Browser
  |
Service Worker
  |
Cache Storage
  |
Server (API / Backend)
  • What is a Service Worker in PWA?

    A Service Worker is a background JavaScript file that runs separately from the web page and enables features like offline support, caching, and push notifications.

    Main Responsibilities:

    • Cache assets
    • Enable offline functionality
    • Handle network requests
    • Enable push notifications
    Example: Register Service Worker

if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) {
  navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js')
    .then(() => console.log("Service Worker Registered"));
}
  • What is a Web App Manifest in PWA?

    The Web App Manifest is a JSON file that provides information about the application such as name, icons, theme color, and display mode. It allows the app to be installed on a device. 

    Example: manifest.json

{
  "name": "My PWA App",
  "short_name": "PWAApp",
  "start_url": "/index.html",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#ffffff",
  "theme_color": "#000000",
  "icons": [
    {
      "src": "icon.png",
      "sizes": "192x192",
      "type": "image/png"
    }
  ]
}
  • What are the advantages of Progressive Web Applications?
    • Works offline
    • Fast performance
    • No need to install from app store
    • Lower development cost
    • Cross-platform support
    • Push notification capability
  • What is the difference between PWA and Native Applications?
    Feature PWA Native App
    Installation Installed via browser Installed via app store
    Development HTML, CSS, JavaScript Java, Swift, Kotlin
    Offline Support Yes (Service Worker) Yes
    Updates Automatic Requires app store update
    Cost Lower Higher
  • When should we use Progressive Web Applications?

    PWA is useful in the following scenarios:

    • E-commerce websites
    • News websites
    • Social media platforms
    • Content platforms
    • Low network connectivity regions
    Real Companies Using PWA:

Twitter Lite
Pinterest
Starbucks
Uber

  • Event-Driven Architecture: Node.js vs Kafka (with examples and architecture diagram)
    Feature Node.js Event-Driven Architecture Apache Kafka Event Streaming
    Definition Node.js uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model where events trigger callbacks or listeners. Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used for building real-time data pipelines and event-driven systems.
    Scope Works inside a single Node.js application. Works across multiple distributed systems and microservices.
    Architecture Type In-process event system using EventEmitter. Distributed publish-subscribe messaging system.
    Data Persistence Events exist only in memory unless explicitly stored. Events are persisted in Kafka topics and stored on disk.
    Scalability Limited to the Node.js application instance. Highly scalable across clusters and partitions.
    Reliability No built-in fault tolerance. Provides replication, durability, and fault tolerance.
    Use Case Handling async operations like HTTP requests, file I/O, streams. Real-time analytics, event sourcing, microservice communication.
    Latency Very low latency within the same process. Low latency but involves network communication.
    Typical Use Backend server logic inside a Node application. Event backbone between services (microservices architecture).

    Node.js Event Driven Example

    
const EventEmitter = require('events');

const eventEmitter = new EventEmitter();

// Listener
eventEmitter.on('orderCreated', (order) => {
    console.log('Order received:', order);
});

// Emit Event
eventEmitter.emit('orderCreated', {
    id: 101,
    product: 'Laptop'
});

    Kafka Example with Node.js

    
const { Kafka } = require('kafkajs');

const kafka = new Kafka({
  clientId: 'order-service',
  brokers: ['localhost:9092']
});

const producer = kafka.producer();

async function sendMessage() {
  await producer.connect();

  await producer.send({
    topic: 'orders',
    messages: [
      { value: JSON.stringify({ id: 101, product: "Laptop" }) }
    ]
  });

  await producer.disconnect();
}

sendMessage();

    Architecture Example

    
Node.js Event Driven (Single App)

User Request
     │
     ▼
Node Server
     │
 EventEmitter
     │
     ▼
Event Listener


Kafka Event Streaming (Distributed)

Service A (Producer)
        │
        ▼
      Kafka
   (Topic / Partition)
        │
        ▼
Service B (Consumer)

Service C (Consumer)
    ✅ **Interview Summary** - **Node.js event-driven** → best for **internal async operations**. - **Kafka** → best for **distributed event streaming between microservices**. --- If you want, I can also give a **“System Design Interview Explanation: Node.js + Kafka Architecture (used in Netflix / Uber)”** which is often asked for **20–30 LPA backend roles**.
  • what is a callback function in Node.js and how does it work?
    Topic Explanation
    Definition A callback function is a function passed as an argument to another function and executed later.
    Purpose Callbacks allow asynchronous operations like file reading, API calls, or timers to run after a task completes.
    Common Usage Used in Node.js asynchronous programming such as events, timers, API responses, and file operations.
    Execution The parent function decides when the callback will run.
    Modern Alternatives Promises and async/await are modern replacements for callback-based code.
  • What is CORS and why is it needed?
    Topic Explanation
    Definition CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security feature that controls how web pages from one domain can request resources from another domain.
    Origin An origin consists of protocol + domain + port.
    Example Frontend: http://localhost:3000
    Backend: http://localhost:5000
    These are different origins → CORS required.
    Purpose Prevents malicious websites from accessing resources on another domain.
    Where enforced CORS is enforced by the browser, not by the server.
  • What are the SOLID principles in software development?
    Letter Principle Description
    S Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) A class or module should have only one reason to change.
    O Open/Closed Principle (OCP) Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.
    L Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) Child classes should be able to replace parent classes without breaking the program.
    I Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
    D Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.
  • Solid Principles in Software Development
    Principle Meaning Example
    S - Single Responsibility Principle A class or module should have only one responsibility. 
    
// Bad: Two responsibilities
class UserService {
  createUser(user) {}
  sendEmail(user) {}
}

// Good: Separate classes
class UserService {
  createUser(user) {}
}

class EmailService {
  sendEmail(user) {}
}
    O - Open Closed Principle Code should be open for extension but closed for modification. 
    
// Base class
class Payment {
  pay() {}
}

// Extended classes
class CreditCardPayment extends Payment {
  pay() {
    console.log("Credit Card Payment");
  }
}

class PaypalPayment extends Payment {
  pay() {
    console.log("Paypal Payment");
  }
}
    L - Liskov Substitution Principle Child classes should replace parent classes without breaking behavior. 
    
class Bird {
  move() {
    console.log("Bird moving");
  }
}

class Sparrow extends Bird {}

const bird = new Sparrow();
bird.move();
    I - Interface Segregation Principle Clients should not depend on methods they do not use. 
    
// Instead of one big interface

class Workable {
  work() {}
}

class Eatable {
  eat() {}
}

class Human extends Workable {
  work() {}
  eat() {}
}
    D - Dependency Inversion Principle High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. 
    
class Database {
  connect() {
    console.log("DB Connected");
  }
}

class UserService {
  constructor(database) {
    this.database = database;
  }

  getUsers() {
    this.database.connect();
  }
}

const db = new Database();
const userService = new UserService(db);
  • Solid Principles with Real Examples
    Principle Meaning Real Example
    S - Single Responsibility Principle Each class should have only one responsibility. 
    
// Handles payment only
class PaymentService {
  processPayment(amount) {
    console.log("Processing payment:", amount);
  }
}

// Handles email only
class EmailService {
  sendReceipt(email) {
    console.log("Receipt sent to:", email);
  }
}
    O - Open Closed Principle You should add new features without modifying existing code. 
    
class PaymentMethod {
  pay(amount) {}
}

class CreditCardPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  pay(amount) {
    console.log("Paid with Credit Card:", amount);
  }
}

class PaypalPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  pay(amount) {
    console.log("Paid with PayPal:", amount);
  }
}

// Add new payment method without changing old code
class UpiPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  pay(amount) {
    console.log("Paid using UPI:", amount);
  }
}
    L - Liskov Substitution Principle Child classes must behave like their parent class. 
    
function makePayment(paymentMethod) {
  paymentMethod.pay(500);
}

const payment = new CreditCardPayment();
makePayment(payment);
    Here any payment type works.
    I - Interface Segregation Principle Do not force classes to implement methods they don't need. 
    
// Separate interfaces

class Payment {
  pay() {}
}

class Refund {
  refund() {}
}

class OnlinePayment extends Payment {
  pay() {
    console.log("Online payment");
  }
}

class RefundService extends Refund {
  refund() {
    console.log("Refund processed");
  }
}
    D - Dependency Inversion Principle High level modules depend on abstraction. 
    
class PaymentProcessor {
  constructor(paymentMethod) {
    this.paymentMethod = paymentMethod;
  }

  process(amount) {
    this.paymentMethod.pay(amount);
  }
}

const payment = new PaypalPayment();
const processor = new PaymentProcessor(payment);

processor.process(1000);
  • what is an arrow function in JavaScript and how does it differ from a regular function?
    Topic Explanation
    Definition An Arrow Function is a shorter syntax for writing functions in JavaScript introduced in ES6. It uses the => syntax instead of the traditional function keyword.
    Main Benefit Provides cleaner and shorter code.
    this Behavior Arrow functions do not have their own this. They inherit this from the surrounding scope.
    Common Usage Used in callbacks, array functions, promises, and asynchronous code.
  • Java Spring Boot vs Python **
    Feature Java Spring Boot Python
    Language Type Statically typed programming language Dynamically typed programming language
    Framework Spring Boot is a powerful enterprise framework for building microservices and web applications Popular frameworks include Django, Flask, and FastAPI

    Learning Curve Steeper learning curve due to complex architecture and configuration Easier to learn because of simple syntax
    Use Cases Enterprise applications, banking systems, large-scale microservices AI/ML, data science, scripting, automation, APIs
    Microservices Support Excellent support with Spring Cloud ecosystem Supported using FastAPI, Flask, and Django
    Development Speed Moderate development speed Very fast development
    Memory Usage Higher memory usage due to JVM Lower memory usage but depends on workload
    Community & Ecosystem Very strong enterprise ecosystem Huge community especially in AI, ML, and automation
    Best For Enterprise backend systems and high-performance APIs Rapid development, data science, AI, automation
    Job Market High demand in enterprise companies and banking sectors High demand in AI, startups, automation, and data science
